Six cipher lines in the regent of Castile’s letter during the Comuneros revolt, printed in 1897 without them as not translatable. Brice Dudout rebuilt the Cardinal’s dotted trigraph code from his other letters, validated it on a fresh pair (0.882 of characters), and read the paragraph: 44 of 46 words. gig. leb. ded. mud. di. qb ga dh oto M & vuh. … que no solamente se mueuen contra [vuestra] magestad … Valladolid → Charles V · dotted trigraph code · 9 September 1520 · key from external plaintext Adrian of Utrecht to Charles V, 9 September 1520 Go to the full text ↓ Six cipher lines in the regent’s letter during the Comuneros revolt, which the editor of 1897 called untranslatable, deciphered with a key rebuilt from his other letters. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 3 November 2026 Method: key recovered based on plaintext from external sources · Extent: partial (87% of the cipher) Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) external text At a glance Key from external plaintext · partial (87% of the cipher) The letter Adrian of Utrecht, Cardinal of Tortosa and governor of Castile for Charles V (sixteen months later Pope Adrian VI), writing from Valladolid on 9 September 1520. He signs “Car.l dertusen”. Where Archivo General de Simancas, Patronato Real, PTR,LEG,2,1,19, f. 1r (PARES 12987122). Danvila printed the letter in Memorial histórico español XXXVI (1897) without the cipher paragraph: “no ha podido traducirse”. The cipher The Cardinal’s “dotted trigraph” code: consonant-vowel-consonant groups followed by a dot stand for words and syllables ( gig. que, leb. no, sa. de), with a homophonic alphabet of signs. It differs from the code of the joint letter of December 1521 , which has its own page. How it was deciphered Key K7 was rebuilt from cipher and plain pairs of the Cardinal’s other letters of 1520–21. One measurement on a fresh pair named before download (PTR,LEG,2,1,99, 5 December 1521) gave 0.882 of characters against at best 0.176 for 200 shuffled keys, and 0.770 of words. What it says The Junta of the Comunidades means to gather all the alcabalas and all the towns and places that had recently been the Crown’s, from the grandees, and it moves not only against Charles but against the great lords. Still open The first cipher word (six signs) and the group fud. are unresolved. The images were not seen here. Credit Brice Dudout rebuilt the key, re-read doubtful signs blind, ran the validation and read the paragraph, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents.

In August and September 1520 the Junta of the Comunidades, meeting at Ávila, seized Tordesillas (29 August) and Queen Joanna. Adrian, at Valladolid, tried in vain to draw it to the town; the mission of the commander Hinestrosa is told in plain text in the letter. Before the cipher paragraph comes the plain sentence “el fin que sobresto tienen sabrá V. Al. por la cifra que va dentro desta”, so an enclosed cipher sheet existed. Its contemporary decipherment survives separately (PTR,LEG,2,1,107) and is not the text of this paragraph. Almost all the Cardinal’s cipher letters of 1520–21 are printed deciphered by Danvila from the contemporary transcriptions. Still without plain text: this paragraph and a struck-out cipher paragraph of 21 October 1520.

K7 was built from the pairs PTR,LEG,2,1,23 and 32 (Bergenroth, Calendar of State Papers, Spain , Supplement, 1868), 2,1,30, 61 and 88 (Danvila), and 2,1,68, 70, 71, 73 and 85 (contemporary transcriptions 2,1,69, 72 and 83). A code group is kept only when attested twice. Sign shapes were re-read blind on three plates, which split confused homophones. Earlier keys failed the criterion fixed in advance: K3 (0.851 of characters but 0.541 of words on 2,1,68), K4 (0.783) and K6 (0.813); their pairs then went into training. Only K7 was frozen before its test pair was named.

The paragraph, with probable words in braces and restored words in brackets: “… esto, dará … a estos [tales], que no {solamente} se mueven {contra} [vuestra] majestad, {mas} aun contra todos los grandes, de los cuales {entienden} {primeramente} [juntar] todas las {alcabalas}, y {después} todas las [villas] {y} lugares que de {poco} {tiempo} en {fueron} de la {corona} real.” Abolishing or reducing the alcabalas and returning to the Crown the towns alienated to lords were among the Comuneros’ demands. Of 46 cipher words, 28 are certain, 12 probable, 4 restored and 2 unresolved: 44 of 46, or 95.7%, so the 95% bar is met narrowly. The translation justifies every probable, restored or unresolved word. The full Spanish text and an English translation are under Full texts.

The first cipher word (six signs, one uninventoried shape) and the group fud. are unresolved. Signs still outside the key: the first signs of [tales] and [juntar], the second sign of [villas], and three more. Twelve probable words rest on one sign or group attested once. The transcription was made by AI and the sign shapes re-read by the contributor from plates; no person checked them against the images here.

Adrian of Utrecht to Charles V, Valladolid, 9 September 1520 (AGS PTR,LEG,2,1,19), cipher paragraph read in part On 9 September 1520 Adrian of Utrecht – Cardinal of Tortosa, regent of Castile for Charles V, and sixteen months later Pope Adrian VI – wrote from Valladolid while the Junta of the Comunidades was settling at Ávila. In the middle of the letter are six lines in cipher. Danvila, who printed the letter in 1897, noted only: “Sigue un párrafo cifrado que no ha podido traducirse”. The cipher is the Cardinal’s dotted code; we rebuilt it from his other letters of 1520–1521 whose plain text is known, validated it on a letter held out, and applied it to this paragraph. It tells what the Junta meant to do to the grandees: take from them the alcabalas and the towns that had belonged to the Crown. Builds coherent sentences, but under the read bar of 95% of words read as sense (87% here); the holes are marked in the reading. An intercepted code letter from the French ambassador at The Hague to the ambassador at Vienna, filed with ten letters to Rouillé and Bernis but written in another code. The key rebuilt for those letters gives nonsense on it, no decipherment was imaged with it, and no key record was found: 761 groups, none deciphered. 1013 · 161 · 966 · 240 · 413 · 158 · 161 · 877 · 569 · 648 · 123 · 736 not deciphered 761 groups · 357 distinct · values to 1198 The Hague → Vienna · numerical code (not d’Affry’s 1757 code) · August 1757 The comte d’Affry to the Marquis de Stainville, August 1757 to Étienne François de Choiseul (Marquis de Stainville) An intercepted letter from the French ambassador at The Hague to his colleague at Vienna, filed with ten letters to Paris but written in another code, for which no key or decipherment has been found. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 27 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained · On the map At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letter Louis-Auguste d’Affry, French ambassador at The Hague, to Étienne François de Stainville (later Duc de Choiseul), ambassador at Vienna, August 1757 (4 August on the copy, 7 August on DECODE). Three pages of figures, an intercept copy made for the stadholder’s cabinet. Where Koninklijk Huisarchief, The Hague, Prins Willem V inv. 192; DECODE R1071, listed there as not decrypted. The cipher A numerical code: 761 groups, 357 different, numbered up to 1198. It is not the code of d’Affry’s letters to Paris. How it was tried The key rebuilt for the letters to Paris was applied and gave nonsense; the images hold no decipherment; no other key of d’Affry or Stainville was found on DECODE. Why it resists No key, no decipherment and no crib. Lyonet’s decipherments, which may include this letter, are in the Nationaal Archief and not digitised. This letter was filed with d’Affry’s letters to the foreign secretaries Rouillé and Bernis, which share one code whose key was rebuilt from the Dutch codebreaker Lyonet’s decipherments. It is in a different cipher; those letters have their own page: the comte d’Affry’s intercepted letters, 1757–58 .

D’Affry’s despatches went by the Dutch post, and the stadholder’s cabinet had them opened, copied and passed to Pierre Lyonet, the Republic’s cipher secretary. Inv. 192 of the Prins Willem V archive holds the copies of nineteen of them, catalogued on DECODE as R1052–R1076 and R2067. All but this one are to Rouillé and then Bernis at Versailles, January 1757 to January 1758. This one is to Stainville at Vienna, written days after the French victory at Hastenbeck (26 July), when France and Austria were fighting Prussia and Hanover together. The copy carries the number 485 and the date 4 August; DECODE gives 7 August. The three pages are photographed sideways and hold only figures, separated by dots. The groups used here are DECODE’s transcription, not re-read from the images. Comparing the first page with it for the figure above showed two differences: the image has 240 where DECODE has 24 in the first line, and 1116 and 1158 at the end of the seventh line are run together in the transcription.

A comparison of group frequencies across all the inv. 192 letters set this one apart. The letters to Paris, first split into two codes the same way, turned out to share their common values: one code. The key of that code, 651 groups recovered by aligning Lyonet’s decipherments with their cipher, gives nonsense on R1071. On 27 October 2026 every machine-readable key of the period in this project was applied to R1071 and scored against shuffled copies of itself: d’Affry’s code, the Van Swieten–Cobenzl table, the Hanoverian army code of 1743, the Prussian code of the Michell letters (1751) and Croiset’s Dutch codebook of 1765. The same test picks out d’Affry’s key on one of his own letters at once; on R1071 none fits ( keytest_R1071.py ). Eight of the sibling records carry Lyonet’s clear copy among their images. R1071 does not. The DECODE catalogue was searched for other records of d’Affry, Stainville or Choiseul: only the inv. 192 letters and a Choiseul record of 1763–64 in the British Library, and no key. Karl de Leeuw’s history of the Dutch black chamber (2000) says Lyonet broke d’Affry’s first code by June 1756 and “two more French ones”, and d’Affry’s code to Choiseul from December 1758 later. Bussemaker’s 1906 extracts of Lyonet’s decipherments do not give this letter’s text.

Lyonet’s decipherments of d’Affry’s letters for July 1757 to December 1758 are in the Nationaal Archief, Stadhouderlijke Secretarie 1.01.50 inv. 223, “grouped by the cipher used”, and not digitised. They, or the French embassy code for Vienna in 1757, would give the key. Without them, 761 groups of a large code with no crib are too few for a reconstruction from the ciphertext alone. With either, the letter should first be transcribed again from the images.

A news-letter from League Paris (BnF fr. 3623 no. 23), copied in clear except for nine persons and provinces coded by small numbers, with the name key bound after it on f. 36r. Both pages transcribed and deciphered in full (99.6% of words read): Madame de Nemours and her son, the Pope, Spain and Mayenne, and Bienvenut shut out by Mendoza. The writer is probably Bienvenu, the Duke of Savoy’s secretary, and the recipient Charles-Emmanuel I. 36 · 53 · 10 · 1 · 35 Madame de Nemours · M. de Saint-Sorlin · le Pape · le Roy d’Espagne · Mayenne the key slip, f. 36r Paris → “Vostre Altesse” (probably the Duke of Savoy) · name code with its key · 28 February 1590 · known key applied Bienvenut to “Vostre Altesse”, Paris, February 1590 to Duke of Nevers Go to the full text ↓ A news-letter from League Paris, copied in clear except for nine names and provinces coded by small numbers; both pages are now transcribed and deciphered with the key slip bound after it. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 27 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete Credits · Alain Dufour (identification) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) At a glance Known key applied · complete The letter Bienvenut to “Vostre Altesse”, Paris, the last day of February 1590: a copy of two pages, in clear except for 26 code numbers for persons and provinces. The writer is probably Bienvenu, secretary of Charles-Emmanuel I of Savoy. Where BnF français 3623 no. 23, ff. 35–36 (DECODE R9453, catalogued there as a key record); catalogue item 30, with the Champagne news-letters. The cipher A name code of nine numbers between 1 and 53: the King of Spain, the Pope, the King, Mayenne, Madame and M. de Nemours, Saint-Sorlin, the towns of the Union or Provence and Dauphiné, the Duke of Parma or Picardy. How it was deciphered The key is bound with the copy on f. 36r and every number in the letter is on it. Both pages were transcribed line by line from the Gallica images on 26 October 2026, the doubtful words re-read at full resolution on 27 October, and the key applied to the whole text. What it says Madame de Nemours wants her son in Spanish service or back in his government; the Pope, Spain and Mayenne have agreed that Spanish aid will pass through the Pope; Mendoza and Moreo keep Bienvenut out of the council, and he means to leave Paris in March. Still open Four doubtful words and a doubtful heading; which value of the two dual entries (15, 17) applies in two places; the places Roccas and Vier; and the recipient, probable but not proven. This letter was filed with three news-letters of June 1590 that use a two-digit alphabet, a different cipher with its own page ( Champagne news letters, June 1590 ); their numbers conflict with this key (there 35 is a , here Mayenne).

Fr. 3623 f. 36r, the key bound after the letter: 1 Le Roy d’Espaigne, 10 Le Pape, 15 Les villes de l’Union ou Provence & Dauphiné, 17 Le Duc de Parme ou Picardie, 36 Madame de Nemours, 35 Monsieur du Maine, 37 Monsieur de Nemours, 26 Le Roy, 53 Monsieur de St Sorlin. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3623 f. 36r, via Gallica (btv1b525245007). Every number in the letter is on the slip, so every code decodes (grade H). The copy marks twice where its original was in cipher (“Ce qui suyt mys en chiffre”, “Et apres en chiffre”, f. 35v): the copyist wrote those passages out in clear and left only the names in numbers. F. 35v, lines 6–9: “d’accabler 26 . Si nous voyons que 10 se resolue a cela … entre 1 . 10 . & 35 . sans que v[ost]re Alt[esse] y aye participation, sinon qu’elle y remedie en 15 ”: the King, the Pope, the King of Spain, the Pope, Mayenne, Provence and Dauphiné. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3623 f. 35v, via Gallica (btv1b525245007).

Both pages were transcribed line by line from the full-resolution Gallica images (canvases 79–80) on 26 October 2026: 33 lines on the recto, 35 on the verso, 1,259 words, abbreviations expanded and struck words kept ( texts/n23_transcription.md ). The 26 code numbers stand where the earlier list of 14 October put them. With the codes resolved, 99.6% of the words read as sense (963 words, none unread, four doubtful, after a second pass at full resolution on 27 October that settled eight doubtful words and corrected two); the full French and an English translation are under Full texts below. Four passages: [Madame de Nemours] me pourmena hyer par la gallerie du logis de la Reyne plus d’une heure … elle me monstra plusieurs avis qu’elle avoit eu de [St Sorlin], qui contenoient principallement que pour les émotions et pratiques qui se commencent a faire en celle province l’on appelle [Monsieur de Nemours] en son gouvernement avec toute l’instance qu’on se peult. Madame de Nemours had asked Juan Moreo to have Philip II take her son into his service; Moreo did not answer a word, and she said in anger that Nemours might do best to withdraw into his government, where he could make himself sought after by whichever party survived. She also showed Bienvenut news of the siege of Grenoble, the demolition of the castle of Gex and the siege of Bonne, “qui nous travaille grandement”. J’ay advis … qu’il y a une tres estroicte intelligence entre [le Pape] et [le Roy d’Espaigne], et que despuys l’arrivée du Legat il a esté avisé entre luy, [Monsieur du Maine] et les Ambassadeurs de [15] que … la pluspart du secours que [le Roy d’Espaigne] fera a ceste cause se donnera par voye du [Pape], tant d’hommes que d’argent, et que soubz main [le Roy d’Espaigne] l’en remboursera avec les interestz a taux de banque, et par ce moyen la guerre se fera au nom du [Pape]. If the Pope sends forces from Italy, “the game will be played out entirely between [the King of Spain], [the Pope] and [Mayenne]” without the Altesse, unless the Altesse acts in Provence and Dauphiné. Panigarola explained to Bienvenut why Moreo and Don Bernardino de Mendoza had shut him out: they feared he wanted to “mettre le nez dans le conseil”. [Ce qui suyt (?) mys en chiffre:] Qui me faict resouldre, voyant que je suys icy inutille a son service … de me mettre en chemin a la premiere commodité que je pourray avoir de passer et m’en retourner, qui pourra estre a mon avis dans tout le moys de mars prochain, que j’entens que Monsieur de Nemours s’en ira avec quelques trouppes en son gouvernement. [Et apres en chiffre:] Si pour la guerre que vostre altesse a presentement sur les bras elle avoit besoin de 1000 ou 1200 harquebuziers, m’en donnant avis, je luy en ferois recouvrer des meilleurs de [17].

The letter is in the Nevers papers and was first taken as written to him. The full text points to Charles-Emmanuel I, Duke of Savoy. Bienvenut signs as the Altesse’s “subject”; Gex and Bonne, Savoyard places attacked by Geneva and Bern in 1589–90, are a siege “qui nous travaille”; the remedy he proposes lies in Provence and Dauphiné, where Savoy intervened in 1590; and the Altesse has “ministres” in League Paris whom Spain keeps out. Nevers was with Henri IV in 1590. The writer has a name in the Savoyard record. The letters of René de Lucinge, the Duke of Savoy’s ambassador in France, mention “le sieur de Bienvenu, qui est icy” in 1585, sent on League business, and their editor Alain Dufour calls “le secrétaire Bienvenu” the side of the Duke’s policy committed to the League. A Savoyard secretary already working with the League in 1585 is the natural author of this report from League Paris in 1590. The recipient is therefore probably Charles-Emmanuel I, and the copy in fr. 3623 an intercept or a copy that reached Nevers. It is not proven until the hand or a copy in Turin is matched.

Doubtful words (grade C), with folio and line: fer[r]oit (35r.11, ending written over), empieter (35r.29, the letter after p looks like r), baste l’ame (35v.5), me (35v.12), and the heading “Ce qui suyt mys en chiffre” (35v.20). The second pass corrected two first readings: “parmy les aff[air]es de ce Royaume” (35r.24) and “de bon lieu” (35r.26, where only “ne part” is struck). Roccas and Vier (35r.22): the letters are certain, the place and its captor are not identified. Cramer and Dufour’s history of the Geneva–Savoy war of 1589–93 is the book to check; M. de Riddes (35v.22) is also unidentified. The dual entries: 15 reads as Provence and Dauphiné at 35v.9 (a place where the Altesse can act) and 17 as Picardy at 35r.30 and 35v.19; at 35r.28 (“les Ambassadeurs de 15”) and 35v.33 (“des meilleurs de 17”) the context does not choose, and both values are kept. The recipient: probable, not proven (section 03).

Paris, 28 Feb 1590, BnF fr. 3623 no. 23, ff. 35r-v (key f. 36r) Bienvenut reports from Paris to 'Vostre Altesse' (probably Charles-Emmanuel I of Savoy, whose secretary Bienvenu was) that Madame de Nemours wants her son Nemours in Spanish service or back in his government; that news has come of Grenoble, Gex and the siege of Bonne; that the Pope, Spain and Mayenne have agreed Spain's aid will pass through the Pope, who is to send 8 or 10,000 men; that Mendoza and Moreo keep the Altesse's ministers out of affairs; and, in cipher, that he means to leave Paris in March with Nemours's troops, and can raise 1,000-1,200 arquebusiers. (?) = doubtful in the French; [?] = not read. --> # Bienvenut to "Your Highness", Paris, 28 February 1590 (BnF fr. 3623 no. 23, ff. 35r-v): English translation [f. 35r] Yesterday [Madame de Nemours] walked me through the gallery of the Queen's lodging for more than an hour, where she talked to me of many things. Among others she showed me several reports she had had from [Saint-Sorlin], which said chiefly that because of the risings and intrigues beginning in that province, [Monsieur de Nemours] is being called to his government as urgently as can be. Not for anything in the world will she let his departure be delayed any longer, for she wants him from now on to set the whole foundation of his fortune on his government. She complained to me that, speaking to Señor Moreo, she had let him understand that since [Monsieur de Nemours] now found himself without a master she would wish it to please [the King of Spain] to make use of him; that if it pleased him to take him into his service, and him [Moreo] to arrange it, she would see to it (?) that he would serve with such fidelity that His Majesty would be entirely satisfied. And on this she said that Moreo had not answered her a single word, at which she was very indignant, and she told me, almost in anger, that it might well be [Monsieur de Nemours]'s good fortune to withdraw into his government and there do as he could, since means were failing him on every side. I have considered this, and I judge she may mean that through his government he will always have the means to make himself sought after and respected by one party or the other, should either of them go under. She also showed me a report covering the siege of Grenoble, the taking of Roccas by Vier (neither identified), the ruin and demolition of the castle of Gex, and the siege of Bonne, which troubles us greatly. The Legate finds himself very much hampered amid the affairs of this kingdom, seeing the mortal hatred the French have for the Spanish name. I have word from a good source, and from a person in a position to know, that there is a very close understanding between [the Pope] and [the King of Spain], and that since the Legate's arrival it has been agreed between him, [Mayenne] and the ambassadors of [Provence and Dauphiné, or the towns of the Union] that, to satisfy France and remove the belief that [the King of Spain] wants to encroach (?) on [Picardy] under pretext either of protection or of religion, it will be better from now on that most of the help [the King of Spain] gives to this cause be given through [the Pope], in men as well as money, and that [the King of Spain] will secretly repay him with interest at the bankers' rate; and in this way the war will be waged in the name [f. 35v] of [the Pope]. And that this is true I have learned for certain, through the man of whom I wrote to Your Highness in an earlier letter, that the courier the Legate sent to Rome carried orders to have ready money sent promptly to keep the war going until [the Pope] can send 8 or 10,000 men of war, with whom he may put heart (?) into [Mayenne] and carry them on, without his having to crush [the King]. If we see [the Pope] resolve on this and send forces from Italy, there is no more doubt that the game will be played out entirely between [the King of Spain], [the Pope] and [Mayenne] without Your Highness having any part in it, unless you take your remedy in [Provence and Dauphiné], or else choose to come to terms with the other party, which in my opinion would be the worst counsel. I do not know what to make of what Monsieur Panigarola told me of the reasons Moreo gave him for the affront (?) that Don Bernardino and he dealt me: he says it was because he foresaw that I wanted to put my nose into the council and learn its business, and that it was not good for so many people to know what is being negotiated. I judge that they want only to keep me and all Your Highness's other ministers as far back and as far from affairs as they can, for fear that you (whose great heart they hold suspect) should get wind of the enterprises and plots they are running in [Picardy]. [What follows (?) put in cipher:] This makes me resolve, since I see I am useless to your service here, inasmuch as the diligence and fidelity of Monsieur de Riddes, who is very practised and very well known here, is quite enough to keep you informed of what happens, and since I also see that the means Your Highness gave me are already beginning to run short, to set out at the first opportunity I can have to cross and return, which in my opinion may be at any time in the coming month of March, when I hear that Monsieur de Nemours will go with some troops to his government. Otherwise I shall find myself so committed and cornered that I shall be here until next winter, for want of being able to cross in safety. [And afterwards in cipher:] If for the war Your Highness now has on your hands you needed 1,000 or 1,200 arquebusiers, on your sending me word I would get you some of the best of [Picardy, or the Duke of Parma]. Paris, the last day of February 1590. Your Highness's most humble and most devoted subject and servant, Bienvenut.

The four DECODE images are out of archive order. P4 is f. 110r (scan 0408) and opens “Sacra Cat. ca & Ces. a M. ta ”. It is in clear, on the Dauphin and the Grand Master crossing with munitions, the King at Briançon, and “Mons. or di Marnol” with the Colonel of the Isola working to recall the Swiss in French service. P1 is f. 110v (scan 0409), with clear text on the Grisons and then the eleven cipher lines. P3 is f. 111r (scan 0410). It has one cipher line struck through, then the clear close, dated “In M. lo ali xiiij de Nov. e M. D. xxxvij” and signed “il Car. l Caracciolo”. P2 is the address leaf, with the docket “del Cardenal Caracciolo xiiij de Nov. e 1537”. Cifrario 38 (Luo 2021, p. 657, from AGS Estado leg. 38 doc. 190) has three parts. An alphabet of invented signs with homophones. a has six signs, and e , i , l , n , o , p and u have two to four each. A syllabary. A consonant’s base sign takes a superscript digit for the vowel: 5 = a, 6 = e, 7 = i, 8 = o, 9 = u. For example, 2 is the base for s , so 2⁷ = si . Nulls, marked by the superscripts 2, 3 and 4, and a few code words. The first cipher line shows the system at work: 2⁷ a̱o⁸ 3⁶ + 9 ṉo⁵ θ 4⁷ a+⁵ ṉo⁶ = si do ve a p ra c ti ca re . F. 110v (scan 0409). The clear text ends at the struck words and the cipher begins. Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1184 f. 110v (scan 0409), via DECODE R9966.

Epso Marno a 9 se accorge hora de la malignita et perfidia de 10 Suizari et [..] et soi ministri. Se deve ne recor- 11 dare, e quante volte io ha dicto che epsi Suizari far- (f. 111r, cancelled) riano quello hora fan po[..] In substance, Caracciolo reports on Marnol’s work with the Grisons. Marnol was to find out whether they would come to terms as the Swiss had. Caracciolo had written to him several times to send Panizone in Caracciolo’s name and to pay him. The Grisons were to be given, as the Swiss had been, the tratta of grain free of duty, on suitable articles. So far it had not seemed good to them, and they would have done as the Swiss did. Marnol now saw the malice and bad faith of the Swiss and their ministers. Caracciolo reminds the Emperor how often he had said what the Swiss would do “hora”. The last words are in the line the writer cancelled.

Tomokiyo’s page on the Spanish ciphers of Charles V, in its section on Luo’s thesis, names the key and gives a rough decipherment of lines 1–4 (“… pagabo quale e a e f ressolvi perche io se r ri a conbento”). That note was found before the work and led to the key. Here the letter was deciphered line by line from the DECODE images, and the key needed no change. Line 3 gives pagato and line 4 contento , where Tomokiyo had pagabo and conbento . Luo’s thesis does not edit this letter.

The first pass left about fifteen percent open. A second pass at 4× with contrast on every line settled most of it with four rules: A superscript belongs to the sign before it. In line 5, 3⁶ 4⁷ et decrypts as ve ti i , so the word is “Elvetii”. A bare ♀ is the letter r, and ♀ with a superscript is the p-syllable. This gives “harriano” in line 8 and “parso” in line 7. The g-shaped sign with a bar is an f homophone, which gives “frumento” in line 6. Dotted signs are nulls. About ten of roughly 330 signs (an estimate, not a sign-by-sign count) stay doubtful: Line 4: “a fe”, decrypted letter by letter, and “serria”, where the sign taken as n stands where an a is expected. Line 5: two a-homophones after “como a”. Lines 7 and 8: one sign each. Line 10: “2 a” after “et”. The cancelled line: one syllable after “po”.

Clairambault 1225 3 avril 1714 f53r Monseigneur, J’ay receu la lettre qu’il a plu à Votre Excellence me faire l’honneur de m’écrire le 19 du mois dernier ; je luy en rend très humbles graces. M. l’abbé Lomelini m’écrit encore de Venise qu’il y sera jusqu’à la fin du mois prochain, et qu’il me prie de luy marquer si j’ay receu quelque avis touchant l’isle de Tabarque , et comme je luy avois déjà fait f53v connoître que tant qu’il ne donnera pas les éclaircissemens necessaires il ne sera pas possible d’en venir au fait, il m’ajoute par sa lettre du 24 mars dernier qu’on les donnera aussitôt que on verra quelque personne [à] Genes pour veue d’une procuration pour trait[te]r avec eu[x] . Les autres par ticipes de l’isle , qui ont sceu les conférences que j’avois eues avec l’abbé sur cette affaire et qui ont cru que je ne traittois que pour une portion , m’ont envoyé demander une entrevue dans laquelle ils m’ont fait connoître qu’ils estoient informés de ma negociation avec l’abbé et qu’ils me prioient de faire en sorte que le traitté se fit pour toute l’isle . Je leur ay répondu qu’il ne tenoit qu’à eux de me faire leur proposition en me remettant les éclaircissemens en question ; ils m’ont répondu à peu près comme l’ abbé qu’ils donneront tous ces f54r éclaircissemens lors qu’ils verront &c. J’ay remarqué qu’ils concourent tous avec empressement à la vente? de cette isle . Votre Excellence aura la bonté de me marquer ce qu’Elle souhaitte que je leur réponde à cet égard. Chacun parle en ce pays-cy fort diversement de la paix qui vient de se conclure entre la France et l’Empire ; les uns veulent que le Roy de Sicile n’y soit pas compris et que l’Empereur se soit mesme reservé dans le traitté de pouvoir luy faire la guerre pour luy reprendre les places qui luy ont esté cedées du Milanois, s’il ne se met en devoir de les rendre à l’amiable, sans que la France puisse le secourir directement ni indirectement. D’autres au contraire disent que le Roy de Sicile ne sera point troublé par l’Empereur dans les Etats qu’il possede presentement, et que s’il doit restituer ce qu’il f54v tient de la part de l’Empire il le fera à l’amiable ; il y a toute aparence que les choses se passeront ainsi, ne paroissant pas qu’on se dispose en Lombardie ni en Piemont pour commencer une nouvelle guerre, quoy qu’on assure que l’Empereur fait filer actuellement quelques troupes dans le Milanois. Au surplus on est fort impatient en ce pays-cy de voir ce que porteront les articles de cette derniere paix, qui a esté traittée si secretement par les deux generaux, dont on ne sçait rien jusqu’à cette heure, et ce que l’on en dit n’est que par conjecture. Il est mort à Rome un fameux banquier appellé le marquis Pallavicin, genois, agé d’environ 55 ans, qui s’y estoit estably depuis long temps. Il a laissé plus de six cents mille écus romains, dont la maison Rospillosi de Rome auroit herité, à ce qu’on dit, si le deffunt avoit fait son testament f55r mais une mort subite l’a surpris et n’a pu donner ordre à sa succession, de maniere que ses plus proches parents pretendent par raison de nature heriter des biens qu’il a laissez. Il estoit fils naturel de M. Carlo Pallavicino, qui estoit noble genois extremement riche, lequel se servoit de ce fils dans son comptoir comme d’un homme ordinaire à gages. Un jour qu’il l’envoya à la loge pour parler à un courtier pour quelque negociation, ce dernier surpris d’un acte d’impatience maltraitta l’autre en parolles et luy dit entre autres, oste toy de devant moy fichu bastard, ce jeune en s’en retourna fort mortifié, et le pere s’en estant aperçu en voulut sçavoir le sujet ; le garçon luy compta la scene qui venoit de se passer, et lors qu’il fut à l’endroit qu’on l’avoit appellé fichu bastard il se mit à pleurer à chaudes larmes ; le pere attendri voulant le consoler le mena sur le champ à la f55v banque de St George et luy fit une cession de cent mille croizats en luy disant, tiens voilà de quoy te consoler, et lors qu’on t’appellera bastard, dis que tu l’es, mais avec cent mille croizats. Le pere long temps apres estant devenu fol et mort dans cet état laissa des biens immenses à un seul fils legitime qu’il avoit, lequel se voyant tant de bien crut que Genes estoit trop petit pour luy et fut s’établir à Rome, où il épousa une fille de la maison Rospillosi, mais il mourut un an apres sans enfans. Le bastard qui s’estoit allé établir en mesme temps à Rome avoit pris une si forte inclination pour la maison Rospillosi qu’il l’a toujours conservée mesme apres la mort de son frere, de maniere que ses plus proches parents n’esper[o]ient rien de sa succession ; mais estant mort sans faire testament ils sont en pretention. M. le marquis Estienne Pallavicin qui a esté f56r souventes fois à Paris pour son plaisir est un des pretendants. Un autre gentilhomme appellé Carlo Lomelino l’est aussi par la mesme raison, estant fils de deux sœurs qui se trouvent les plus proches parentes des deffunts. M. Alexandrin Grimaldy qui est actuellement envoyé de la Republique à Rome, ayant apris la mort subite de ce banquier, se transporta sur le champ chez luy et fit mettre le sceau à la maison et donna en mesme temps part de cette mort à M. le marquis Estienne Pallavicin par un courrier qu’il luy expedia à cet effet, en luy marquant que sa presence seroit necessaire à Rome ; on dit qu’il doit partir incessamment pour s’y rendre. Cependant la chambre apostolique pretend cette succession attendu que le deffunt estoit bastard, ainsi il y aura indubitablement des procès. Un avocat de mes amis a esté déjà consulté là-dessus et son opinion est que les parents l’emporteront f56v sur la chambre apostolique. Lors qu’on s’attendoit icy à reformer bient[o]st entierement la quarantaine qu’on fait observer à tout ce qui vient du costé d’Allemag[ne], et qu’on l’avoit mesme déjà reduite à la moitié, on vient d’aprendre par des voyes indirectes que la peste a recommencé à se faire sentir en Allemagne dans quelques villes où elle n’avoit pas encore esté ; ils attendent pourtant d’en sçavoir la verité avant de prendre les precautions convenables à cet égard. Quoy que nous eussions déjà apris de divers endroits la signature de la paix entre la France et l’Empire, ce que Votre Excellence a bien voulu m’en marquer me donne une parfaitte consolation, esperant que c’est le temps que par vos bontés, Monseigneur, je sortiray enfin du triste état dans lequel je me trouve f57r depuis long temps. Je supplie très humblement Votre Excellence de vouloir bien m’envoyer mes expeditions pour aller remplir le consulat de la nation en Sardaigne qu’Elle a bien voulu me destiner ; trop heureux si je trouve en ce pays-là des occasions à pouvoir donner des marques de mon zele et de mon aplication pour le service du Roy. Si Votre Excellence veut bien se souvenir du petit memoire que je pris la liberté de luy envoyer en avril 1712 touchant les devoirs d’un consul, Elle ne doutera pas que je ne le sçache executer ; mais quel meilleur memoire peut-on avoir que les instructions et les ordres de Votre Excellence ? Elle les sçait distribuer avec tant de bonté qu’ils donnent une entiere émulation à ceux qui les reçoivent, f57v j’en suis tout remply, et l’excès de mon zele m’a porté à communiquer au nouveau vice consul, que le Sr Aubert a fait venir depuis cinq mois, les demarches qu’il est necessaire d’observer en ce pays-cy pour penetrer ce qui? s’y passe en secret . Ce vice consul est un nommé Laugier de Toulon que j’ay remarqué estre fort entendu dans les affaires et dans tout ce qui regarde la marine, duquel ce consul peut retirer un grand secours pour se fai[re] honneur auprès de Votre Excellence, à moins que les avantages qu’il luy fait ne soient pas suffisants pour le retenir auprès de luy. Je suis avec un très profond respect, Monseigneur, de Votre Excellence, Le très humble et très obeissant serviteur, Paget? À Genes le 3e Avril 1714. 28 août 1714 f58r Monseigneur, J’ay receu les trois lettres qu’il a plu à Votre Excellence me faire l’honneur de m’écrire le 13 de ce mois, à deux desquelles M. Aubert s’est chargé de répondre, et je me suis reservé de luy marquer ce qu’Elle souhaitte sçavoir concernant la princesse de Parme et ses 2 oncles. Cette princesse qu’ on reconnoit déjà pour reyne d’Espagne a toutes les belles f58v qualitez qu’on peut desirer. Elle achevera sa 22e année le 25 Octobre prochain , estant née le mesme mois en mil 692. Elle est bien faite, blonde, le visage rond, les traits fins et assez reguliers, et la taille belle , quoy que moyenne, beaucoup d’esprit et un air fort modeste . On ne luy a pas reconnu des inclinations particulieres, mais une entiere soumission et une complaisance aveugle pour ? Mada[me] la duchesse sa mere qui l’a toujours tenue sous ses yeu[x] , et s’en faitte une attache particuliere à luy donner une belle education , à quoy Elle a parfaittement bien reussy, à ce qu’on dit. Votre Excellence n’ignore pas que cette mere , apres la mort de M. le duc de Parme son mari, espousa en 2es noces le prince François Farnese , qui est le duc de Parrme re[g]nant, frere du deffunt , duquel elle n’a pas eu d’enfans et a perdu l’esperance d’ en avoir, se trouvant agée de 44 ans , quoy que f59r ce dernier duc n’en ait que 36. Il y a encore le prince Antoine de Parme, frere du duc, qui n’a que 35 ans. Mais il n’est pas marié et n’a nulle inclination pour le mariage . Ainsi la jeune princesse semble devoir attendre tous les biens de sa maison , se trouvant unique et de premier lict , et adorée de ses 2 oncles qui sont charmés de la voir espouser le Roy d’Espagne , d’autant plus qu’il est issu de France , pour laquelle ils ont toujours montré une grande partialité . Au contraire Mada[me] la duchesse qui est de la maison de Neubourg a toujours esté de genie alleman[d] , et on pretend que la jeune princesse est plustost du party de ses oncles sur cela que de celuy de Mada[me] sa mere . Je suis avec un très profond respect, Monseigneur, de Votre Excellence, Le très humble et très obeissant serviteur, Paget? À Genes le 28 Aoust 1714. The right key sits in Cobham’s own earlier letters in the same volume, where the cipher was deciphered between the lines at the time. Most of the alphabet was recovered from those glosses. They are clear English with passages in Greek-like signs. Where British Library, Harley MS 287 ff. 80–81, 88, 92–93 and 96–97 (DECODE R8490, R8492, R8495, R8496), catalogued with no decipherment. The key record the catalogue suggested (Bodley’s 1590 cipher) does not fit. The cipher A polyphonic sign cipher: one sign stands for s, t and a, another for r and y. Code numbers include 7 the Queen, 10 the Lord Admiral, 15 Parma and 16 the King of Spain. How it was read The key comes from Cobham’s own April letters in the same volume, deciphered between the lines at the time. About sixty glossed words aligned at full scan resolution give a sign inventory ( signs.tsv ). A solver ( solve.py ) matched cipher words against a word list from the Calendar of State Papers Foreign for 1588. What it says Cobham reports on the talks, a captain gone into Scotland, Italians arriving and the haven of Rain, in fragments such as “within France”. The graded decipherment is in targets/cobham1588/READING.md . Still open About a third of the cipher words are deciphered. The rest could not be resolved from the scans: the L-shape and K-shape signs on f. 88, the square on f. 80 and the codes 4, 22 and 27 are unglossed.

William Brooke, Lord Cobham, was one of Elizabeth’s commissioners sent to treat with Parma’s deputies in the spring of 1588. The talks moved from Ostend to Bourbourg while the Armada was fitting out. The Calendar of State Papers Foreign (vol. 21 pt 4) calendars his letters in SP 77, but not these Harley copies. No printed decipherment of them was found. On f. 89 (R8493) the glosses give “what may be”, “further hoped for at their hands” and “our abode in this towne is so advantagious”. Aligning them gives the following table. A second session working on Cobham’s March letters (R8477–R8487) reached the same values independently from its own cribs, and deciphered most of those letters: see Cobham at Ostend, March 1587/8 (key in targets/harley287/key.tsv ). Its table separates s (a narrow ∧) from t (a wide one), which may resolve the s/t ambiguity here.

A third pass worked from the scans at full resolution (7,200 pixels wide), aligning about sixty glossed words on ff. 75, 79 and 89 sign by sign. The result is targets/cobham1588/signs.tsv . The families that look alike at normal size separate cleanly. p is a loop with its tail swept down-left (“upon”, “popes”, “perswade”). l is a circle crossed by a straight stem (“arrival”, “holding”). h is a stem with a bowl to the right (“harken”, “thought”). m is a horizontal S with a loop (“made”, “commission”), and w a dot and stroke (“willing”, “sworne”). The glosses also show that several signs are polyphonic. Λ is s and t (and probably a), γ is r and y, c is o and once a, and the l sign once stands for t. The code numbers are glossed too: 7 = her Majesty, 10 = the Lord Admiral, 15 = the Duke of Parma, 16 = the King of Spain. f. 80r: the word first taken for ARMADA (“as usuall in all armadas”) is treaties : its third sign is the 7-form e, not the m sign (re-checked 22 October 2026), so the passage reads “as usuall yn all treaties in [?numbers], that at the treaty of [?Breda]”. Also “hoping theym in the [?ex]pances”; a run with vertical word dividers ending “ to these termes ”; and “[22] is so forwarde yn the action that he promised Q[ueen]”. (M) f. 88r: “15:” is the Duke of Parma . The first cipher run probably begins “[?captain] …” before a name, “with 40 men of […] have promised the haven of […]”. The rest turns on signs no gloss shows. (M) f. 92r: “4 sent by […]” and “of words of [?letters]” (M); the September guess “the Portugals” is withdrawn.

The sign inventory is now fixed, so the images are no longer the obstacle. Several signs are polyphonic and a few (an L-shape and a K-shape on f. 88, the square on f. 80, the codes 4, 22 and 27) are unglossed. The next step is to transcribe the runs sign by sign from the full-resolution crops, give each sign its set of possible letters from signs.tsv , enumerate each cipher word’s possible decryptions against a word list of the 1580s, and let the clear context choose.

The leaf carries a clear dateline and nine lines of figures, 189 tokens separated by commas, with no address or signature. Brussels was then the capital of the Austrian Netherlands, and ecclesiastical business there went through the nunciatures, so the slip was probably sent by someone at Brussels to the nuncio at Cologne, in whose archive it is kept. Nothing on the leaf proves this. The key, as Lasry rebuilt it, gives letters and a few syllables fixed homophones of one to three digits (a 6|77, e 04|40, i 17|71, o 16|61, r 14|41, s 01|38, che 35, di 53, ma 74). The nulls 2, 22 and 222 stand between words, and four-digit codes in the 9300s and 9400s stand for words or names. Because the groups are separated by commas, the text divides into units without ambiguity.

Brusselles 9 ott.re 1721. Sopra il curato [45] [9441] [43]te divinis, g(rat)s di sapere qualche cosa di [9336] [9485] di Tournai. Sopra l’affare di Colonia, ma egli, a quel che vedo, ne è informato. Se stima a proposito che io [76] scriva in [9356] ad un suo corrispondente, lo farò volentieri, ma attendo i suoi ordini in questo. “About the curate […] a divinis [suspended from his office?], [I would be] glad to know something of [9336 9485] of Tournai. About the Cologne affair: he, as far as I see, is informed of it. If you think it right that I write [76] in [9356] to a correspondent of yours, I will gladly do so, but I await your orders on this.” Bonavoglia’s decipherment is the same, except where the values below change it.

18 = qu, not que. It occurs in qu-a-l-che, a qu-e-l che and in qu-e-st-o. With que every one of the three has a doubled e . Grade C. 55 = gli : “ma e-55, a quel che vedo, ne è informato”, ma egli . Grade C. 67 = g? : “67-r-a-t-s di sapere”, most likely grato with a slip in the last figure. Grade M. Lasry’s three queried values, 81 ne , 86 se and 88 st , each fit their context ( ne è informato , se stima , questo ) and are kept.

45, 9441, 43 in “curato 45 9441 43-te divinis”. The phrase must be a suspension a divinis , perhaps with the curate’s parish, but none of the three occurs again, so no value can be confirmed. 9336 9485 in “di [9336] [9485] di Tournai”: probably a title and a name, perhaps the bishop. 9356 in “scriva in [9356]”: a place or a word such as cifra . 76 in “che io [76] scriva”: ne , le or gli would all fit. The sender and recipient are not named on the leaf. The other contents of Colonia 5 might identify them.

His text was transcribed here from the Google Books page image on 23 October 2026. What it says The Pope’s encouragement to Climent at the court of Castile; in cipher, that Don Bartolomé is not fit to govern the church of Zaragoza, and that Don Gil [Sánchez Muñoz] at Barcelona “rouses the prelates who are asleep” (translation). Puig’s note cites another letter of Comuel, doc. 661, which he does not print. Still open The ciphertext: no image of the letter exists, so the cipher and its key are unknown. Francesc Climent, called Çapera, was Benedict XIII’s chamberlain and treasurer and later bishop of Barcelona; he left his papers to the cathedral chapter. Among them Sebastián Puig y Puig found fourteen letters partly or wholly in cipher, deciphered them, and printed them in the appendix of Pedro de Luna, último papa de Aviñón (1920). This is one of them: Pedro Comuel to Climent, 27 Jun 1416 (appendix CXXXV, p. 578; Çapera no. 670). Of its 401 words Puig prints 85 in italics as his decipherment; the last deciphered clause is Catalan, not Latin. The reading audit of 22 October 2026 found no text of the letter in the repository; on 23 October Puig’s page was fetched as an image from Google Books and transcribed ( texts/comuel1416_reading.md , with an English translation). The letter ends on p. 578; p. 579 is the next item. Puig’s note cites another letter of Comuel, doc. 661, which he does not print. The originals are not digitised, and the archivist Josep Mas noted that Puig studied many of the Schism papers at home in 1920–30 and did not return them all. Puig’s print may be the only witness.

Puig never printed a key, and the only image of any of these ciphers is his facsimile of one page of Benedict XIII’s own letter of 22 June 1400. From that page the key of Benedict’s letters was rebuilt here: a plain substitution, one sign per letter. Puig writes of “la clave o claves”, the key or keys, he recovered, and nothing shows whether this letter, from another writer, used the same one. So it has its own entry. Benedict XIII’s letters are on Benedict XIII to Climent, 1399–1403 (a different or unverified cipher, with its own page); the other letters of his circle each have their own page for the same reason: Santa Cruz to Climent, 1399 , Jafet to Climent, 1400 , Exea to Climent, 1408 , Comuel to Climent, December 1415 .

The ciphertext. No image of the letter exists, so its cipher, its key and Puig’s reading cannot be checked. Blocker: needs the original in the Arxiu Capitular de Barcelona. Another letter of Comuel , doc. 661, cited in Puig’s note 2 and not printed. Blocker: needs the original.

Item quare non scripsi mandavit mo. scribere vobis _quod quamvis dns. bartolomeus amisit bonus non tamen est ad regendam eccliam cesaraugustam; dicit etiam quod illos iuvenes de vera et alius dimitatis redire ad studium et non turbetis eos item quod habeatis recommissum iohannes ugueti qui bonus est; scribatis vel mitatis aliquem ut papa sit informatus de mente vestra et de statu negociorum et cetera,_ et dirigat deus p. v. in agendis cui me recomendo _dominus egidius est barchinone pro epo. valentino et facit mirabilia ut dicitur et excitat prelatos qui dormiunt e desengana los clarament veus que fa un hom que gos parlar._ Script. XXVII junii P. servitorum vestrum. — Reverende in Xpo pri, et dno. meo metuendmo. dno. The passages Puig deciphered are in _italics_. Names modernised here only. Holes: none. ## Translation Most reverend father and most dread lord. With due commendation first made: after Guillem Ortolà left I wrote to Your Reverend Paternity by Pedro Soriano how our lord had written to you that you, who know the business, should see in what state things remain at the court of the King of Castile, whether you ought to go back there or come to this kingdom, since he is content with what Your Paternity decides on it. He warns you of one thing, of which, it seems from your letters, you are already well warned: that you will have to bear many great dangers for the faith of Christ and the service of the Pope, perhaps greater and harder than he wrote to you and you to His Holiness. Therefore put on the armour of God and prepare yourself, as he not only believes but is certain you will, to bear whatever and whatsoever may come or befall. He says that this is the time in which God wills that those who are good be made manifest; for he knows that you care little for temporal goods or the honours of the world, would not willingly trade them for the glory of paradise, nor break your loyalty for any danger that might befall you. Monsignor repeated these words to me so many times that I can hardly set out His Holiness's mind; and though he knew that I had written to you, I wished to write again. He also said and ordered me to write what follows: that you should not strike such terror into yourself that you throw yourself to the ground, since many prelates resisted strongly in many things and few granted letters on the revenues of the Camera to be raised by commissaries, and those afterwards had recourse to His Holiness asking absolution, rehabilitations, dispensations and even new provisions of their dignities, and I was present at at least two of them. He trusts in God that you will act as you have always been used to act well, will make up the failings of others who act less well, strengthen the weak and timid, and carry off the crown. Item, because I had not written, he ordered me to write to you _that although Don Bartolomé lost [his] goods, he is still not fit to govern the church of Zaragoza; he also says that you should let those young men of Vera and the other return to their studies and not trouble them; item, that you keep Juan Ugueti, who is good, commended; that you write or send someone so that the Pope is informed of your mind and of the state of affairs, etc._ And may God direct Your Paternity in your doings, to whom I commend myself. _Don Gil [Sánchez Muñoz] is at Barcelona for the bishop of Valencia and does wonders, they say, and rouses the prelates who are asleep, and undeceives them plainly: you see what a man does who dares to speak._ Written 27 June. P., your servant. — To the reverend father in Christ and my most dread lord, the lord Archbishop of Zaragoza.

Fourteen cipher despatches of 1786–87 from the Polish legation at St Petersburg, in the one-part code of 1783 whose key survives in the same fonds. Brice Dudout transcribed the key and read the pieces blind, without opening the cabinet’s clear texts: 81.8% of 7,040 words, on the Russian regiments in Poland and the Empress’s journey to the Crimea. 2345 981 95 1647 669 871 573 … · . na iu trze Y sze … St Petersburg → Warsaw · one-part code of 1783 · December 1786 – October 1787 · read with the key of the time Deboli and Gołuchowski, St Petersburg, 1786–87 Go to the full text ↓ The Polish envoy in St Petersburg reports on the Russian regiments in Poland, Potemkin and the Empress’s journey south, in a code whose key of 1783 survives and was applied here blind. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 6 November 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (82% of the cipher) · On the map With Brice Dudout (solution) · Also credited · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) · Daniel Bourdeau (pointer to a source) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (82% of the cipher) The despatches Eleven despatches of Antoni Augustyn Deboli, Polish envoy in St Petersburg, to King Stanisław August (29 December 1786 – 16 October 1787), and three letters of Gołuchowski to one of the King’s ministers, all in the older code. Where AGAD Warsaw, Zbiór Popielów (zesp. 12), sygn. 3, “Deboli. 1787 (cyfry)”, 83 pieces; the key in sygn. 444. Not on DECODE. The cipher A one-part Polish code in shuffled letter blocks: groups 1–1969 for syllables, words and names, signal group 2345, nulls from 1970. The same volume also uses tables 9933, 3865, 12282 and the code of 1789–91, which are not deciphered here. How it was deciphered With the key of the time, “Cyfra polska” of 8 March 1783, transcribed in full (1,965 entries) and applied without changing a value from the sense. Read blind: the cabinet’s clear texts of 1786–87 were not opened. What it says Deboli presses Vice-Chancellor Ostermann for the withdrawal of the Russian regiment stationed in Poland, as the Sejm instructed; everything depends on Potemkin; the Empress’s journey and Joseph II’s meeting with her. Still open 1,281 unresolved words, partly misread digits and partly values that do not fit; the key scores 0.837 on a held-out 1788 pair, under the 0.90 set in advance; the pieces in the other tables. Credit Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée) transcribed the key and the despatches and read them, working with Claude Opus 5.5 agents. The key itself is the cabinet’s of 1783.

Volume 3 of the Zbiór Popielów holds Deboli’s cipher despatches of 1787, 83 pieces, and four inserted letters of Gołuchowski. Sorted by their opening group, 22 pieces are in the older code (signal 2345), 19 in table 9933, 14 in table 3865, 3 in table 12282, 3 in the code of 1789–91 and 3 mostly in clear. The fourteen deciphered here are the older-code pieces that were transcribed. The code of 1789–91 has its own pages ( Deboli 1789 , Deboli 1788 ). The cabinet’s clear texts of 1786–87 are in AGAD, Archiwum Królestwa Polskiego 269. By its header index, a clear of the same date exists for 8 of the 14 pieces; for those the content is probably already known, and the reading here is a blind reading of them, not a first one. For six pieces (p13, p21, p28, p33, g1, g3) no clear text was found.

Sygn. 444, “Cyfra polska”, 8 March 1783, is a one-part code: blocks of groups for each initial letter in shuffled order (M from 1, N from 92, O from 211, P from 326 … D from 1323), endings and alternatives written with the values. It was transcribed from its nine scans (98% legible) and re-read on the image only for 21 values; no value was changed from the sense of a despatch. It is not the code of 1789–91 (8 is mi here, do there). The key was tested on three despatches of 1788 in the older code against their cabinet decipherments, the ciphers hashed before the clears: 0.874, 0.874 and 0.837 on the held-out one, against shuffled-key controls of 0.08–0.12. The threshold fixed in advance was 0.90, so the test failed at that level while confirming 444 as the key of 1783–88; most misses are alignment artefacts and misread digits.

Counted by script on each reading file, the fourteen pieces come to 7,040 words: 5,499 certain, 256 probable, 4 restored and 1,281 unresolved, 81.8% read by sense. The share per piece runs from 0.70 to 0.91, so none reaches the 95% bar. The unresolved syllables are left in place. A few digits were settled by blind shape questions answered by Brice Dudout. The readings, in Polish or French, are under Full texts; the English file gives summaries of the deciphered parts, not full translations. Deboli tells the King that Ostermann’s evasive answer about the Russian regiments in Poland kept him from asking formally; he presses for their withdrawal, as the Sejm instructed him, and judges that everything depends on Potemkin, who wants the affair sent to a commission he fears. Other pieces follow the Empress’s journey and Joseph II’s plan to meet her at Kherson rather than Kiev.

1,281 unresolved words, isolated syllables that do not construe: partly misread digits of the despatches, partly values of 444 that do not fit, and four places where the key itself is torn or rubbed out (1215, 1216, 1398, 1405). The key fails its own test at 0.90 (0.837 on the held-out pair); a new test on three despatches of 1786 with clears in AKP 269 is pre-registered and not yet run. The digits were transcribed once, from the scans; blind questions were used only where one digit changes the reading. The pieces in tables 9933, 3865 and 12282 and in the code of 1789–91 are not deciphered; no key of the time for them was found. For eight pieces the cabinet’s clear texts exist and were deliberately not opened, so the reading has not been compared with them.

Written by AI agents for Brice Dudout, 5-6 Nov 2026, from the readings in reading/; not checked by a historian. ## Deboli to the King ### p01 (29 Dec 1786) Deboli tells the King that the Vice-Chancellor's (Ostermann's) evasive answer about the Russian regiments stationed in Poland kept him from asking formally, for fear of an explicit refusal; he considers an approach through Potemkin and mentions abuses committed by the regiments. Last Wednesday he pressed the Vice-Chancellor, who said neither yes nor no, so the silence has to be read. Since the King's despatch of the 16th, he sees that Russia is not disposed to withdraw the regiments. At the next conference he will use the Department's despatch of the 9th and the argument that the Emperor, travelling to Kiev, will see Russian regiments in Poland with his own eyes. Partly read passages: Buchholtz (the Prussian envoy) spreading a "falsehood"; a visitor explaining his interests; a count's memorial on estates of Polish families in Ukraine. To the Department he writes only pro forma. ### p04 (9 Jan 1787) Deboli expects an answer at tomorrow's conference on the King's letter of the 16th (Dec.). The aim is finally to be rid of the regiment in question (cf. piece 1). The Empress's departure remains as announced. By the last Vienna courier, Joseph II will come to Kherson rather than Kiev and cannot stay long because the Neapolitan sovereigns are expected in Vienna. Potemkin will go to Krichev (his estate) to receive the Empress and will wait for her at Kiev; otherwise he could not finish his tours. The affair of the Princess of Württemberg (Augusta of Brunswick) troubles the grand-ducal couple: there was talk of sending her to Reval during the Empress's absence pending an answer from her father the Duke of Brunswick, who reportedly wrote urging her to win her husband's affection and declines to take her side or recall her; since yesterday it is said the Empress will take her along. A general, taken seriously ill on Saturday, is better. Deboli received the King's letter of 7 December yesterday. ### p07 (18 Jan 1787) Deboli reports a talk with Vice-Chancellor Ostermann about the Russian regiment stationed in Poland. Deboli presses for its withdrawal, as the Sejm instructed him. Ostermann answers that the Poles complain now of the Emperor, now of the King of Prussia, while also demanding the withdrawal. He adds that the regiment keeps the peace and that the Hetman himself complained of it. He blames Deboli's vehemence and tells him to put these points to the King. Deboli notes that he has waited for an answer for almost a year. For three years, he says, he has answered foreign envoys vaguely. The French minister, speaking to the Dutch one, assumed the King would raise the matter when he met the Empress. In Deboli's view everything depends on Potemkin, who wants the affair sent to a Commission. Deboli fears such a Commission: the grievances (Igelström, a detachment entering a district in 1783) would be turned back against Poland. He suggests the King write to Potemkin before Kiev. He will not use the King's letter of the 3rd. He also mentions Potemkin's plan to buy an estate in Poland ("S mila", probably Smiła). The letter then covers: - the affair of the Palatine of Ruthenia, with Chernyshev, General Komarzewski and Razumovsky; - a young castellan's son who came to St Petersburg via Riga with neither his father's leave nor a passport. He claimed to carry a letter from the Hetman to Potemkin. Deboli refuses to protect him, lends him 300 roubles against a bond and sends him home via Połock. ### p13, p15, p21 - **13 (27/7)** — Foreign ministers await an audience with the Empress. She received three of them at Tsarskoye Selo, in a small circle and in very good humour. Hetman Branicki and his wife are to come to St Petersburg this winter (news from Cobenzl). There are hopes he will regain the King's favour. Deboli answers that the King does not push him away. - **15 (31/8)** — Three posts came with no letter. The answer to the King's letter will come from the Empress herself, since Ostermann's chancery has no orders. The British envoy (Fitzherbert) has left and was given the Empress's portrait. On Tuesday Ségur's tragedy "Coriolan" was staged at the Hermitage, with only Cobenzl and the author invited. Comedies and proverbs are played in the small theatre; the other ministers come on Thursdays. Ségur leaves within a week with the Prince de Ligne, after M. de Sainte-Croix's arrival. The letter is left unsigned as Deboli leaves for Pavlovsk. - **21 (17/8)** — Deboli asks how the King's letter and its allegorical idea were received. The Empress came back to town, without saying whether she would return to Tsarskoye Selo. A ceremony was held at the Summer Palace for the Preobrazhensky regiment's feast. She then moved into the Winter Palace, to everyone's satisfaction. ### p23, p28, p30 - **23 (14/9)** — Courier to Warsaw; Cobenzl and the Austrian courier; the Turks have declared war; French mediation; Ostermann on France and Berlin; Sardinia; Prussian recruitment (2 × 500); the prince de Ligne wishes to write to the king. - **28 (25/9)** — Back from Gatchina; the king's letter of the 12th; Cobenzl says the alliance binds the Emperor to war; Council debate on peace with the Turks; Ligne's letter sent with the Austrian courier; Ligne asks about an extraordinary sejm; Deboli jokes he will propose him as deputy for Wilno. - **30 (3/8)** — Pisarz Wielhorski has arrived on business of the castellan's wife Ogińska of Wilno (probable), with the chancellor's letters to the vice-chancellor, Count Bezborodko and Prince Vyazemsky (probable); Deboli has introduced him. Starosta Potocki: 200,000 roubles would have been lost had they not been withdrawn, merchants having failed (partly unresolved); creditors will get barely 5 %. Potocki still loses through the exchange rate, down to 36 stuivers (probable) per rouble against 42 at the start of winter, on the 400,000 roubles he sent. ### p33, p37 - **33 (7 Oct.)** — At tomorrow's conference Deboli will carry out the king's order (dispatch of the 24th of last month): Field Marshal Rumyantsev's division has hastened its entry into Turkish territory to screen Poland; he will ask when to expect the answer on the alliance project with Russia ("in hand"); there is hesitation here about starting anything in Poland and fear of trouble from Prussia; Deboli answers that inaction would be taken as abandoning Poland and would help Prussian intrigues. Three conclusions: 1) no long war is wanted: take Ochakov (this autumn or rather in winter), then make peace; 2) according to Bezborodko the Emperor will do little; Herbert has not yet sent a courier because Joseph II wants to be ready and to concert with Russia; the attack will come when the Russian army enters Ochakov Tartary and Moldavia, the Emperor also attacking from Pokutia if Kamieniec is secured; the theatre of war will move to the Danube; 3) a Franco-Russian union is hard: England would join Prussia; the Danish minister (Saint-Saphorin, probable) foretells an English fleet in the Baltic, but has a second plan: Russia will humour both England and France. Ségur is almost the only one to speak of the prince of Nassau with respect; ministers here mock him. 200,000 roubles in gold and silver sent under escort to Rumyantsev to pay for provisions in Poland. Rumour of a 5-million loan (probable) at the Berlin bank, spread on purpose by Berlin, and false. - **37 (16 Oct.), 444 part** — Written in the morning before leaving for Gatchina; the courier announced in the king's letter of the 3rd has not arrived. With the vice-chancellor away, a long talk with Markov on the dispatch: he is heard kindly and told Russia still wants to shield Poland from any damage in this war and to come to an agreement; but on guaranteeing a territory for Poland (asked in the king's letter) Markov protests and gives a "dissertation": in the last Turkish war circumstances forced Russia into the partition; if Poland makes difficulties Russia might again have to consent to its loss; the aim should be keeping, not enlarging, the country; Russia cannot promise unconquered land; anything would rather come from conquests over the Turks; above all Polish possessions must be preserved; spreading the plan would be most harmful. Deboli answers in two parts: 1) troubles in Poland will be prevented if Russia joins in the means of keeping Poland under the watchword of union; the nation, used to fear, would read Russian inaction as abandonment, and individuals would scatter "like lost men who fall into snares while seeking help"; 2) the idea of gains from the Turks is no sine qua non; he asks that it not be misconstrued; the proposal, known to few, is to come through Stackelberg and stay secret, as the vice-chancellor urged. He must now treat the matter with the vice-chancellor on these lines; Markov repeats that the disposition to an agreement remains and calls the use of the Polish army against the Turks a way to occupy minds and turn them from harmful ties. He denies what was reported about Prince Repnin (a sum of roubles and a place in the suite): it is untrue. Buchholtz reportedly announced the coming entry of 10 Russian regiments, causing alarm in Warsaw; questioned by the Prussian minister in St Petersburg, Gołuchowski said what he knew and refrained from saying more, since the matter was not clear enough in the report of the Palatine of Ruthenia. ### g3 (30 Mar 1787) On Sunday at court the foreign ministers (Danish, St-Saphorin; Portuguese, Horta?) pressed him about the 10 regiments said to be entering Poland; he answered he had nothing certain. The Danish minister then asked about Şahin Giray: Hamburg papers said he would be sent to Persia and later return to the Crimea, where the Empress is to go. Gołuchowski said he knew no more than the Hamburg papers and ended the conversation to avoid further questions. ### g4 (18 May 1787) Charged (by Prince Stanisław Poniatowski's household) with finding out Grand Duke Paul's taste in saddle horses to be sent from Poland, Gołuchowski questioned the riding master who had been at Tsarskoye Selo. The horse must be: 1) very calm; 2) unafraid of firing, attacks, arms drill, soldiers' shouts and cannon — not even moving its head when the Grand Duke, as he does, rides up to the guns; 3) lively when needed and well schooled; 4) sound and strong-legged, since the Grand Duke rides his chosen horse every day: he sets off at a gallop to a fixed point, then walks, out twice a day, sometimes up to 40 versts. The Grand Duke complained he had no good horse to sit before his regiment's front without fear and wants a Polish horse for the May review (Old Style). Written by AI agents for Brice Dudout, 5-6 Nov 2026, from the readings in reading/; not checked by a historian. ## Deboli to the King ### p01 (29 Dec 1786) Deboli tells the King that the Vice-Chancellor's (Ostermann's) evasive answer about the Russian regiments stationed in Poland kept him from asking formally, for fear of an explicit refusal; he considers an approach through Potemkin and mentions abuses committed by the regiments. Last Wednesday he pressed the Vice-Chancellor, who said neither yes nor no, so the silence has to be read. Since the King's despatch of the 16th, he sees that Russia is not disposed to withdraw the regiments. At the next conference he will use the Department's despatch of the 9th and the argument that the Emperor, travelling to Kiev, will see Russian regiments in Poland with his own eyes. Partly read passages: Buchholtz (the Prussian envoy) spreading a "falsehood"; a visitor explaining his interests; a count's memorial on estates of Polish families in Ukraine. To the Department he writes only pro forma. ### p04 (9 Jan 1787) Deboli expects an answer at tomorrow's conference on the King's letter of the 16th (Dec.). The aim is finally to be rid of the regiment in question (cf. piece 1). The Empress's departure remains as announced. By the last Vienna courier, Joseph II will come to Kherson rather than Kiev and cannot stay long because the Neapolitan sovereigns are expected in Vienna. Potemkin will go to Krichev (his estate) to receive the Empress and will wait for her at Kiev; otherwise he could not finish his tours. The affair of the Princess of Württemberg (Augusta of Brunswick) troubles the grand-ducal couple: there was talk of sending her to Reval during the Empress's absence pending an answer from her father the Duke of Brunswick, who reportedly wrote urging her to win her husband's affection and declines to take her side or recall her; since yesterday it is said the Empress will take her along. A general, taken seriously ill on Saturday, is better. Deboli received the King's letter of 7 December yesterday. ### p07 (18 Jan 1787) Deboli reports a talk with Vice-Chancellor Ostermann about the Russian regiment stationed in Poland. Deboli presses for its withdrawal, as the Sejm instructed him. Ostermann answers that the Poles complain now of the Emperor, now of the King of Prussia, while also demanding the withdrawal. He adds that the regiment keeps the peace and that the Hetman himself complained of it. He blames Deboli's vehemence and tells him to put these points to the King. Deboli notes that he has waited for an answer for almost a year. For three years, he says, he has answered foreign envoys vaguely. The French minister, speaking to the Dutch one, assumed the King would raise the matter when he met the Empress. In Deboli's view everything depends on Potemkin, who wants the affair sent to a Commission. Deboli fears such a Commission: the grievances (Igelström, a detachment entering a district in 1783) would be turned back against Poland. He suggests the King write to Potemkin before Kiev. He will not use the King's letter of the 3rd. He also mentions Potemkin's plan to buy an estate in Poland ("S mila", probably Smiła). The letter then covers: - the affair of the Palatine of Ruthenia, with Chernyshev, General Komarzewski and Razumovsky; - a young castellan's son who came to St Petersburg via Riga with neither his father's leave nor a passport. He claimed to carry a letter from the Hetman to Potemkin. Deboli refuses to protect him, lends him 300 roubles against a bond and sends him home via Połock. ### p13, p15, p21 - **13 (27/7)** — Foreign ministers await an audience with the Empress. She received three of them at Tsarskoye Selo, in a small circle and in very good humour. Hetman Branicki and his wife are to come to St Petersburg this winter (news from Cobenzl). There are hopes he will regain the King's favour. Deboli answers that the King does not push him away. - **15 (31/8)** — Three posts came with no letter. The answer to the King's letter will come from the Empress herself, since Ostermann's chancery has no orders. The British envoy (Fitzherbert) has left and was given the Empress's portrait. On Tuesday Ségur's tragedy "Coriolan" was staged at the Hermitage, with only Cobenzl and the author invited. Comedies and proverbs are played in the small theatre; the other ministers come on Thursdays. Ségur leaves within a week with the Prince de Ligne, after M. de Sainte-Croix's arrival. The letter is left unsigned as Deboli leaves for Pavlovsk. - **21 (17/8)** — Deboli asks how the King's letter and its allegorical idea were received. The Empress came back to town, without saying whether she would return to Tsarskoye Selo. A ceremony was held at the Summer Palace for the Preobrazhensky regiment's feast. She then moved into the Winter Palace, to everyone's satisfaction. ### p23, p28, p30 - **23 (14/9)** — Courier to Warsaw; Cobenzl and the Austrian courier; the Turks have declared war; French mediation; Ostermann on France and Berlin; Sardinia; Prussian recruitment (2 × 500); the prince de Ligne wishes to write to the king. - **28 (25/9)** — Back from Gatchina; the king's letter of the 12th; Cobenzl says the alliance binds the Emperor to war; Council debate on peace with the Turks; Ligne's letter sent with the Austrian courier; Ligne asks about an extraordinary sejm; Deboli jokes he will propose him as deputy for Wilno. - **30 (3/8)** — Pisarz Wielhorski has arrived on business of the castellan's wife Ogińska of Wilno (probable), with the chancellor's letters to the vice-chancellor, Count Bezborodko and Prince Vyazemsky (probable); Deboli has introduced him. Starosta Potocki: 200,000 roubles would have been lost had they not been withdrawn, merchants having failed (partly unresolved); creditors will get barely 5 %. Potocki still loses through the exchange rate, down to 36 stuivers (probable) per rouble against 42 at the start of winter, on the 400,000 roubles he sent. ### p33, p37 - **33 (7 Oct.)** — At tomorrow's conference Deboli will carry out the king's order (dispatch of the 24th of last month): Field Marshal Rumyantsev's division has hastened its entry into Turkish territory to screen Poland; he will ask when to expect the answer on the alliance project with Russia ("in hand"); there is hesitation here about starting anything in Poland and fear of trouble from Prussia; Deboli answers that inaction would be taken as abandoning Poland and would help Prussian intrigues. Three conclusions: 1) no long war is wanted: take Ochakov (this autumn or rather in winter), then make peace; 2) according to Bezborodko the Emperor will do little; Herbert has not yet sent a courier because Joseph II wants to be ready and to concert with Russia; the attack will come when the Russian army enters Ochakov Tartary and Moldavia, the Emperor also attacking from Pokutia if Kamieniec is secured; the theatre of war will move to the Danube; 3) a Franco-Russian union is hard: England would join Prussia; the Danish minister (Saint-Saphorin, probable) foretells an English fleet in the Baltic, but has a second plan: Russia will humour both England and France. Ségur is almost the only one to speak of the prince of Nassau with respect; ministers here mock him. 200,000 roubles in gold and silver sent under escort to Rumyantsev to pay for provisions in Poland. Rumour of a 5-million loan (probable) at the Berlin bank, spread on purpose by Berlin, and false. - **37 (16 Oct.), 444 part** — Written in the morning before leaving for Gatchina; the courier announced in the king's letter of the 3rd has not arrived. With the vice-chancellor away, a long talk with Markov on the dispatch: he is heard kindly and told Russia still wants to shield Poland from any damage in this war and to come to an agreement; but on guaranteeing a territory for Poland (asked in the king's letter) Markov protests and gives a "dissertation": in the last Turkish war circumstances forced Russia into the partition; if Poland makes difficulties Russia might again have to consent to its loss; the aim should be keeping, not enlarging, the country; Russia cannot promise unconquered land; anything would rather come from conquests over the Turks; above all Polish possessions must be preserved; spreading the plan would be most harmful. Deboli answers in two parts: 1) troubles in Poland will be prevented if Russia joins in the means of keeping Poland under the watchword of union; the nation, used to fear, would read Russian inaction as abandonment, and individuals would scatter "like lost men who fall into snares while seeking help"; 2) the idea of gains from the Turks is no sine qua non; he asks that it not be misconstrued; the proposal, known to few, is to come through Stackelberg and stay secret, as the vice-chancellor urged. He must now treat the matter with the vice-chancellor on these lines; Markov repeats that the disposition to an agreement remains and calls the use of the Polish army against the Turks a way to occupy minds and turn them from harmful ties. He denies what was reported about Prince Repnin (a sum of roubles and a place in the suite): it is untrue. Buchholtz reportedly announced the coming entry of 10 Russian regiments, causing alarm in Warsaw; questioned by the Prussian minister in St Petersburg, Gołuchowski said what he knew and refrained from saying more, since the matter was not clear enough in the report of the Palatine of Ruthenia. ### g3 (30 Mar 1787) On Sunday at court the foreign ministers (Danish, St-Saphorin; Portuguese, Horta?) pressed him about the 10 regiments said to be entering Poland; he answered he had nothing certain. The Danish minister then asked about Şahin Giray: Hamburg papers said he would be sent to Persia and later return to the Crimea, where the Empress is to go. Gołuchowski said he knew no more than the Hamburg papers and ended the conversation to avoid further questions. ### g4 (18 May 1787) Charged (by Prince Stanisław Poniatowski's household) with finding out Grand Duke Paul's taste in saddle horses to be sent from Poland, Gołuchowski questioned the riding master who had been at Tsarskoye Selo. The horse must be: 1) very calm; 2) unafraid of firing, attacks, arms drill, soldiers' shouts and cannon — not even moving its head when the Grand Duke, as he does, rides up to the guns; 3) lively when needed and well schooled; 4) sound and strong-legged, since the Grand Duke rides his chosen horse every day: he sets off at a gallop to a fixed point, then walks, out twice a day, sometimes up to 40 versts. The Grand Duke complained he had no good horse to sit before his regiment's front without fear and wants a Polish horse for the May review (Old Style).
