The letter Bergenroth could not decipher in 1862 survives in three ciphered copies in AGS Patronato Real leg. 53 doc. 69. Its key is the Cifra general de los Reyes Católicos printed by Galende Díaz in 1994; applied unchanged, it decodes every code group, while about half the runs of single-letter symbols are too small to decipher on the online images. The letter concerns the French attack on Roussillon and asks Henry VII for two thousand English foot. cog · SABEYS · xix · bof · zok · RONPIO · yiz · … · yaz · yui · xuy · zin ya · sabeys · el · rey de Francia · nos · ronpio · los · … · la · guerra · en · Napoles Segovia → London · homophonic alphabet with a two-to-four-letter nomenclator · 20 August 1503 (with duplicates of September and 3 October) Isabella of Castile to the Duke of Estrada, 20 August 1503 from Isabella I of Castile Go to the full text ↓ Bergenroth calendared this letter in 1862 as a despatch he could not decipher, and no decipherment of it has been found since. Tomokiyo named its key, the royal Cifra general printed by Galende Díaz; applied unchanged to a transcription of the three copies, it decodes every code group. About half the runs of single-letter symbols could not be deciphered, because on the online images the symbols are too small to tell apart. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (23% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · Juan Carlos Galende Díaz (key or decipherment used) · Satoshi Tomokiyo (pointer to a source) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (23% of the cipher) The letter Queen Isabella to her ambassador in England, Hernán Duque de Estrada, Segovia, 20 August 1503, with duplicates of September and 3 October. Where Archivo General de Simancas, Patronato Real leg. 53 doc. 69, formerly Tratados con Inglaterra leg. 4 ff. 65–67, on PARES. Bergenroth calendared it in 1862 as a despatch he could not decipher. The cipher A homophonic alphabet, with several symbols for each vowel, together with a nomenclator of two- to four-letter code groups for words. Method Known key applied: on Tomokiyo’s suggestion, the Cifra general de los Reyes Católicos printed by Galende Díaz in 1994. It fits at once, and about 480 code groups all make sense in context. The three copies were transcribed and collated. What it says France has opened war in Naples, Aragon, Guipúzcoa and Galicia. Henry VII is bound by treaty to help defend Spain, and Estrada is to ask him for two thousand English foot. It is not about Catherine of Aragon’s marriage. Still open From recto line 12 on, most lines are mostly unread and cannot be built into sentences (decoded, not read): about half of the 154 runs of letter symbols: on the 988-pixel images a symbol is eight to ten pixels high. With a higher-resolution copy from Simancas the key should decipher the whole letter. Credit Satoshi Tomokiyo suggested the key; the key itself is Galende Díaz’s 1994 edition.

Bergenroth cited it as S. E. T. c. I. L. 4 ff. 65, 66 and 67 : Secretaría de Estado, Tratados con Inglaterra, legajo 4. That series now sits in Patronato Real, Capitulaciones con Inglaterra, leg. 53 , and PARES records 2207985–2207991 are docs. 66–72, all letters of 1502–03 to Estrada. Doc. 69 (dated only “1503” in PARES) has eight images: images 1–2 (pencil f. 322): copy X , 46 lines and 11 on the verso, closing “en madri[d]? a … de setiembre”, endorsed by Estrada as received at Durham House on All Saints’ Day, by the ship Jorja (George): Bergenroth’s no. 380, f. 68; images 3–4 (f. 323): copy Y , closing “en Segovia a xx de agosto de diii” , its dorse marked “Leg. 4 f. 65”. This is Bergenroth’s no. 369; images 5–6: address leaves; images 7–8: copy Z , closing “en Segovia a tres de otubre de diii”, endorsed “en la casa de Durã[m] a ocho de março de diiii. Recebida de uno de Salusbery”: Bergenroth’s no. 381, f. 69. Tomokiyo listed it under 3 October and noticed it was not in Estrada’s usual cipher. The three copies begin with the same words and carry the same text with different line breaks. Isabella’s letter of 3 October in Estrada’s cipher (Bergenroth no. 385, now PTR 53/71–72) explains Z: “in case you may not have received [our letters of 20 August], I have ordered that the duplicate of it should be sent to you along with this letter.” Bergenroth calendared no. 380 (f. 68) as Isabella’s 3 October letter on the ratification of the marriage treaty, “deciphered by the editor”, and no. 381 (f. 69) as “the same despatch”. The leaves carry the August text in the other cipher, so he must have deciphered the ratification letter from its other copies (ff. 74–77) and filed these two duplicates under it by their date and endorsements. The letter he could not decipher was in his hands three times over. That filing probably also gave the catalogue entry its subject, the marriage. The end of copy Y: the last cipher line, then in clear “en Segovia a xx de agosto de diii”, the date Bergenroth gives. The Cifra general de los Reyes Católicos (Real Academia de la Historia 9/15 ff. 7–9) is printed by Juan Carlos Galende Díaz (1994, appendix doc. 1): an alphabet of symbols with several forms for each letter, and 683 code groups of two to four letters beginning v-, x-, y-, z-, b- and c-. It was transcribed here for the Great Captain’s letter of 1500 in BnF Espagnol 318 ( targets/esp318/keys/cifra_general.txt ) and is applied here unchanged. Bergenroth’s “two keys of cipher” is this mixture of code groups and letter symbols; no second key is needed. Estrada’s usual cipher, which Bergenroth did decipher (Tomokiyo lists groups such as cab , gam , raf , ru ), does not occur in the letter. The scribe has two habits that affect transcription: the v- codes are written with a b-like v ( vib Aragón , vud agora , vil ayuda ), and a final z is written like a 3 ( yiz los , zez por , ziz para ).

From copy X, collated with Y and Z ( targets/estrada1503/reading_X.md ). Recto lines 1–11 and 14–15 build sentences; they are written out in PTR53-69_reading.md with the code groups given as their key values, [..] for a run not deciphered and [?word] for a doubtful word: Ya sabeys [co]mo el rey de Francia nos ronpio los dias passados la guerra en Napoles si[n] le dar causa alguna para ello; y que fezimos con el toda quanta justificacion [..] en el mundo pudimos para escusar la guerra, buscando todos los medios que se podian [..] para ello; y nunca lo pudimos [..] quanta [..] fezimos y [?requerimientos] con harto [..] [?siendo] [..] su [..] y en nuestro [..] Narbona; y agora no cierta[mente] contentandose con aquello ha en[..]biado todo su poder por mar y por tierra a las fronteras de nuestros reynos, la mayor parte a la de Rosellon y a la otra frontera de [Fuen]terrabia para nos hazer toda la guerra que pudiere en ellos, como nos ha ya rompido la guerra por el reyno de Aragon y por la provincia de Guipuzcoa, como en el reyno de Galizia, con cierta armada de mar … … de toda la flor de la gente de Francia ha fecho la mayor armada que el ha podido y la tiene [junta] en Lenguadoque para entrar en Rosellon … The rest of the recto and the verso is decoded, not read: the partial reading ( texts/PTR53-69_partial_reading.md ) has unread runs in nearly every clause. Phrases that hold in it include “el rey de Inglaterra nuestro hermano es obligado por virtud de lo […] entre nos y el, de nos ayudar para defender nuestro […]”, “no queremos afrontar […] armas […] que se declare […] por nos ha […] si los franceses entran en nuestros reynos” and “los dichos dos mil peones”. In English: the King of France broke the peace in Naples without cause, though the monarchs gave him all the justification in the world. He has now sent his whole power by land and sea to their frontiers, most of it against Roussillon and the rest against Fuenterrabía, and has already opened war in Aragon, Guipúzcoa and Galicia. The flower of France is gathered in Languedoc to enter Roussillon. From the partial reading, and confirmed by the letter of 3 October below: Henry VII is bound by treaty to help defend Spain; so far the monarchs have not pressed him to declare himself, and now Estrada is to ask him for two thousand foot soldiers and ships to carry them. Lines 17–30 turn to the Spanish response (the grandees, troops, the Navarre frontier) and are too broken to paraphrase with confidence. Copy X, verso lines 5–8: the first line has yiz xor xik zod P E O N E S, los dichos dos mil peones . Image: Archivo General de Simancas, PTR leg. 53 doc. 69, image 2 (copy X, f. 322v), via PARES. The check is the next letter. On 3 October Isabella wrote again, in Estrada’s usual cipher (PTR 53/71–72; a 19th-century clear copy is bound with it). It opens “Por otras nuestras cartas de veinte de agosto … habréis visto como el Rey de Francia había comenzado a nos romper la guerra … y como por entonces no queríamos afrontar al Rey de Inglaterra nuestro hermano a que se declarase por nos … hasta ver que los franceses entraban en nuestros reynos” , sends a duplicate of the August letter, and repeats the request for “dos mil peones ingleses escogidos” , adding that the French had now entered the counties of Roussillon and laid siege to Salses.

Runs of letter symbols : 154 stretches in reading_X.md , about half the cipher tokens of each copy. The alphabet has several symbols for each vowel, and on 988-pixel images they cannot be told apart reliably. Three copies were collated, and runs deciphered in one copy were carried over to the others. The next step is a higher-resolution reproduction from Simancas; with that, the printed key should decipher the whole letter. Code groups : none unknown. zer , zeg and boe / bue are uncertain in two places each. The later notes on copy X (All Saints’ Day) and at the foot of copy Z (“a ocho de março”) are only partly legible. Grades: the code groups are C (the key confirms them in context); the letter runs quoted above are C where they complete a word from both sides and M where marked […] or bracketed.

Isabella to the Duke of Estrada, Segovia, 20 Aug 1503: copy X recto ll. 1-11 and 14-15 read in part Isabella tells Estrada that the King of France broke the peace in Naples without cause, has sent his power by sea and land to the frontiers of Roussillon and Fuenterrabía, and has opened war in Aragon, Guipúzcoa and Galicia; the King of England is bound by the treaties to help defend what is theirs, and Estrada is to ask for two thousand English foot with ships. About half of the letter-sign runs stay unread at the resolution PARES serves. reading_X.md gives code groups with their values and the letter runs as read; the sign-level transcription exists only for copy Y lines 1-10 (work_Y.md). Builds coherent sentences, but under the read bar of 95% of words read as sense (89% here); the holes are marked in the reading. A letter of Florence’s envoy to the Count of Urbino. Gabbrielli built a partial key in 1863 from a few glossed words (printed by Meister in 1902), so DECODE’s “non-decrypted” means only that no decipherment is on the record. His key was applied and extended from the glossed runs of three sibling letters (R3755–R3757): 98% of the 99 cipher symbols now have a value. The letter describes Galeotto’s mission to Urbino after the defeat at Zagonara. perché dice che [ɱ ·: ᴗ ∂ ⟩ E ℘] [π ⊔ 6 ·:’ ⟩ H] [ç …] [+o ⚲ ♀ ⊔ ô +o ʓ H] perché dice che MADONNA [è] PURE FEMINA E SOSPETOSA ·: H ℘ ɣ = A · ⟩ E 9 = N · +o ∂ = O · ô = T · q = null Urbino → the Signoria of Florence · homophonic letter cipher with word signs · early 1425 Galeotto da Ricasoli to the Dieci di Balía, Urbino, early 1425 Go to the full text ↓ Archivio di Stato di Firenze, Dieci di Balía, Responsive 2 no. 171 (old 168), DECODE R3754: a one-page letter of Florence’s envoy to Count Guidantonio da Montefeltro, in fast Florentine cursive with about twenty runs of cipher. The abbé Gabbrielli rebuilt the key in 1863 from a few words he glossed on this letter and three others; Meister printed his table in 1902. The letter itself was never printed. Gabbrielli’s key was applied, and extended from his own glosses over the cipher runs of this letter and of the sibling letters nos. 21, 91 and 92 (DECODE R3755–R3757). With the extended key, 97 of the 99 cipher tokens are deciphered, 94 of them at grade H or M. No fuller key was found in Gabbrielli’s volume, in print or on DECODE. The letter is still decoded, not read: the clear Italian around the runs is a first-pass reading with gaps in nearly every sentence, so the whole could not be built into sentences and translated. A re-read of the clear text on 23 October filled much of the middle of the letter and found its date line, but the opening, line 9 and the close still do not hold (11 of 23 sentences clean). Where Archivio di Stato di Firenze, Dieci di Balía, Responsive 2 no. 171; DECODE R3754, listed as “Non-decrypted”. The cipher An alphabet with two or three signs per letter, eighteen nulls and thirty word signs, plus six clear cover words. How it was read Gabbrielli’s 1863 key (printed by Meister, 1902) was applied and extended from the siblings’ glosses, adding six certain and fourteen probable letter values. What it says The Count of Urbino calls his wife “after all a woman, and suspicious”; her relatives and the citizens were to bind themselves to his wishes in secret. The letter opens “Magnifici potenti Signori miei” and is signed “Vostro servidore Galeotto de Fibindacci”. Its foot, never transcribed before 23 October 2026, reads “[?In] Castello, a dì viij di settembre”, with no year; the dating to early 1425 below rests on the siblings and is not confirmed by it. Its siblings in the same hand, filza 3 nos. 91 and 92, are dated at Urbino on 17 and 28 February, in the Florentine year 1424, that is 1425. Guasti’s edition of the Commissioni di Rinaldo degli Albizzi shows the Dieci sending Galeotto to the Count of Urbino in September 1423, and prints a later clear letter of his from Urbino of 28 August 1425. “Madonna” is the Countess, Caterina Colonna, niece of Pope Martin V, who married Guidantonio in 1424 and reached Urbino on 4 March 1424. The key is page 1 of Gabbrielli’s volume Chiavi delle cifre delle lettere ai Dieci di Balía dal 1424 al 1530 , compiled in 1863–64. The volume is on the Ilardi microfilm at Yale, reel 58, and Meister printed page 1 in Die Anfänge der modernen diplomatischen Geheimschrift (1902), p. 50. It is headed “Cifra di Galeotto Fibindacci da Ricasoli, carteggio dei X di Balía, an. 1424”. It gives an alphabet with two or three signs for most letters, eighteen nulls, and a nomenclator of thirty word signs such as Conte d’Urbino , Duca di Milano , Malatesta , fanti and mille . It also lists six cover words written in clear: Giovanni for the Dieci, Andrea for Galeotto, trombetta for an ambassador, che for horse, con for war and tagliato for loss. Gabbrielli marked the letters he worked from in the margin: filza 1 nos. 163 and 165, filza 2 no. 72 and filza 3 nos. 21, 91 and 92. His interlinear glosses on no. 171 cover a dozen words: paolo , di madona , cintadini , il conte , sarrem andino , a laog. , ambasciatore , puro femina e sospettosa , el conte d’Urbino , cavalli , parenti and madonna . Several of these sit over runs far longer than the gloss, and two of them are misreadings.

Each run was cut from the deskewed scan at four to five times magnification and transcribed sign by sign. The signs were then matched against Gabbrielli’s table and his gloss. Capitals are the decoded text. “Madonna è pure femina e sospetosa” The run after “perché dice che”, with Gabbrielli’s gloss above. It continues onto the next line. Image: Archivio di Stato di Firenze, Dieci di Balía, Responsive 2 no. 171, via DECODE R3754. The clear text runs: “… che […] Giovanni [i Dieci] mandasse trombetta [ambasciatore], perché dice che”. Thirty signs follow. MADONNA is seven signs, all in Gabbrielli’s table. PURE is P, U, R, E from his table with a feathered null after the P. FEMINA is six signs, all his. E is his. Two signs follow that have no value (section 05). SOSPETOSA is nine signs. The two O signs in it stand exactly five places apart, as the two O’s of s-o-spet-o-sa do, and that fixes the alignment. Gabbrielli glossed the whole phrase but never tabulated the signs in it. The sentence reads: “because he [the Count] says that Madonna is, after all, a woman, and suspicious”. “Parenti e citadini” The run before “promettessono e obligassensi”, glossed parenti and cintadini . Image: Archivio di Stato di Firenze, Dieci di Balía, Responsive 2 no. 171, via DECODE R3754. The run has seven signs and then eight. Gabbrielli’s values give P, A, R, E, I, T and D; the others are values recovered from the sibling glosses (9 = N, ɣ = A) or fixed by position (two light strokes = T, ᴗ = C, # = I). The two words are PARENTI and CITADINI, one letter per sign. The sentence reads: “et segretamente MADONNA et PARENTI [e] CITADINI promettessono e obligassensi che, non obstante [ELLA?] dicesse e volesse el [?contrario], essi farebbono quello volesse [IL CONTE]”. In English: Madonna’s relatives and the citizens should secretly promise and bind themselves that, whatever she might say or want to the contrary, they would do what the Count wished. “Acomandino a lo…” Gabbrielli glossed this run sarrem andino and the next word a laog. The first sign is on his own list of nulls. The next ten are A C O M A N D I N O by his table and by the value +o = O, which the siblings confirm. The last three are A L O, and the clear text continues. The 18 September reading took the last sign for I (“a lui”); at three times magnification it is Gabbrielli’s O. The clause is “Ma prosetto che no lo pare che [IL PAPA?] sia [?atento], S'ACOMANDINO A LO[…]” (re-read on 23 October 2026), “that it does not seem to him that the Pope is attentive; that they commend themselves to […]”.

This is a working text, re-read on 23 October 2026 on crops that follow the slope of the lines (they fall about 3% to the right, which had split the old strips): texts/no171_reading.md , with an English translation. The clear hand is fast; [?word] marks a doubtful word, […] an unread place. Cipher is given in capitals and word signs in brackets. Magnifici potenti Signori miei. Io so stato qui [?mostrado] pel tempo cattivo della piena grande che fu […] avere fatto questa mia. Sentito, PAVOLO venne a vedermi e parlato [?seco] d'una cosa e dell'altra, che stemo insieme più che un'ora, scoprendo l'intentione DI MADONN[A] et CINTADINI e [?persone] […] [IL CONTE]. Ma prosetto che no lo pare che [IL PAPA?] sia [?atento], S'ACOMANDINO A LO[…]; sono stati così parechi [?strani] parlari. Ma parebbe fusse più utile che qualunche [?come] [?privata] persona fusse a motivare de' ragionamenti, che […] Giovanni [i Dieci] mandasse trombetta [ambasciatore], perché dice che MADONNA [è] PURE FEMINA E […] SOSPETOSA, pure [?vedendosi] coperto, se sapere a fare. [?Sperra] et bene, ma non sta [?ancora] coperto. Et anno sospetto di questo [CONTE D'URBINO]; detto non credo bisogni, ma pure delle cose perché [?ne dee] avere sospetto. O detto molto [?grave], [?chiarigliene] e [?ancho] [?strignerlo]. El modo gli parebbe: farebbe dimostrare fare [?quanti] [FANTI] et quarche che [cavalli], e segretamente [DIECI] dessi loro opera che [?metassono]; et segretamente MADONNA et PARENTI [e] CITADINI promettessono e obligassensi che, non obstante [ELLA?] dicesse e volesse el [?contrario], essi farebbono quello volesse [IL CONTE]. E ragionamenti furono assai e lungo. […] [?scriverò] tutto conchiudendo se [?sarà] [?secondo] quello altri [?nostra], ma parmi volesse andasse più segreta. Racomandomi alla Signoria vostra. [?In] Castello, a dì viij di settembre. Vostro servidore Galeotto de Fibindacci da Ricasoli. Galeotto, held up by the weather of a great flood, reports an hour’s talk with Paolo, who came to see him, about the intentions of the Countess and the citizens; it does not seem that the Pope is attentive, and some party is to commend itself to someone. He thinks it more useful that someone open the talks as a private person than that the Dieci send an ambassador, because the Count distrusts his wife: “Madonna is after all a woman, and […] suspicious”. Foot and horse are to be engaged quietly, with the Dieci giving them work. Her relatives and the citizens are to bind themselves, in secret, to follow the Count whatever she says. He ends that the business should be kept more secret.

Was a fuller key already available? No. Gabbrielli’s volume has a second key for a Fibindacci in 1424 (key no. 2, “Karolus commissarius”), but it belongs to another sender and gives other values to the shared shapes (+o = B, 6 = S, ∧ = H), which the glossed words here contradict. His keys nos. 3 and 4 are Latin syllabic nomenclators. Meister and Somogyi reproduce key no. 1 only. DECODE holds Gabbrielli’s volume as key records R5687–R5698 (the 1424 frames are R5687–R5690); none is linked to R3754–R3757 and none goes beyond key no. 1. What the siblings add. Gabbrielli glossed most cipher runs of nos. 21, 91 and 92, but tabulated only some of the signs under them. Forty glossed runs were transcribed sign by sign and matched letter for letter with the gloss: la novella della rotta , andarono , tante e tali , non contenterà mai , venuta a Imola , Modigliana twice, d’Oriuolo , promettere , Filippo , mandato , salvo condotto , venne and the word signs for Malatesta, the Duke, Galeotto, Pandolfo, Carlo, the Count, the Dieci and fiorini . Eleven runs could not be matched (faint gloss, blots). The result, with the evidence for each value, is the file key_extended.md . Six new letter values are certain , each spelled out under a gloss: ɣ = A, a 5-shape with a cross-stroke = M, 9 = N (Gabbrielli has B), +o = O, a π with a hooked leg = O, and an open 4 with a long bar = T. Fourteen more are probable , among them three signs with two values (ᴗ = D and C, # = L and I, π = F and S), each resting on one letter so far. Nulls. q is a null, as Gabbrielli has it; ɣ is a variant A, not a null; a heavy filled triangle is a null (in andaro▼no and madon▼na ). His null “o+” (circle then cross) is a different sign from +o (cross then circle), which is O. Nomenclator. A three-stroke sign is pace ; β, Gabbrielli’s con , also enciphers the syllable con inside a word (SALVOβDOTTO). Corrections to the tabulation of 18 September. Rereading the film at full size shows that ▽ is under E in Gabbrielli’s table, and that the cross over a small circle (T), the 8 with a ring below (S) and the ⊓ with a stem (I) are his own signs, not new ones. All 99 cipher tokens were transcribed again from three-times crops and deciphered with the extended key (token list cipher171.tsv ). 72 values come from Gabbrielli’s table, 16 from the recovered values, 5 are nomenclator entries and 4 rest on context. The changes are small: the name is spelled PAVOLO; the Count’s word sign stands three times; the Dieci’s word sign stands on line 11; “a lui” becomes A LO…; the heavy pair on line 4 is a null and one word sign.

The word sign before “sia” (a box with a bar, after a heavy null) is not in Gabbrielli’s nomenclator. He wrote over it a small p with a looped flourish, the usual abbreviation for Papa . The Countess is the Pope’s niece, so “the Pope” fits. Grade I. One single word sign , before “dicesse”, is given the value ella from context alone. Grade I. Two signs before SOSPETOSA , after the E, have no value: an open 4 with a long bar (T in the siblings) and ψ (P by the key). “e t[ro]p[o] sospetosa” would fit, but one occurrence with no gloss cannot fix it. The word sospetosa is not affected. PAVOLO is deciphered cleanly; who he is stays open. He may be messer Paolo da Capranica, whom a Florentine cover list of 1424 calls “Capra”. The clear text : about a dozen words of the opening (lines 1–4), of “O detto …” (line 9) and of the close (lines 12–13) stay doubtful after the re-read of 23 October 2026: the mercantile cursive is fast and faded at the resolution of the DECODE image. Six cipher letters rest on look-alike readings. The date : the foot gives “a dì viij di settembre” and a doubtful “[?In] Castello”, but no year. The key is still partial. B, H and Q have no values beyond Gabbrielli’s, eleven sibling runs are not aligned, and about fifteen glossed runs of no. 92 are not yet transcribed. The three siblings have not been deciphered end to end. The extended table is queued for DECODE as a key derived from Gabbrielli’s (R5687–R5690), with its grades.

Their key was applied here to a fresh transcription of one page and reproduces their plaintext; the date is 15 May 1637. 503 · 67 4 96 82 30 9 30 94 7 8 13 30 70 61 20 → dem 503 ZUWIEDER GEWESEN Kassel → Stockholm · numerical homophonic cipher with code numbers · 15 May 1637 Sigismund Heusner von Wandersleben to Axel Oxenstierna, Kassel, 15 May 1637 to Axel Oxenstierna Go to the transcriptions ↓ Riksarkivet, Stockholm: a letter of five pages from the Swedish commissary-general Sigismund Heusner von Wandersleben to the chancellor, catalogued here twice, as DECODE R4332 (“partly solved”) and R3816 (“not solved”). Both records are one letter. Michelle Waldispühl and Nils Kopal recovered the key and published the decipherment in 2024. Their key was applied here to a fresh transcription of one page and reproduces their plaintext. One letter, in clear German with ciphered words and phrases. Where Catalogue entries 208 and 209, DECODE R3816 and R4332. The three scans are byte for byte the same, pages 2 and 3 in the other order, so they are one letter. The cipher A numerical homophonic alphabet for words and phrases, with three-digit numbers for names and places. How it was read R4332 carries the key and full plaintext of Michelle Waldispühl and Nils Kopal (HistoCrypt 2024). Applied to a new transcription of one page of figures, their key gives their plaintext, except for three slips in the new transcription. Still open What they left open: some sixteen code numbers. Credit Waldispühl and Kopal, HistoCrypt 2024: the deciphered text is theirs.

DECODE R4332 image 1 (letter page 2), top: dem 503 · 67·4·96·82·30·9·30·94·7·8·13·30·70·61·20 = zuwieder gewesen , then vnd die 764 and übergeben in figures. Image: Riksarkivet, Stockholm, Heusner to Oxenstierna 1637, letter p. 2, via DECODE R4332 (image 1). The letter is written in clear German, and the sensitive words and phrases are in figures separated by points. The alphabet has 22 letters with one to eight values each: E has eight (8, 30, 31, 61, 100, 110, 120, 200) and H six, while K and P have one each. The values run from 2 to 202, and nothing marks word divisions inside a run. Three-digit numbers from 147 to 808 stand for persons and places. The key file on the record lists 47 under both O and U. The plaintext is Waldispühl and Kopal’s. Heusner has fallen out with Field Marshal Banér and, warned about Franz Heinrich of Saxe-Lauenburg “wegen der Hamburger sache”, has withdrawn to 164. The Kassel court has turned away from Sweden: So erfahre ich aber das HERR UND KNECHT SEHR GEENDERT UND AM GANZEN HOFE AUSSER DER 503. NICHT EINER MEHR UFFRECHT SCHWEDISCH, IA DER 628. FAUORISIRET vnd CARESSIRET alzo die so in SEINEM ABWESEN dem 503. ZUWIEDER GEWESEN vnd die 764. UBERGEBEN wollen A campaign is talked of, “WOHIN IST STILL”, but the force is not there. Then comes the secret war material: Man hat hier in der aller größen geheimb etlich 385. CENTNER METALLISCHE SPEISSE ZUSAMMEN GESCHMELZET vnd solche verdecket auf 147 geführet, daselbst etliche schon hierzu gemachte STUCKE ZU TAUSCHEN Johan von Uffeln is to be commandant of 571, and Gunterot is to take the field. The letter ends “CASSEL den 15. May 1637”.

The figures on letter page 2 (259 tokens with the clear-text breaks) were transcribed from the scan without using the published plaintext. The published homophone table turns them into ZUWIEDER GEWESEN … UBERGEBEN … NEGOCIIREN … FORCE … BASTANT … AUS DEM LANDT ZU TREIBEN … BESTALLUNG … GELDER … GROSSES HERANTZ … RECHT IM DIRECTORIO FASSEN, the published decipherment. Three single figures differ (SOHL for SOLL, FEOD for FELD, CLAM for CLAR), and each is a slip in the new transcription.

The codes 147, 164, 184, 255, 289, 321, 384, 385, 503, 571, 617, 628, 703, 708, 747 and 764, left as numbers by Waldispühl and Kopal. 747 is in their plaintext but not in their key file. From context alone, 503 is the one person at the court still loyal to Sweden, who “SOLL IN DAS FELD”, most likely Landgrave Wilhelm V of Hesse-Kassel (grade M). 147 is where the guns are cast, and 764 a place some wanted to surrender. The Hessian correspondence of 1637 would settle these.

Two letters of an Este agent in Hungary in a two-tier cipher of graphic signs (DECODE R1126, R1127, catalogued as ‘Jantini’); not solved. The cipher was transcribed and tried ciphertext-only and with Caprile’s 1519 values; controls show this syllabic system with word codes cannot be solved without a key or crib. … per la mandata dil duca Lorezo in Franza m/n L/m [f] m/m s/7 d/7 l/n c/n [&] … the clear text breaks into the two-tier signs and stays in them for two pages Buda and Eger → the Este court · two-tier cipher of graphic signs (syllabic family) · 1517–1518 Benedetto Fantini, Buda and Eger, 1517–1518 Go to the full text ↓ Archivio di Stato di Modena, Ambasciatori, Ungheria b. 4, “Benedetto Fantini” nos. 5 and 6 (Vestigia 1849, 1851; DECODE R1126, R1127, where the writer appears as “Benedetto Jantini”). Two letters of a Ferrarese in Cardinal Ippolito d’Este’s household in Hungary, one with two full pages of cipher. The cipher was transcribed column by column and tried from the ciphertext alone and with the values of the only related key, Caprile’s of 1519. It was not deciphered. No earlier decipherment, clear copy or key is known. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained · On the map With Brice Dudout (solution) not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The document Ciphered letters of Benedetto Fantini (catalogued as “Jantini”), Ferrara, 1517–18. Vestigia has the whole file, nos. 1–7 (1515–1518); only nos. 5 and 6 carry cipher. Where Two DECODE records catalogued “partially decrypted”, which reflects the clear passages. None of the seven items has a decipherment, clear copy or gloss. The cipher Same family as Giuliano Caprile’s 1519 letters from the household: a base stroke with a small sign above, plus bracket signs. Caprile’s letter of 1 May 1519 and its 1882 decipherment show it to be syllabic: small sign for the consonant, base for the vowel, brackets for whole syllables. How it was tried Fantini’s two cipher pages (1,370 columns) were run through a syllabary solver (simulated annealing). It recovers a control text of the same length and structure even with a tenth of its signs corrupted, but on Fantini produces no Italian, and Caprile’s values make the fit worse. Still open The text. It needs a key or decipherment from the Este chancery, or a paired letter in Fantini’s own key.

R1126 p. 1: the clear opening (“Da Buda … scripsi a V. S. Ill.ma … il negotio dla restitution de Modena et Regio per la mandata dil duca Lorezo in Franza”) and the start of the cipher. Image: Archivio di Stato di Modena, Fantini letter (R1126 p. 1), via DECODE R1126. DECODE ASMo no. Date, place Cipher R1126 Fantini no. 5 (Vestigia 1849) [spring 1518?], Buda. Vestigia and DECODE give “1517”, the file year p. 1 after six clear lines (18 lines) and all of p. 2 (25 lines): 1,370 columns; pp. 3–6 clear R1127 Fantini no. 6 (Vestigia 1851) 6 March 1518, Eger (“Agria”) five short lines, about 46 columns, in a torn and faded leaf The letters are addressed to a lord styled “Vostra Signoria Illustrissima” and “Vostra Eccellenza”, most likely Duke Alfonso I. The clear opening of no. 5 asks for news of the restitution of Modena and Reggio and of Lorenzo de’ Medici’s journey to France. The clear pages 3–6 report the Hungarian diet and the governors appointed around the young Louis II. They continue the letter; they are not a decipherment. Fantini’s other letters (nos. 1–4 and 7, 1515–1518) are in clear.

Each unit is a base stroke written on the line (shapes like 7, m, n, g, y, 4, t, a) with a small sign written above it (o, 2, 1, b, &, c, L, s, d, 9 …), or an L-shaped bracket enclosing a small sign. The transcription ( t1126.txt ) counts 1,370 columns: 167 distinct forms, 299 of them brackets (22%) with 22 different inner signs. The commonest columns are 2/7 (77), -/7 (63), o/7 (60), -/y (47), -/g (46) and &/m (44). Caprile’s letters of 1519 use the same kind of script. His letter of 1 May 1519 (DECODE R1130) mixes clear sentences with short cipher runs, and the 1882 archivist’s decipherment (Vestigia 1860, “4c”) covers them. Aligned by hand, the runs decrypt as syllables. intertenere is seven columns, y/7 9/7 [y] c/7 [y] z/m [m]: i, n, te, r, te, ne, re. The same opening recurs in intertenerlo and in che termine . oratore is o [ra] [to] [re], twice. In that key base 7 carries no vowel, m gives e and n gives o. Tested on stretches not used to build it, the values placed 16 of 18 letters in the true text, against 8.1 on average for shuffled text.

Siblings, clear pages, print. All seven Fantini letters on Vestigia. Bonzagni’s letters of 1512–14, the other Este–Hungary cipher, use a different, simple alphabet. DECODE has no key record from Modena for 1490–1540, and nothing turned up in print. Caprile’s key. Three pairings with the 1882 decipherments. R1131 is water-stained, and its alignment was no better than shuffled controls. R1134’s supposed interlinear decipherment is a second letter in clear with cipher insertions. R1130 gave the syllabic structure and about twenty values. A syllabary annealer ( syl_anneal.py : consonant for each upper sign, vowel for each base, a syllable for each bracket, scored with a sixteenth-century Italian 5-gram model). On a control of 2,200 letters from sixteenth-century Italian, enciphered in the same structure with two homophones per consonant, it recovers the text almost word for word once three base values are fixed. It still does so with 10% of the signs corrupted. On Fantini , eight restarts of 150,000 moves each, on the raw transcription and with the frequent pairs -/7 -/y and -/7 -/g merged as ligatures. The result is Italian-looking syllable salad that differs from restart to restart, scoring −2.37 per letter against −1.77 for the control’s true key. Seeding Caprile’s values drops the score from about −140 to −1,250. The solver recovers the syllabic control at this length and noise, so the search itself is sound. A later check read Fantini’s roughly 290 brackets as word codes, as they are in Caprile’s letter R1133. A control of that shape recovers only 7% of its text, so a ciphertext-only attack cannot decipher this letter at any transcription quality. Fantini’s key is not Caprile’s.

A key or decipherment in the Este chancery (ASMo, Cancelleria, Cifrari), or a letter to or from Fantini with its decipherment. A better image of R1126 from ASMo for the faint upper signs. Page 1 was transcribed twice (90% agreement) and page 2 three times, with an estimated error of 2–3%; the pairing of small signs to bases is sometimes doubtful. R1127 is too short and too damaged to attack on its own.

Words in [ ] are restored from the period clear copy on pp. 3-4; (?) marks a doubtful phrase; … an unread stretch. … of which I very much doubt, the term having passed without my hearing anything from there. I have nothing to report to Your Lordship, except that this kingdom goes on in its usual disorders, and at the last diet, which lasted so long, nothing good or stable was concluded. Eight lords were appointed to govern the King of Hungary and the kingdom during His Majesty's youth; four of them, that is two spiritual and two secular, were always to stay at court, dividing the time so that each should have his turn, to dispatch the business arising from day to day without waiting for the diet, as has been done until now; and I was one of the first named. But I believe this order will not be kept, because it would be a very great expense to each of the said eight, and each gladly avoids it, as did the Cardinal of Esztergom (Strigonio) and the lord palatine, who govern everything so as to do as they please. They do not care that the matter goes forward, because if the others stayed at court they would want to do as they please too; and the officials and ministers of the King, who have all been placed by means of the said two lords and are at their pleasure, could no longer obey the said two as they do now, and so little by little the great authority of the said [Cardinal] of Esztergom and of the palatine would be taken away. It had been ordered that the lords and the whole kingdom should impose on their subjects a levy of one ducat per hearth for the benefit of the King and kingdom, because the lords now … their life, and of it they are very sparing (?), as is known, and the poor King is dying of hunger. The counties, that is the nobility, will not consent to this payment by their subjects; they have gathered and decided that every county send four nobles, in the midst of another of theirs (?), for the next feast of St James, where they say they will summon these lords to make them understand their mind. This could easily stir up a new and dangerous fire in this kingdom, which God forbid. … we must go back to Buda, and each must bring with him all his men-at-arms, who are unanimously to be sent against the Turks, which will be a very great expense for all without any fruit. I have strongly dissuaded this, in general to all at the diet and in particular to each one individually, as it seems to me a very dangerous thing, with nothing to be gained, since these troops are sent only to make raids, which they will do when they find the enemy unprepared, otherwise not; and when they did, one must fear for certain that the Turks would make some effort with troops to defend themselves, and would come to the frontiers at a time when our men …

Where An eighteenth-century copy, BnF Clairambault 331 f. 157. The copyist omitted a page and three lines of the original cipher; they are outside the percentage. The cipher A letter substitution in which a dot over a sign makes it a different letter. How it was read Key recovered from the ciphertext alone after a new transcription that kept the dots and separated straight strokes from curved numerals. No key, decipherment or parallel text was found. A token audit counts 386 (96.0%) as coherent Italian after thirteen listed emendations. What it says Wolsey’s wealth “in denari contanti”, gold and silver vessels and household goods; the last passage names Winchester, St Albans and York. Five signs once taken for clear “in summa” give un ann , completing un anno . Still open Three rare signs and a financial junction. All values are inferred; there is no contemporary key to check them against.

The copy's heading dates a letter to the king and its accompanying letter for the Grand Master to 15 March 1530. The sender is attributed to Giovan Gioacchino da Passano, the French agent in London; this is not a decrypted signature. The predominantly clear Italian body discusses English affairs and recovering payments and quittances from Wolsey. The cipher account precedes the royal letter's valediction. There are sixteen physical cipher lines: an introduction, six short listed items, and a longer final financial passage. Seven amounts stand in the right margin. The earlier description of “nine entries” came from provisional transcription blocks and should not be mistaken for the manuscript's line count. The reference at the head appears to be “Vol. 79, fol. 78”; its modern shelfmark has not been established. The recto account. Dotted and undotted signs are different letters; the clear amounts do not supply a decipherment. BnF, Clairambault 331 f. 157r, Gallica. Spacing, punctuation and u/v display are editorial. All key values are I (inferred); none is taken from a contemporary key or parallel plaintext. M marks uncertainty. The three labels below preserve signs that are not letters of the alphabet: [D] is identified below from context as the Cardinal, [Q] as the King, and [S2] may be a royal title. These context readings are not counted as decoded words. Sapera vostra magesta che questo [S2] de gli beni del [D], per quanto si dice, son pervenuti circa [clear amount] , in l'infrascrite par[u?]tite, cioe: The opening expressly qualifies its report: “according to what people say.” The source has parutite ; partite is likely intended, but the extra stroke is retained as a doubt. No missing preposition or royal title is silently supplied. Recovered entry Established sense Clear numeral component In denari contanti Ready cash CL In crediti de so [D] per [Q] interditi et poi levati Credits; restriction and subsequent recovery, with agency unresolved L Per gli fruti de un anno de lo intrate de so [D] One year's revenues; the reference to [D] remains abbreviated or uncertain LX In baghe circa Probably jewels or rings, approximately XX In vasele d'oro et d'argento Gold and silver vessels CCL In supelectili de casa per el meno Household furnishings, at least CC The amounts in the right margin are written as a Roman numeral, a raised sign like a small 9, and Scuti : CL, L, LX, XX, CCL and CC here, XX after the final passage. The raised sign stands for m , thousands: the total at the foot is DCCL with M written over it, the introduction’s round figure is DCCC with m over it, and the seven components add up to exactly DCCL. Context readings of the three signs (30 September 2026). [D] occurs four times, always where a masculine person is named: de gli beni del [D] , crediti de so [D] , intrate de so [D] , and al deto [D] insieme con lo arcivescoato de Diorch . The clear text a few lines above the cipher speaks of “el predetto Cardinale”, and al deto [D] echoes it; the account deals with Winchester, St Albans and York, the three benefices Wolsey held until February 1530, when he kept York and gave up the other two. [D] is taken as [Cardinale] , grade I. [Q] occurs twice: the credits were per [Q] interditi et poi levati , and after the deduction for the Cardinal havera [Q] per ano circa XX[m] scuti . The XX of that last clause is one of the seven sums that make up the DCCL gathered in by questo [S2] , so [Q] is the party that received the goods: [il Re] , Henry VIII, grade I. [S2] (once, “questo [S2]”) is the cipher sign for a with a raised stroke; questo [Re] or questo [Signor] (the copyist writes a raised r in the same way in S.ria ) both fit, and it is left open. The literal so before [D] is kept; it may be the northern so , “his”. With these readings the first part of the account runs without a gap: … de gli beni del [Cardinale], per quanto si dice, son pervenuti circa DCCC[m] scuti in l'infrascrite partite, cioe: in denari contanti CL[m] scuti; in crediti de so [Cardinale] per [il Re] interditi et poi levati L[m] scuti; per gli fruti de un anno de lo intrate de so [Cardinale] LX[m] scuti; in baghe circa XX[m] scuti; in vasele d'oro et d'argento CCL[m] scuti; in supelectili de casa per el meno CC[m] scuti. “… of the goods of the [Cardinal], as it is said, about 800 [thousand] scudi have come in, in the items below, namely: in ready money, 150 [thousand] scudi; in credits of the [Cardinal], sequestered by [the King] and then collected, 50 [thousand]; for the fruits of one year of the revenues of the [Cardinal], 60 [thousand]; in jewels, about 20 [thousand]; in gold and silver plate, 250 [thousand]; in household furnishings, at least 200 [thousand] scudi.” The sums stand in the margin in clear; partite is the copy’s parutite without its extra stroke. The final passage continues across the verso. Its emended letter reading is: Per l'intrate del vescoato de Vinchiestri et abadia de sancto Albano, rebatuti [stacked clear notation, scuti] dese intrato al deto [D] insieme con lo arcivescoato de Diorch, asignati et ordinati, havera [Q] per ano circa [XX + abbreviation, scuti] . Winchester, St Albans and York are identifiable. Rebatuti means deducted; the signs do not support restituti , restored. The literal dese is an attested regional word for ten, but its connection with the stacked monetary notation and intrato is not secure. The passage concerns revenues, a deduction, and assigned annual income; a precise translation of who receives which sum would exceed the evidence. The final account passage and the explicit omission notice. BnF, Clairambault 331 f. 157v, Gallica. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, Clairambault 331, via Gallica. The seven right-margin Roman components sum exactly: CL + L + LX + XX + CCL + CC + XX = DCCL (750). The apparent thousand multipliers suggest 750,000 scudi, compared with the introduction's approximate 800,000. This scale remains an interpretation of the notation. The inline stacked amount is not an eighth right-margin entry; its role is unsettled. The list mixes assets and revenues.

The earlier transcription merged significant dots and inconsistently classified numeral-like strokes. Several substitution searches therefore failed, although their synthetic controls worked. A fresh dotted inventory of 397 signs and 28 aliases gave connected Italian under a seeded many-to-one four-gram annealer. A frequency penalty was necessary: without it the model preferred repeated i . The shared model was it-cinquecento ; no target plaintext was supplied. The recurring distinctions include 3=i / 3d=d , 7=o / 7d=p , 8=i / 8d=q , 9=o / 9d=t , and S=a / Sd=g . The suffix d marks the dot; it is part of the same cipher sign. Linguistic extension and image checking established further values. Some apparent homophones may instead be the copyist's variants. Recognizing 1 m S m m 7 as un anno restored five previously excluded cipher signs. The final 402-token inventory has IC 0.0602. It happens to equal the old transcription's token count but differs in segmentation and sign classes. The independent-looking place names, repeated words, ordinary Italian clauses and sum of the numeral components provide internal checks. They do not amount to an independent contemporary decipherment.

Three rare sign types: D four times, Q twice, S2 once. D = the Cardinal and Q = the King are context readings (grade I, above), not key values; S2 is open between a royal title and Signor . The two so [D] expressions, the extra stroke in parutite , and the four-letter dese financial junction. These nine additional tokens are excluded from coherent coverage. Thirteen local contextual emendations, mostly misplaced or missing dots, are individually listed in the key and token audit. They are included in the 96.0% measure; the literal, uncorrected output is also supplied. A page and three lines of original cipher, expressly omitted by the historical copyist. No token count or decipherment is available. The extent figures apply to the surviving account only. All sixteen extant lines and every residual occurrence were rechecked. The nearby cipher and the Ferrara Passano/Sormano material have different inventories. No matching key or complete parallel copy was found. The related printed Passano report, Letters and Papers IV no. 6307, is dated 4 April 1530 and cannot validate this March account. An original or independent complete copy is the next evidence needed; further confident expansion from this short text alone would be conjecture. The exact audit is 395/402 assigned, 386/402 coherent, 16 M tokens, 13 emendations . These are reproducible counts of editorial judgments; the token accuracy is not independently known. Read on 23 September 2026. The heading dates the copy 15 March 1530; the sender is attributed to Giovan Gioacchino da Passano. The body addresses Francis I. The page also contains a subsequent letter for the Grand Master. **This is a reconstructed reading, with explicit gaps and emendations, not a contemporary decipherment.** The account is substantially read; it is not a claim to have recovered the omitted continuation or every word. Run `python targets/joachim1530/decode.py` to regenerate the literal reading, the edited unspaced reading, the 402-row audit, and the coverage figures. ## Conventions and coverage - `[S2]`, `[D]`, `[Q]` preserve three rare signs whose expansions are not established. `[D]` probably refers to Wolsey; `[S2]` may be a royal title. These contextual identifications are **not** entered as solved key values. - Italicized editorial comments and punctuation are not encrypted words. Spacing below is editorial. u/v is displayed as v where appropriate; the decoder retains u. - All established values are **I**, inferred from the ciphertext; none is H (historical key) or C (independent known plaintext). **M** marks residual uncertainty. Thirteen local substitutions are listed by exact line and position in `key.json` and `reading_tokens.tsv`; most concern displaced or missing dots. - 402 observed tokens, 28 aliases; **395/402 assigned (98.26%)**, **386/402 coherent on the conservative audit (96.02%)**. The 16 excluded tokens comprise seven rare-sign occurrences, four letters in the two `so [D]` expressions, the four-letter `dese` financial junction, and one apparent extra stroke in `parutite`. This is an editorial measure, not an independently measured cryptanalytic accuracy. The 13 emendations are included in coherent coverage and exposed individually. - The final 402 count is coincidentally the same as the old transcription's count. It is a different segmentation and inventory. The first fresh dotted transcription had 397 tokens; recognizing `1 m S m m` as encrypted `un ann` added five. The old file had wrongly called it clear “in summa.” ## Italian reading, in manuscript order **Introduction, f. 157r, lines 1–3** > Sapera vostra magesta che questo [S2] de gli beni del > [D], per quanto si dice, son pervenuti circa **[clear amount: m over DCCC, scuti]**, > in l'infrascrite par[u?]tite, cioe: The literal third line has `parutite`; *partite* is the likely intended word, but the extra stroke is kept outside the coherent count. The opening's syntax and royal-title expansion are not silently repaired by supplying an “a” or a verb. The gist is a report, expressly qualified by “per quanto si dice,” about goods associated with the person `[D]`. | Entry | Edited Italian | Clear numeral component | |---|---|---| | 1 | In denari contanti | CL, followed by a raised abbreviation, scuti | | 2 | In crediti de so [D] per [Q] interditi et poi levati | L, raised abbreviation, scuti | | 3 | Per gli fruti de un anno de lo intrate de so [D] | LX, raised abbreviation, scuti | | 4 | In baghe circa | XX, raised abbreviation, scuti | | 5 | In vasele d'oro et d'argento | CCL, raised abbreviation, scuti | | 6 | In supelectili de casa per el meno | CC, raised abbreviation, scuti | `so [D]` is literal; an abbreviated reference to the person is plausible but not expanded. `baghe` is kept as written, tentatively jewels/rings in this asset list. `vasele` means vessels and `supelectili` household furnishings. `per el meno` is “at least.” `interditi` is the recovered word; the precise legal meaning and agency of `[Q]` remain unsettled. **Final passage, f. 157v, lines 2–6** > Per l'intrate del vescoato de Vinchiestri et abadia de sancto Albano, rebatuti > **[clear stacked m/m-like notation, scuti]** dese intrato al deto [D] insieme > con lo arcivescoato de Diorch, asignati et ordinati, havera [Q] per ano circa > **[XX + raised abbreviation, scuti].** The toponyms identify Winchester, St Albans and York. *Rebatuti* (“deducted”) is supported; the earlier tempting *restituti* (“restored”) is **not** the recovered word. `de Diorch` is retained, not silently changed to `de Iorch`. `asignati` is the spelling with one s. The first four letters on the middle line decode literally `dese`; this is an attested regional word for “ten,” but its attachment to the stacked notation and following `intrato` is not settled here. No precise deduction or allocation is asserted in translation. **Bottom total:** a large M above `DCCL . Scuti`, introduced by a separate sum mark. The seven right-margin numeral components add correctly: CL + L + LX + XX + CCL + CC + XX = DCCL, or 150 + 50 + 60 + 20 + 250 + 200 + 20 = 750. Their apparent thousand multipliers suggest 750,000 scudi, versus the introduction's approximate 800,000; that scale remains an editorial interpretation of the financial notation. The inline stacked notation is not an eighth right-margin item. The list mixes property and revenue descriptions, so it must not be represented as a modern audited balance sheet. ## English rendering of the established sense Your Majesty will learn that, according to what people say, goods of `[D, probably the Cardinal]` have come to the amount written, in the following items: ready cash; credits, with an unresolved reference to their restriction and subsequent recovery; one year's income; jewels or rings; gold and silver vessels; and household furnishings, “at least” the amount stated. The final passage concerns the revenues of Winchester and the abbey of St Albans, a deduction whose numerical wording remains uncertain, and income assigned or ordered together with the archbishopric of York. It ends with what `[Q]` will have annually. The rare signs are left visible because substituting “king,” “cardinal,” or “he” at every occurrence would give an unwarrantedly definite account of the transfers. ## Context readings of [D], [Q], [S2] and the margin sums (30 September 2026) Added for George Lasry's quotation list. The benefices named (Winchester, St Albans, York) are Wolsey's; in February 1530 he kept York and gave up the other two, which is what the final passage describes. - **[Q] = [il Re].** Two places: "per [Q] interditi et poi levati" and "havera [Q] per ano circa XX[m] scuti". Six letters of João IV to his ambassador in Paris, copied into the embassy letter-book (ANTT Manuscritos da Livraria 1017) with passages in cipher. Two substitution alphabets were rebuilt from clear text in the same volume: clear copies of three 1642 letters, and a leaf listing two 1645 passages in clear. The 1642 letters concern the captive Infante D. Duarte and Richelieu’s death; the 1644 letter, which had no decipherment, keeps the marriages of Prince Teodósio and the Infantas secret. 398 of 438 cipher words read; the 1643 runs are illegible at the scan resolution. o pagetfofc fu aEℓinc fuz fxotnc zcx zxanu ozofu … a liberdade do Infante Dom Duarte meu muito amado … o = a · c = e · f = d · t = r · z = m · ft = ElRei Christianíssimo · ⊕ = Castela Lisbon → Paris · two substitution alphabets · 1642–1644 · key from adjacent plaintext João IV to the marquês de Nisa, 1642–44 from João IV of Portugal Go to the full text ↓ The king of newly independent Portugal wrote to his ambassador in Paris partly in cipher; both alphabets were rebuilt from clear text bound into the same letter-book, and the 1644 passage that has no decipherment in the book is now deciphered in part (Laranjo Coelho’s 1940–42 edition not checked). Daniel Bourdeau · posted 27 October 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: partial (91% of the cipher) · On the map Credits · Brice Dudout (unpublished earlier solution, verification) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · partial (91% of the cipher) The letters Six letters of João IV to Vasco Luís da Gama, marquês de Nisa, his ambassador in France, copied into the embassy’s letter-book, December 1642 to September 1644. Where Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, Manuscritos da Livraria n.º 1017, letters 9, 13, 44, 49, 56 and 153, scans on DigitArq. Catalogue no. 380. The cipher Letter-for-letter substitution written as pseudo-words with the word breaks kept, a symbol for Castile and a code word for the King of France. In 1644 the alphabet changes to signs shaped like Greek letters. How it was deciphered The 1642 alphabet from three letters copied in clear beside their cipher; the 1644 alphabet from a leaf near the end of the volume that gives two later passages in clear. What it says The release of the Infante D. Duarte, held by Spain; Richelieu’s death and French ships for Madagascar; and in 1644 the marriages of Prince Teodósio and the Infantas, to be kept from everyone. Still open Short cipher runs in three 1643 letters that the 1060-pixel scans cannot resolve, and five words at the end of the 1644 passage. Credit Brice Dudout had rebuilt the 1642 key from the same clear copies earlier the same day and pointed out that letter 153 was the unread piece.

Manuscritos da Livraria 1017 is the second volume of the copies of João IV’s letters to the marquês de Nisa (conde da Vidigueira), sent to Paris in 1642 to win French support for the Restoration of 1640: 284 letters, 1642–45. Torre do Tombo catalogues each letter separately and marks six as written “in great part in cipher”. Those six make up catalogue no. 380. The flags are incomplete: letter 8 (25 October 1642) is mostly in cipher, and so are passages in letters of December 1643, January 1644 and January–February 1645. Two systems are used. Until 1644 the cipher is written in ordinary cursive letters, so that a run such as o pagetfofc fu aEℓinc fuz fxotnc looks like a foreign language inside the Portuguese. Each plain letter has one cipher letter, two have two (s is r or v ; u/v is x or z ). Names are spelled out; Castile is a crossed circle ⊕, and the King of France is the two-letter code ft . From September 1644 a second alphabet appears whose signs look like Greek letters (ε, η, ρ, χ, β, ν). Letter 8, 25 October 1642: the cipher passage on the Infante D. Duarte, then the “Papel junto à dita carta” on the same business in clear. This pair and letter 13’s clear copy gave the first alphabet. Image: Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, Manuscritos da Livraria 1017 f. 15 (scan m0019), via DigitArq.

The 1642 alphabet. The letter-book copies some letters twice. Below letter 8 a “papel junto” covers the same matters in clear ( ecinarcinu = sentimento, fxotnc = Duarte, atrou = irmão, etcfanur = créditos); letter 9 is copied in clear on the next leaf; letter 13 is followed by a “Carta inclusa” giving the whole letter in clear ( paecico = licença, iozeur = navios, Eurcinox = fomentava). Aligning them gives the alphabet: plain a b c d e f g h i l m n o p q r s t u v z cipher o g e f c E d b a p z i u g s t r v n x x z l The October and November 1643 letters use it unchanged. A statistical check of 1,164 cipher letters from letters 9 and 13 against a Portuguese letter model passes (the reading scores far above random keys and above keys fitted to shuffled text). The 1644 alphabet. Letter 153 (21 September 1644) has four lines in the Greek-shaped signs. The 1642 alphabet does not read them, nor does any shift of it, and three solver runs on a Portuguese model found nothing: 148 letters is too little. A sweep of all 289 scans found the same alphabet in letters of 14 January and 7 February 1645 (Cartas 187 and 212), and a leaf before the index (m0276) that lists the volume’s cipher passages in clear, those two among them. The leaf’s “Do Pr. e sobre todos meu m. to amado, e prez. do f. o ” against the cipher infeqtix bxv nEqmx oEuEn bvfoEp bpuEx imxt puE zfacE gives most of the alphabet (E = o, b = m, e = n, f = i, i = p, m = r, n = s, p = a, x = e, z = f, q = c, a = l, c = h, o = t). The volume’s own list of deciphered passages. The last two entries, Cartas 187 (f. 174) and 212 (f. 185), are in the 1644 alphabet and gave its key. Image: Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, Manuscritos da Livraria 1017, leaf before the index (scan m0276), via DigitArq.

Letter 9, 28 December 1642 (149 of 158 cipher words). The cipher carries the business of “a liberdade do Infante Dom Duarte meu muito amado e prezado irmão”, the king’s brother, held by the Spanish since 1641. The French king’s letters to Prince Thomas and the Duke of Longueville were to have the troops escorting him to Milan intercepted. Spanish prisoners of rank were to be got from France to exchange for him. Any attempt by force or flight would be “mui arriscado para a vida do Infante”, since his guards had orders to kill him if anyone tried to take him on the road, and secrecy was “o ponto mais essencial deste negócio”. Letter 13, 31 December 1642 (199 of 207 legible words). The French king had licensed his vassal Rigão and others to send ships to the island of São Lourenço (Madagascar), trade there and build forts, which Portugal claimed. The cardinal-duke of Richelieu was reported dead. He was held to be the man who most fomented the wars with Castile, and on his account offers of a cessation of arms had been refused; if the report was true, Castile might now succeed. Nisa was to penetrate “com recato e segredo” the secrets of Castile and the mind of the French king and his ministers. Letters of 9 October and 20 November 1643 (24 of 42 transcribed words). These are short runs: the congress of Münster, news of the Infante from Genoa, and the instructions of France and Castile for the general peace. Letter 153, 21 September 1644 (26 of 31 words). Nisa was to leave the business he had in hand to the marquês de Cascais, except one matter: Letter 153: the passage in the 1644 alphabet, between “visto se não entende tão no” and the date line. Image: Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo, Manuscritos da Livraria 1017 f. 153 (scan m0157), via DigitArq. … visto se não entende tão no[s] dos casamentos do Príncipe meu sobre todos muito amado e prezado filho e das Infantas , sobre que vos mandei escrever: porque estes não comunicareis nem confiareis ao Marquês nem a outra alguma [?] pessoa , mais que […] mandado […]. “… since it does not extend to the marriages of the Prince, my son beloved above all, and of the Infantas, about which I had you written: for you shall neither tell nor entrust these to the Marquis nor to any other person, except […] ordered […].” Cipher in italics. Prince Teodósio was ten. The February 1645 passage in the same alphabet says the same: “porque este negócio não quero que saiba mais que vós e Luís Pereira”.

The 289 DigitArq scans were downloaded through the archive’s open API. They are 1,060 pixels wide, the only size served. Letter 8’s cipher and its papel junto, then letter 13 and its Carta inclusa, were aligned word by word to rebuild the first alphabet ( key.py ). Letters 9 and 13 were transcribed and checked against their clear copies, and the 1643 letters were located and transcribed. Letter 153 was transcribed. The 1642 key and its shifts were tried, then a homophonic hill climb and two simulated annealers on a Portuguese n-gram model: all failed. A sweep of the whole volume found the two 1645 passages and the list on m0276. Aligned, they gave the second alphabet, which was then extended from letter 153’s own context.

The cipher runs of the 1643 letters (44, 49, 56) and five faint lines of letter 13 (m0025) are rubbed or show-through at the scan resolution. Better images from Torre do Tombo would close them; letter 13’s text is known from its clear copy. Letter 153: pn Evcv Eno nE before “mandado” and purzmofm after it are unread here. “alguma” is grade C. The values of d, g and r in the 1644 alphabet rest on one or two occurrences. A parallel reading of letter 153: Brice Dudout read it the same day, independently, and published it on Europe chiffrée ; his files are in the repository folder ( dudout/ ). The two readings agree on the first two passages. He reads the five words left open here (“as que vos {tenho} [mandado] advertir”), three of them partly from sense, and took two corrections from this page (the z of “confiareis” and c = h). The clear text before the cipher differs: “entenderá no” in his reading, “entende tão no[s]” here. His five words are not yet checked here against the scan. In letter 9, a duke’s name (Duque de O[..]a) is blotted. P. M. Laranjo Coelho’s edition of these letters (1940–42) was not seen. It may print the clear copies; whether it prints letter 153 is unknown.

Two royal despatches of February and April 1593 (BnF fr. 16093 ff. 406, 410) in Maisse’s Cipher of 1592–93, the key the King also sent to Savary de Brèves. Contemporary clear copies in Brienne 13 give the full text, and f. 406 is the duplicate of f. 404, which carries a partial interlinear decipherment. Where Bibliothèque nationale de France, Français 16093 ff. 406 and 410 (catalogue item 17), with their twins f. 404 and f. 412; clear copies in Brienne 13 (BnF NAF 6984) fol. 171r and 193v. The cipher Maisse’s Cipher (1592–93): letter-shaped symbols for the letters, homophonic, with two-digit figures for a nomenclator of common words and names. The King calls it the copy of the cipher he sent to Savary de Brèves. How the text was obtained The old Harlay pièce numbers on the leaves lead, through Berger de Xivrey’s Lettres missives , to clear copies in Brienne 13, which copy the ciphered passages in clear. f. 406 turned out to be the duplicate of f. 404, which carries a partial interlinear decipherment. What they say Rome: the marquis de Pisany and Cardinal Gondi should stay where they are; Maisse’s long-standing judgement of “les affaires de Rome” proved right. Still open The Brienne 13 copies are located but not transcribed, so no text of either letter is in this repository and neither counts as read (reading audit, 22 October 2026). Tomokiyo’s key for this cipher is in hand but was not applied: neither leaf is transcribed sign by sign, so the cipher is not verified on these leaves. Credit Found and contributed by Arya Sanketbhai Patel (PR #7), with the November 1592 letters. Other ciphers The King’s letters of November 1592 in the same file are in a different, numerical cipher, deciphered on their own page . f. 404, the twin of f. 406: letter-shaped signs carry the letters and two-digit figures carry the nomenclator; 27, 10, 26, 23, 19, 21 and 24 are the commonest figures here. BnF Français 16093 (formerly Saint-Germain-Harlay ms. 1024) is the file of despatches from the Court to Maisse at Venice, digitised as btv1b90074656 . Tomokiyo puts ff. 406 and 410 in Maisse’s Cipher (1592–93) , the long series ff. 344 to 444, which includes four leaves (ff. 398, 401, 402 and 404) that carry a partial decipherment written between the lines. folio canvas date on the leaf pièce Brienne 13 confirmed by f. 406 457 Chartres, 8 February 1593 247 fol. 171r (canvas 176, right) heading Coppie de lettre du Roy audict sieur de Maisse de Chartres le huictiesme febvrier 1593 ; preamble identical f. 410 461 Mantes, 27 April 1593 251 fol. 193v (canvas 199, left) heading Mante le vingt huictiesme Avril 1593, receue le vingt douxiesme May The route to the clear copies is the one described on the page for the 1592 letters : each leaf carries an old Harlay pièce number, Berger de Xivrey cites the letters by it with a reference to “Fonds Brienne, Ms. 13” , and Brienne 13 (BnF NAF 6984, btv1b100904592 ) copies the despatches in clear, ciphered passages included. f. 406 is not a separate letter. Tomokiyo lists f. 404 as carrying a partial interlinear decipherment and f. 406 as having none, as though they were two despatches of February 1593. They are the same despatch: both are docketed Chartres 8 Féb. 1593 , both open with the same words, and Brienne 13 copies the letter once, at fol. 171r, under pièce 247. f. 406 is the duplicate sent by the other route; the King says in these letters that he writes “par double voye” . Tomokiyo already records that f. 412 is the duplicate of f. 410; f. 406 is the same case, unrecognised. So the plaintext of f. 406 is attested twice, by the Brienne copy and by the interlinear decipherment on its twin.

Quotations are transcribed from the Brienne copy; spelling is the copyist’s. f. 406, with f. 404: Chartres, 8 February 1593 (pièce 247) The King has answered every despatch as it came and has docketed the dates of each in his replies, so that Maisse can tell what has gone astray. The ciphered matter turns on Rome: the insolence of the Spaniards and what His Holiness will resolve; it would be very much to the purpose that the marquis de Pisany should not leave where he is, and that Cardinal Gondi should be told the same, “ce que j’ay faict à l’instant mesmes” , for if that fails neither of them has much hope of going to Rome, and their entering among those of the League “pourroit faire naistre parmy eux quelque plus grande division” . This is also the letter that says in clear, of the cipher itself, that Maisse has kept “le double du chiffre que j’ay envoyé aud. de Brèves” , which explains why the same key turns up in the Savary de Brèves correspondence. f. 410: Mantes, 27 April 1593 (pièce 251) The copy heads it 28 April, received 22 May. The King acknowledges Maisse’s letters of 20 February and 7 and 23 March, the last of which arrived first because the duc de Nevers had kept the other courier some days with him in Champagne. Maisse shows him so clearly the disposition and state of everything there, and in what touches his service, that he takes great contentment in it and recognises more and more the usefulness of his good offices; he asks him to be assured “que j’en estime vostre merite tel envers moy que vostre absence a cette occasion ne vous y fera rien perdre” . And experience has shown that Maisse was not deceived in the judgement he had long since formed of “les affaires de Rome” .

Tomokiyo reconstructed the key from the sibling letters and published it as an image, “Maisse’ Cipher 2 (BnF fr.16093, f.344 etc.)” . It is homophonic, mixes letter-shaped symbols with figures and carries word codes for vous, ceulx, est, faict, de, des, fort, par, pour, que, qui, advis, ces, comme, bon, avec, et, jay, les, luy, moy . It was not applied to ff. 406 and 410: neither is transcribed sign by sign, so the reading on this page is the clerk’s, not a decipherment checked on the leaves. Transcribing the cipher is a much larger job than for the 1592 letters; the content of both letters is settled by the Brienne copies regardless.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. f. 406 (twin f. 404), Chartres, 8 Feb 1593, from the Brienne 13 clear copy; cipher decrypted on its first lines (WAINUT, 27 Oct 2026) read in part Henri IV to Maisse at Venice: he has answered every despatch and noted their dates, approves Maisse's sending of duplicates, hopes the despatch for the Pope was not delayed, and has written to the Grand Seigneur and his ministers (Maisse can read the letter to Breves if he kept the copy of the cipher). From the start of the cipher block on (its end is not fixed): Rome; Pisany's arrival in Italy; the war in Piedmont and a letter sent through Lesdiguieres' men with a further charge for Lesdiguieres; Gondi at Nancy with the King's passport; the King going down to Saumur, where his sister is. The earlier summary of f. 406 in this entry and in NOTES (the Spanish insolence, Pisany and Cardinal Gondi not to leave Rome) describes the top of fol. 171r, which is the end of Maisse's own letter to the King of 10 Apr 1593. The end of the letter (fol. 173r) is not transcribed. ## In clear on f. 406 Monsieur de Maisse, I have always answered your despatches as I received them and noted their dates in my letters, so as not to leave you in doubt, and so that you could tell whether any of them had been lost. Because of that uncertainty, I approve your practice of sending duplicates of the previous despatch with the most recent ones. Since the last letters I wrote to you, I have received together yours of 26 December and 1 January; the latter reported the arrival with you of the ambassador[?] with his despatch. If you found that despatch out of season in some respect, you will nevertheless have understood that this was not for want of his being sent back early enough to reach in time the place where he must go, had he not met extraordinary hindrances on his journey. Had the remedies for these been in my power and had I not provided them, I would regret this inconvenience the more; but since I could do no more than I have done, one must still do what one can for the rest and wait, as in all other things, for the fruit that it will please God to bring from it. I believe that in the said despatch you will have found an answer to all the points on which you thought an answer from me was needed concerning my affairs over there. Or if you saw anything lacking, you will have supplied it, as I left it to your judgement; and I am confident, as regards the Pope, that you will have seen to it that it was not delayed on that account, as your letter gave me hope. Once this step is taken, we shall wait for what the first news after the receipt of the said despatch brings us from that quarter. Meanwhile, having thought it fitting to make some reply to the letters I received from the sieur de Brèves, I have by the same means chosen to write a word of thanks to the Grand Seigneur, and likewise to write to his chief ministers about the refusal to let the ambassador of Spain go to Constantinople, which they say in their letters, that you sent me earlier, was made out of regard for me. If you have kept the copy of the cipher that I sent to the said sieur de Brèves, as I understood you would, you will see what I write to him; for I wish you to know all that comes and goes in that quarter, because of the connection between the two charges, and because of the value I set on the good advice you can give in it. ## From "Le surplus" on: in cipher on f. 406 and f. 404 (where the cipher block ends is not fixed) The rest of your letters concerns the affairs of Rome, the journey of the marquis de Pisany and the war in Piedmont. I was very glad to hear of the said marquis's arrival in Italy, as I saw from your said letters, having still had nothing from him myself. I am waiting for the outcome of his said journey, and likewise of the new means you have sought for the relief of my said affairs in Piedmont. In which, although I know that you do what you can, yet with the other despatches I sent to the sieur de Lesdiguières by those who had come to me from him, I sent him a letter that I wrote to you specially on that matter, so that he can forward it to you by whatever route he thinks fit. And I have nevertheless[?] told his people what I saw in all your letters of the care you take there, so that they might bear witness to the said sieur de Lesdiguières that, without being asked, you were doing of your own accord what he could wish. Still, so as to leave out nothing that may depend on me, I have chosen to add this further charge, which he will use if he sees fit, so that he can see even more clearly what he may expect from it. And although there is already justification enough for doing so, I have not wished to reject the advice given me not yet to let Cardinal de Gondi or the marquis de Pisany come back. Two intercepted letters of the French command in Spain, kept in Spanish copies at the Archivo Histórico Nacional with the cipher passages left as numbers (Diversos-Colecciones 134, N.34 and N.73). Brice Dudout deciphered them with the French table of the 1812 Grand Chiffre, the British “Great Paris Cipher”, whose cells he read on Jean-François Bouchaudy’s photographs and froze before Jourdan’s letter was decoded: 259 of its 267 numbers, and about 85% of Marmont’s, whose copy is faulty. After the fall of Almaraz, Jourdan orders Soult to reinforce d’Erlon against Hill or send him over the Tagus at the bridge of the Arzobispo to cover Madrid.
