Daniel Bourdeau · posted 27 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: partial (92% of the cipher) · On the map Contributed by Brice Dudout (solution) · Also credited · Jean-François Bouchaudy (pointer to a source) · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) known key At a glance Known key applied · partial (92% of the cipher) The letters Marshal Jourdan, King Joseph’s chief of staff, to Marshal Soult, commanding the Army of the South, Madrid, 28 May 1812; and Marshal Marmont, commanding the Army of Portugal, to Jourdan, Salamanca, 1 June 1812. Both were intercepted and survive in Spanish copies that keep the cipher passages as numbers. Where Archivo Histórico Nacional (Madrid), Diversos-Colecciones 134, N.34 (Jourdan’s letter, in a Spanish translation of the time, PARES 3156392, images 2–3) and N.73 (Marmont’s, PARES 3109832, images 2–3; catalogue no. 751 here). The cipher The Grand Chiffre of 1812, which the British called the Great Paris Cipher: a table of numbers for letters, syllables, words and names, extended to 1,400 with additions for Spain (1300 Lord Wellington, 1383 the Tagus), with several numbers for frequent words. How it was deciphered With the French deciphering table of the time (Service historique de la Défense, “B n° 30”), whose cells Brice Dudout read on Jean-François Bouchaudy’s photographs and froze before decoding. Jourdan’s letter was kept out of that work: decoded with the frozen entries, it scores above 998 of 1,000 tables with the values shuffled. What they say Jourdan orders Soult to reinforce Count d’Erlon’s corps so that it can beat General Hill on the Guadiana or, if Wellington calls Hill back, to send it over the Tagus at the bridge of the Arzobispo to cover Madrid. Marmont writes that only certainty and great operations begun in the South could outweigh an operation in the North. Still open In Jourdan’s letter, eight numbers that do not give the expected value and are restored from the sense. In Marmont’s, about 26 of 176 numbers: the Spanish copy has too many miscopied figures. Scovell, Wellington’s cipher officer, deciphered Marmont’s letter in 1812; his decipherment was never printed. Credit Brice Dudout ( Europe chiffrée ), working with Claude Opus 5.5: the table cells read and frozen, both transcriptions, the held-out test, the French text and the English translation. His write-up . The deciphering table of the time is kept at the Service historique de la Défense; the photographs of it are Jean-François Bouchaudy’s.

On 19 May 1812 General Hill took and destroyed the forts and the pontoon bridge at Almaraz, the only solid crossing of the Tagus between Marmont’s Army of Portugal and Soult’s Army of the South. Joseph, now commander-in-chief in Spain, with Marshal Jourdan as his chief of staff, was trying to bring into action the corps of Count d’Erlon (General Drouet), detached from Soult’s army. Eight weeks later, on 22 July, Wellington beat Marmont at Salamanca. The Archivo Histórico Nacional keeps, in the Depósito de la Guerra papers of its Diversos-Colecciones, French despatches of that year that fell into Spanish hands. Two of them are in the Grand Chiffre: Diversos-Colecciones 134, N.34 : a Spanish translation, made at the time, of Jourdan’s letter to Soult (“el Mariscal Duque de Dalmacia”), Madrid, 28 May 1812, initialled “Monsalud”. The translator put the clear parts into Spanish and copied the three cipher passages as numbers, 267 in all, without deciphering them. Diversos-Colecciones 134, N.73 : a copy of Marmont’s letter to Jourdan, Salamanca, 1 June 1812, in a Spanish hand, with its cipher passages as numbers, 176 in all. Catalogue no. 751 here. The Spanish copy of Jourdan’s letter, image 2. The first cipher passage follows se disponía a marchar adelante ; the second, below the paragraph on Hill and Almaraz, begins 642. 397. 90. 87. 693 , Vous sentez , and is interrupted near the end by Es dificil , words the original had in clear, which the translator put into Spanish. Image: Archivo Histórico Nacional, DIVERSOS-COLECCIONES,134,N.34 image 2, via PARES (the copy published by Brice Dudout, Europe chiffrée). A third piece of the same collection, Colonel Jardet to Marmont, Paris, 6 March 1812 (133, N.29; catalogue no. 724), is in a different cipher and needs no work: it is a copia descifrada conforme , the Spaniards’ full decipherment, with their reconstruction of its key attached, 48 numbers built on a line of Voltaire’s Tancrède , “À tous les cœurs bien nés que la patrie est chère”, with the numbers from 49 up as nulls. It is also no. 1 of George Scovell’s file of intercepted ciphers (Oman, A History of the Peninsular War V, appendix XV).

The Grand Chiffre of 1812, which the British called the Great Paris Cipher, is a repertory of 1,200 numbers for letters, syllables and words, extended to 1,400 with additions for Spain: 1211 l’armée du Centre, 1214 l’armée anglaise, 1300 Lord Wellington, 1383 le Tage. Frequent words have several numbers. The groups are written with points between them, and words are spelled out of syllables where the table has no entry: 909 168 424 946 is Mi-ra-ve-te , 217 894 954 173 637 Ar-zo-bi-s-po . The French deciphering table survives at the Service historique de la Défense (“B n° 30”), and Jean-François Bouchaudy has published photographs of it. Brice Dudout had already read 226 of its entries to decipher a letter of King Joseph of December 1812 ( his edition ); for these letters he read the cells they needed. The entries used are in targets/marmont1812/key_1812_entries.tsv , each with the source of its reading; the photographs are not reproduced.

No cryptanalysis. The numbers 2–1400 of Army of Portugal traffic in 1812 pointed to the Grand Chiffre, and the first line of Marmont’s letter, decoded with the 226 entries already read, gave French. The rest is applying the table of the time unchanged. A frozen table and a held-out letter. Both transcriptions were frozen with a SHA-256 hash. The cells needed for Marmont’s letter were transcribed from the photographs and frozen; Jourdan’s letter was kept out of that work and decoded only afterwards. Each decoding, taking the main value of every entry with no correction by the sense, was scored with a French letter-trigram model learnt on an independent text (Marmont’s Mémoires , vol. IV) against 1,000 tables in which the same values are given to the numbers at random. Jourdan’s letter scores −2.184 with the frozen entries, against −2.217 at the 99th percentile of the shuffled tables, and only 2 of the 1,000 score higher; after seven cells were looked at again on the table (424, 132, 276, 1120, 525, 320, 642, kept in a separate list), none does. Marmont’s letter passes narrowly with the frozen entries (−2.248 against −2.249) and clearly after the re-readings. Two word-coverage scores tried afterwards did not separate the real table from the shuffled ones, because long multi-word entries flatter the shuffled tables, and they are not used. The text. Every number was then given its value and the French built into sentences, checked against Jourdan’s parallel letter to Marmont of the same day, printed in Marmont’s Mémoires , and his order to d’Erlon of 7 May 1812 (Du Casse, Mémoires du roi Joseph IX, p. 6), which use some of the same words.

Brice Dudout’s text of the three cipher passages; the clear parts of the letter, which the Spanish copy gives in translation, are summarised. {x} probable reading; [x] restored from the sense. The letter opens in clear: the King has received a letter of the 26th from Marmont (the Duke of Ragusa), who reports that Wellington is north of the Tagus with his whole army except Hill’s division, that the English army will have moved against him by about the 8th, and that two divisions have already crossed the Douro. Then the first cipher passage: le duc de Raguse a rappelé à lui la division {Foy}, de manière qu’il ne va plus rester dans la vallée du Tage que trois bataillons et environ huit cents chevaux de l’armée du Centre, sous les ordres du général Treillar[d]. The Duke of Ragusa has recalled Foy’s division to him, so that there will remain in the Tagus valley only three battalions and about eight hundred horse of the Army of the Centre, under the orders of General Treillard. A clear paragraph follows: the King believes Marmont all the more because it is Hill’s division that has made the expedition against the bridge of Almaraz, well supported by other troops. Then the orders, in cipher: Vous sentez, monsieur le maréchal, que dans cette circonstance vous deve[z] renf[or]cer le corps du comte d’Er{lon} autant que cela vous sera possible, afin de le me{tt}re en état de [ba]{tt}re le corps du général Hill s’il reste sur la Guadiana. Si [au] contraire lord Wellington rappelle à lui le général Hill, alors le comte d’Er{lon} doit se porter sur Miravete et venir pas[ser] le Tage au pont de l’Arzobispo, pour co[u]vrir Madrid ou pour se porter sur le flan[c] droi{t} de l’armée anglaise, suivant les circonstances. Le passage du pont de l’Arzobispo es difícil pour l’artillerie, mais il n’est pas impraticable. Le général d’Er{lon} devroit me[ner] avec lui le moins el equipaje posible. Es muy importante que este general se ponga en correspondencia avec le général Treillar[d], qui va commander dans la vallée du Tage. You will feel, Monsieur le Maréchal, that in this situation you must reinforce Count d’Erlon’s corps as much as you can, so as to enable it to beat General Hill’s corps if he stays on the Guadiana. If on the contrary Lord Wellington calls General Hill back to him, then Count d’Erlon must move on Miravete and come to cross the Tagus at the bridge of the Arzobispo, to cover Madrid or to move against the right flank of the English army, as circumstances require. The passage of the bridge of the Arzobispo [is difficult] for the artillery, but it is not impracticable. General d’Erlon should take with him as little [baggage as possible. It is very important that this general put himself in correspondence] with General Treillard, who is to command in the Tagus valley. The words in Spanish were in clear in the original; the translator put them into Spanish with the rest of the clear text, and the English gives them in brackets. The third cipher passage, from avec le général Treillard , ends the orders; the clear closing is signed Jourdan, “Mariscal del Imperio, Jefe del E. M. de S. M. C.”

Marmont’s letter of 1 June, from Salamanca, is in the same cipher, but the copy is poor: the Spanish copyist confused the forms of 1, wrote 3 for 9 and the reverse, and transposed figures. About 150 of its 176 numbers give a value (about 85%), and some 26 do not. The passages that build sentences, as Brice Dudout gives them, with a few words restored from the sense: “C’est qu’il n’y a qu’une certitude absolue et des opérations capitales commencées dans le Midi qui puissent l’emporter sur les probabilités d’une opération dans le Nord”; “J’écris itérativement au général Caffarelli”; “Il serait bien désirable que le général Drouet suivît les mouvements du général Hill”; “en préparant un matériel d’artillerie à Talavera”. “It is that only an absolute certainty and capital operations begun in the South could outweigh the probabilities of an operation in the North”; “I write repeatedly to General Caffarelli”; “It would be most desirable that General Drouet should follow the movements of General Hill”; “by preparing artillery material at Talavera”. Wellington had this letter too. On 7 June 1812 he wrote that he had “one intercepted letter from Marmont to Jourdan; which I am endeavoring to decipher” (Gurwood, Dispatches IX). It is no. 28 of George Scovell’s file of ciphers; his manuscript decipherment of it has never been printed, and Oman gives only a one-line summary. The line-by-line decoding of what this copy gives is under Full texts below; Brice Dudout’s working notes on it are in reading_N73_partial.md .

Foy’s division , of the Army of Portugal, had been guarding the Tagus valley. Foy’s name is written 1011 , a cell given as “Foi s” in Brice Dudout’s notes and as “soir” in his list of entries: the reading {Foy} is probable. Treillard commanded the troops of the Army of the Centre in the Tagus valley. Miravete is the pass and fort above Almaraz; the bridge of the Arzobispo crosses the Tagus upstream, on the Talavera road. Jourdan’s parallel letter to Marmont of the same day calls it difficult for the artillery, “but I do not think it impracticable”, and speaks of the same eight hundred horse. Monsalud. The Marqués de Monsalud commanded Spanish troops in Extremadura. On 11 June 1812 Wellington wrote to Hill that Monsalud believed Joseph had ordered Soult to approach the Tagus, but “did not send me the paper on which he founds this notion”. The paper may be this copy; that is only a hypothesis.

Jourdan’s letter. Of 267 numbers, 259 give their value in the table (97.0%): 250 certain and 9 probable. By the project’s grades the certain values are H (read from the key of the time), the probable ones M, and the restorations I. Eight numbers do not give the expected syllable and are restored from the sense: 208 renf[or]cer, 598 [ba]ttre, 88 [au] contraire, 62 pas[ser], 1085 co[u]vrir, 266 flan[c], and 981 372 me[ner]. They are copying errors by the translator, who at places confuses 1 and 7, 3 and 9, 5 and 6, or cells the photographs do not show clearly. The probable readings are 320 (a T-shaped cell), 525 lon and 1011 {Foy}. Two observations made here on the PARES image, not part of the contributed text and not checked against the table: the number transcribed 88 (line D5) has an overwritten first figure that looks like the copyist’s 5, and 58 is aux in the table, which, read au as in line D8 ( 58 before pont ), would give au contraire without a restoration; and the number transcribed 62 (line D8) ends in a figure shaped like the 4 of 74 on the next line, so it may be 64 , a cell not yet transcribed from the table. Marmont’s letter. About 26 of its 176 numbers are unresolved and several words are restored; the passages around them do not build sentences. The Spanish copy is the limit: a better copy would settle them, the intercepted original among Scovell’s papers or the French minute; neither has been consulted. Earlier work. Jourdan’s letter to Soult is not in Scovell’s list (Oman V, appendix XV, where nos. 26–27 are letters of 26 May to Soult on the fall of Almaraz), nor in Du Casse’s Mémoires du roi Joseph IX, Marmont’s Mémoires IV, Jourdan’s Mémoires militaires , Wellington’s Dispatches IX or his Supplementary Despatches VII (Brice Dudout’s search, 28 October 2026). No decipherment of it was found.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. Jourdan to Soult, Madrid, 28 May 1812 (AHN DIVERSOS-COLECCIONES,134,N.34) Eight weeks before the battle of Salamanca, Marshal Jourdan, King Joseph’s chief of staff, orders Soult to reinforce Count d’Erlon’s corps against General Hill, or to send it across the Tagus at the bridge of the Arzobispo if Wellington calls Hill back to him. The letter was intercepted: a contemporary Spanish translation survives in the Archivo Histórico Nacional, with the enciphered passages left as numbers, undeciphered. They read with the table of the 1812 Grand Chiffre. Each announces a Soviet key change in the enciphered weather broadcasts and gives the method and key to read it. Where National Institute for Defense Studies, Tokyo, online through JACAR, Ref. C01004558500, C01004559200, C04120597300, C01004559500, C01004816800, C01004816500, C01004816400, C01004816900, C01004816700, C01004832500, C01004832600, C01004818600. The images are all rights reserved and not reproduced. The cipher Groups of five figures, the international synoptic report, enciphered by subtracting or adding a key figure by figure without carrying. Four generations follow each other, from a fixed additive in the Far East in 1938 to Moscow tables of 1940. How it was read By the Japanese, in 1938–1940. Here the reports’ method passages were transcribed and translated, the tables of June–July 1940 transcribed cell by cell and frozen before any check, and the worked examples recomputed. What it shows The eleven rows of each June 1940 table are one 109-figure cycle, shifted; the key group only gives a starting point, so the tables could be rebuilt from a few days of traffic. The figure 0 almost never occurs in a Soviet key. Still open One figure too many in the October odd-day grid, not located; one key cell of 29 April 1940 probable (8, 6 possible). No enciphered Soviet broadcast of 1940 was found online to test the tables independently. Credit Brice Dudout ( Europe chiffrée ) found the reports, transcribed and checked the tables and reviewed doubtful cells on the images; sent on 29 October 2026, working with Claude agents. The British side of the system is Brian Audric’s (2000).

The plain text under every cipher is the international synoptic report: groups of five figures for station, cloud, weather, wind, pressure and temperature. Every system subtracts or adds a key figure by figure without carrying. key.tsv holds every key of the reports. August 1938, Far East. Groups 1↔3 and 2↔5 exchanged, +3 on every figure (+4 on the station index). Read the same day, ten hours after it came into service. From September 1938 one additive group per broadcast group, changed every two to four weeks. February 1940, Far East. Eleven symbols (0–9 and X); group 1 substituted and then used as running key for the line. February–June 1940, Moscow “types” 17040, 05104, 05080, 05188. One indicator figure per group is substituted and fixes the subtractor of the other four. This is the “Russian code” described from the British side by Brian Audric (Met Office IDA unit, 2000); his example deciphers by the same method. June–October 1940, Moscow. A key group aaabb sent in clear; 7 and X exchanged; a 109-figure cycle subtracted from the starting point the key group designates. Two tables at a time (odd and even days in Moscow), changed 10 June, 26 June and 12 October 1940. The report of 16 July 1940 encloses the four June tables complete; that of 16 October 1940 the two new grids.

Brice Dudout transcribed the four June–July 1940 tables cell by cell from the photographs (4 tables × 11 rows × 109 figures = 4,796 figures) and the two October grids, and froze them before any check. He then found the structure the Japanese had exploited: the eleven rows of each table are the same 109-figure cycle, shifted ( cycles_109.tsv ). Every station enciphered with another key yields another overlapping fragment, which is how the tables could be rebuilt from a few days of traffic. The October grids are the same thing condensed, one figure per key, the struck-out cell being the one duplicate of 110 keys for 109 positions.

The report of 16 July 1940 prints one example: two stations received on 6 July 1940 at 04:00 Japan time (5 July in Moscow, an odd day, so table 3), key group 22244 (row 222, column 44). Station 1 reads 84110 03862 12212 43127 30803 00290: station 841, pressure 943.1 mb, temperature 27, wind direction code 12 force 2. Station 2 (station 933) continues in the same cycle: pressure 1013.2 mb, temperature 28. The clear text is figures, not prose: the code meanings follow the international synoptic code as summarised by Audric; the Soviet variant of 1940 and the station indexes were not checked.

Rotation: 0 disagreements on 4,796 figures; 3 figures illegible on the photograph (table 3: row 111 col 99, row XXX col 11, row XXX col 88) restored from the structure as 4, 4, 2. Held-out example: the key stream drawn from the transcribed table equals the stream printed in the report, and the decipherment gives back the report’s clear text: 60 of 60 figures. Type 17040 (February 1940): the example is reproduced, 25 of 25; it settles a figure blurred on the photograph (33556). Audric’s British example: 25 of 25 with his key. Visual review by Brice Dudout (28 October 2026): the fifth additive of 12 November 1938 is 34235 (first transcribed 34135); the subtractor for cipher figure 6 on 29 April 1940 is badly stamped (8 probable, 6 possible); ten October cells confirmed. No 200-control statistical test: no key was recovered here and no language read; the keys are Japanese, transcribed and checked against the reports’ own examples. The British files (TNA HW 54/4, HW 40/31) are not digitised.

Count by the 95% rule, in figures: June–July tables, 4,796 figures, 4,793 certain, 3 restored from the cyclic structure, 0 unresolved; worked example, 60 of 60 certain; October grids, 218 figures, not checkable by rotation (one figure per key): in the odd-day grid 2 and 5 occur 13 times and 4 only 11, so one figure is probably misread, not located; the key list has one probable cell. The October grids are key material only, with no cipher text.

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: key recovered based on adjacent plaintext · Extent: complete · On the map Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) adjacent text At a glance Key from adjacent plaintext · complete The letter “Famulus et servulus Ricc. de Mutiliana” (Modigliana) to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, lord of Mantua, Forlì, 6 November 1428. Italian, clear text with runs of cipher. Where Archivio di Stato di Mantova, Archivio Gonzaga. DECODE R1854, image 3; the record was catalogued as one letter of unknown sender. The cipher A homophonic substitution in graphic signs with nulls and three name signs: the lord Malatesta, the marquess’s sons, the pope. How it was deciphered A contemporary hand wrote the plaintext letter above each graphic sign; about two-thirds of that gloss is legible. Thirty values of signs taken from it, and a few rare signs from context, decipher every run from its signs. What it says The governor of Forlì secretly favours the marquess’s sons; with the pope, the lord Malatesta and the count of Urbino, the lord of Mantua could become “una grande signore in pocho tempo”. Still open Two unglossed signs and about 25 signs in doubtful words. This letter is image 3 of DECODE R1854, which holds four letters to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga in four ciphers. The others have their own pages: a Gonzaga agent in Rome, 9 August 1428 , Francesco de’ Cattanei, February 1430 and Pandolfo Malatesta, 22 April 1428 (not solved). They were written up together until 14 October 2026.

This letter is in Italian, clear text interrupted by cipher runs. Over every sign a contemporary hand has written the plaintext letter in small faint script, and three word signs are glossed as names: el signor Malatesta , li fioli del signor marchese and el papa . About two-thirds of the gloss is legible. Thirty values of signs attested in it (each two to fifty-six times), plus a handful of rare signs fixed from context, decipher all 894 signs: … a ciascuno pare che questo acto sia molto dannoso a le signor Malatesta et cusì, perché [el] dà ad intendare a molti che el papa fia cum loro. Se la S.V. havesse da papa fare questa impresa insieme cum lo signor Malatesta [e] conte d’Urbino, la S.V. se faria una grande signore in pocho tempo. Bene che el signor Malatesta è riputato così povaro, molti se copriano per lui … The informant reports that the governor secretly favours the marquess’s sons, and that Guidantonio da Montefeltro, count of Urbino, is in secret contact with Giovanni de Ramberto, which has aroused suspicion. Full text: reading_p3.md .

One pass transcribed the gloss ( p3_gloss.md ), a second the signs ( p3_signs.txt ). The key comes from the gloss, and every run was deciphered from its signs rather than from the faint gloss, so the legible gloss checks the reading. A test against chance and overfitting with an Italian letter model ( docs/_validate.py ) passes.

869 of 894 signs read as sense, re-counted 5 October 2026. Two unglossed signs (one of them twice) and about 25 signs in doubtful words (“de Ianus(?) ubi(?)”, “dice cavad(?)”). The writer’s first name is abbreviated, “Ricc.”.

L'amico *che m'à dicto quel che scrive, e el conte sa l'à octo da chi serci li* vostro servidore et *del signor Malatesta* et inimico *de li fioli del signor marchese* per molti respecti. *El qual dice* discreto sa ch' *d li fioli del signor marchese de Ianus(?) ubi(?)to rompare cum [?] lo signor Malatesta* et però ch' *s'à anno speran[ç]a, o veramente i[n] una de l'eletere* principe, o veramente in una o più *de le lor persone, et sa me certo che tucto i popoli* sopra *è mal contenti et vorriano el signor Malatesta* et firme. Certo ch' *questo governatore* nel segreto *savore[g]gi li fioli del signor marchese* et ch' *questa gente* ch' [cm] *tenea le pronti; ered[e] e questi fioli del signor marchese* non *la tenu[t]e se non* in *lor favore*, o veramente per *levarsu qualche cosa de me[?]o* ... *adendo el caso*: a ciascuno pare che questo acto sia molto dannoso *a le signor Malatesta* et cusì, perché *[?] dà ad intendare a molti che el papa* fia *cum loro*. Se la S.V. havesse *e(?) da papa* fare questa *impresa insieme cum lo signor Malatesta [e] conte d'Urbino*, la S.V. *se faria una grande signore in pocho tempo*. Bene che *el signor Malatesta è riputato così povaro*, molti *se s[e] copriano per lui*, ma ciascheduno teme *no gle possa adiutare de dice cavad(?) li bisognando*. [L21, clear line] Adviso la S.V. che io comprendo et sento *se [el] papa non* [struck] *da contra el signor Malatesta havese punto de fiato*, et spetialmente *se el signor conte d'Urbino fus cum lui*. Pensimo la S.V. *che saria giugnargle la vostra signoria*, maxime *de consentimento del papa*. E da un altro amico de so di fede ho *che Lunardo* et ch' *certo m'è stato questione*. Ancho che *ocultamente el signor conte d'Urbino* tene *[una] grande pratica cum Giovanni de Ramberto*, et per questo che se ne *è acorto alcuno*, se ne presso *admiratione et sospecto cum lo conte d'Urbino. Forlivii 6 novembris. ## Summary (English) A Gonzaga informant at Forlì reports that his contact, a friend of the Malatesta and an enemy of the marquess's sons, says the governor (of Forlì, for the pope) secretly favours the marquess's sons; everyone thinks the matter very harmful to the lord Malatesta, because it is put about that the pope is with them. If the lord of Mantua undertook this enterprise together with the lord Malatesta and the count of Urbino, he would become a great lord in a short time; the lord Malatesta is thought so poor that many would shelter behind him but fear he could not help them. The count of Urbino (Guidantonio da Montefeltro) is secretly in close contact with Giovanni de Ramberto, which has caused wonder and suspicion. ## Measure 905 cipher signs (`p3_signs.txt`; the gloss confirms most runs). Unread or doubtful: Z (2), fk (1), the one '?' sign, and short doubtful spans (L04 "d … de Ianus ubi", L05–06 "speran[ç]a o a", L10 "ered", L12 "de me[?]o", L20 "dice cavad") — about 25 signs. Read as sense ≈ 880/905 = 0.972. The three name codes are read (glossed). R1854 image 3: Ricc(ardo?) de Mutiliana to Gianfrancesco Gonzaga, Forlì, 6 November 1428: English translation Translation (Claude Opus 5.5, 23 Oct 2026) of the "Italian" section of `reading_p3.md`: clear text with the cipher runs (in *italics*), re-deciphered from the signs with the key taken from the contemporary interlinear gloss. Same holes: `[?]` an unread sign, `[x]` letters supplied, `(?)` doubtful. Where the 1428 Italian is garbled or uncertain (the doubtful spans the reading lists) the English follows the words and marks the uncertain sense `[?…]`. ## Translation Illustrious and most excellent lord, my most singular lord. The friend *who has told me what he writes, and the count knows it [?from whom he heard it]*, your servant and *[friend] of the lord Malatesta* and enemy *of the sons of the lord marquess* for many reasons — *he says*, discreetly, that he knows that *[?the] sons of the lord marquess [?…] [?would] break with [?] the lord Malatesta*, and therefore that *they have hope, either truly in one of the electors(?)* princes, or truly in one or more *of their persons; and he is certain that all the peoples* above *are ill content and would like the lord Malatesta* and firm. Certain that *this governor* in secret *favours the sons of the lord marquess*, and that *these people* that [cm] *kept them ready; [?believe] and these sons of the lord marquess* did not *hold it except* in *their favour*, or truly to *get something of me[?]o for themselves* ... *the case arising*: it seems to everyone that this act is very harmful *to the lord Malatesta*, and so, because *[?] gives many to understand that the pope* is *with them*. If Your Lordship had *[?from the] pope* to make this *enterprise together with the lord Malatesta [and the] count of Urbino*, Your Lordship *would make himself a great lord in a short time*. Although *the lord Malatesta is reputed so poor*, many *would shelter behind him*, but each one fears *he could not help them [?…] if they needed*. [L21, clear line] I advise Your Lordship that I understand and hear *[?that if the] pope did not* [struck] *[?…] against the lord Malatesta had any breath*, and especially *if the lord count of Urbino were with him*. Let Your Lordship consider *what it would be to join Your Lordship to him*, above all *with the consent of the pope*. And from another friend I know of [?good] faith I have *that Lunardo* and that *certainly there has been a dispute with me*. Also that *secretly the lord count of Urbino* holds *[a] great dealing with Giovanni de Ramberto*, and because *someone has noticed* it, *wonder and suspicion* has arisen from it *with the count of Urbino. I expect to hear much*. I commend myself always to Your Lordship. Forlì, 6 November. Key: key3_p3.txt

Two letters from Lyon to the Duke of Nevers in substitution ciphers of graphic signs, each with its own contemporary decipherment. Birago’s cipher flap covers a complete clear copy, transcribed in full; the duchess’s interlinear decipherment is faded and was transcribed only in part. No key was applied: the similar 1584 Nevers alphabet does not fit. F = E · 9 = Q · X Y Z IN CLEAR · LYON 1574 Lyon → the duke of Nevers · substitution cipher of graphic signs · September 1574 Henriette de Clèves and Renato Birago to the Duke of Nevers, Lyon, September 1574 from Henriette de Clèves → to Duke of Nevers Go to the full text ↓ BnF français 3315 ff. 15–16 and 21, two letters from Lyon in September 1574. One has a minute word-by-word decipherment between its lines and a clear ending; the other keeps Renato Birago’s cipher flap over a complete clear Italian fair copy. The text was taken from these contemporary decipherments: f. 21 from its clear copy, and f. 15 from its interlinear decipherment, checked word by word against the cipher decoded with an alphabet rebuilt here from the gloss (22 October 2026). Only four overwritten lines of f. 15v and a dozen single groups stay open; with them the f. 15 reading builds coherent sentences but reads at 94.1% of its words, under the 95% a complete reading needs. Tomokiyo had described the system but published no decipherment. It does not use the Nevers key at ff. 12–13; it resembles Nevers no. 2 (1584, BnF fr. 3995 f. 16) but differs in decisive assignments. How it was read Both leaves carry their own decipherment. On f. 21 a folded cipher sheet covers a clean, signed Italian copy of Birago’s whole letter; on f. 15 an early hand wrote French plaintext between the cipher lines. No key was rebuilt and no solver was run. What it says Birago says Nevers’s visit is late, Piedmont is better discussed orally, and Their Majesties wish to provide Nevers with a government. Henriette writes at midnight, her eyes hurt from weeping. Still open On f. 15 the interlinear decipherment is transcribed only in part and the ciphered middle lacks a reliable line-by-line transcription. One phrase on f. 21 is uncertain, and the exact 1574 alphabet is not rebuilt. Credit Satoshi Tomokiyo observed that the leaves do not use the key at ff. 12–13 and are close to Nevers no. 2.

The Gallica viewer’s sequence obscures the physical arrangement. Image f17 shows manuscript f. 15r, and f18 shows its verso next to a clear ending on f. 16r. Image f23 shows f. 21r with Birago’s pale cipher flap covering much of the Italian fair copy. In image f24 the flap is folded away, revealing the whole clear text on the same recto. The next image is the verso and bleed-through, not another ciphertext. BnF fr. 3315 f. 21r with the cipher flap covering the clear text; a small Italian decipherment is written between the signs. The same recto with its flap folded away: the complete clear copy, dated Da Lione alli xxviii di settembre 1574 and signed Renato Birago. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3315 f. 21r, via Gallica view 24.

Birago had expected Nevers at Lyon throughout the month for the feast of St Michael. Since he has not come, Birago hopes to see him shortly, though not as soon as he would like. The bearer’s purpose has come at a bad time: affairs of the kingdom are such that virtually anything else would be considered before it. He therefore returns with the dispatch that will make the answer clear. Et quanto alle cose dil Piemonte, ella intenderà similmente com’elle siano passate … rimettendomi a parlargliene poi più minutamente di bocca, quando Iddio mi farà la gratia di vederla. Birago will not commit the Piedmont business to a fuller written discussion. He adds that Their Majesties are very willing to provide Nevers with a governorship and every other thing he deserves, and that he has done and will continue to do every good office of a true servant and friend. A semi-diplomatic transcription of the whole leaf is in targets/nevers1574/f21_transcription.md ; only one short expression in the first sentence remains uncertain.

The cipher fills two dense pages and the first 19 lines of f. 16r. Above almost every run a smaller contemporary hand has supplied its plaintext. The letter opens: Monseigneur, je ne veulx faillir a vous advertir que ce jourd’huy a esté rendu a monsieur de Savoye Pignerol et Savillan, au grant contentement du Roy et de la Royne mere, qui ont faict ce beau chef d’euvre. The duchess then went to the Queen Mother’s council. Catherine asked why Nevers should not pass through, since he did not lose his government for that; the duchess answered that, cut down as it was, she held it for lost. At court it had been told to the King that Nevers had written of “une ligue aupres du Roy de quatre ou cinq”. Two governments “qui ne pouvoient faillir, comme Picardie et Languedoc” are in prospect, and his friends say that if he keeps his government as it now stands “vous vous feriez beaucoup de tort”. The reading ( f15_reading.md , English f15_en.md ) has 4 holes in 402 tokens on f. 15r and f. 16r; on f. 15v lines 2–5 are overwritten and their gloss is faded. Over the whole letter the reading builds coherent sentences but reads at 94.1% of its words (measured 24 October 2026), under the 95% a complete reading needs. The outer address is clear: A Monsieur, Monsieur le duc de Nevers, pair de France . The cipher runs on from the foot of f. 15v into the first 19 lines of f. 16r (“Je luy ay” continues there), and then gives way to a clear ending in the duchess’s hand. The writer says it is midnight, her eyes hurt from weeping, she wishes herself in paradise rather than suffer the way they are being made to suffer, and asks God to grant her “bon frère” patience. The closing reads “De Lyon ce 16 de septembre”; the year 1574 is inferred from the archival setting. A superficially similar appeal of Henri III to the duchess printed by Lavisse belongs to an earlier occasion, before his departure for Poland, and cannot serve as a crib for this letter. F. 15r: the large cipher signs and the much smaller French decipherment compete for the same narrow spaces. The page carries its own decipherment, transcribed line by line on the Gallica native images. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3315 f. 15r, via Gallica view 17.

Tomokiyo observed that ff. 15 and 21 do not use the Nevers key copied at ff. 12–13. They closely resemble Nevers collection no. 2, issued a decade later in 1584 and preserved in BnF fr. 3995 f. 16, but differ in decisive assignments: on the 1574 leaves F is e , 9 is q , and x, y and z are left in clear. The 1584 table therefore shows the design of the system (an alphabet of graphic signs, special signs for doubled consonants, and nulls), but it cannot be applied to this text as it stands. BnF fr. 3995 f. 16: Nevers no. 2 (1584), the close sibling identified by Tomokiyo. Mechanical substitution from this table gives wrong plaintext on the 1574 leaves. Image: Bibliothèque nationale de France, fr. 3995 f. 16, via Gallica btv1b525085665. The 1574 alphabet was rebuilt on 22 October 2026 by aligning the f. 15 signs with the French gloss above them ( f15_key.md ): a=1, c=C, d=a b-shape, e=F or E, g=0, i/j=7, l=3, m=+, n=2, o=8, q and s=9, r=T, t=4, u/v=6, with a doubling sign, name signs for the King, the Queen Mother and the Queen, and XX with digits for a number. Every value is attested in several words. It is close to the 1584 no. 2 alphabet but not the same.

F. 15v ll. 2–5 and the gloss-only line at its head (about 70 words). The decipherer wrote over the cipher signs and the gloss above is faded or struck; the original or a multispectral image might recover them. About a dozen single groups on f. 15v (ll. 7, 10, 12–16, 20–23) and f. 16r (ll. 1, 14), which neither the signs nor the faded gloss settle; the group XX before “une ligue” is not spelled. One phrase on f. 21 (grade I). The fair copy appears to write per saluato suo ; it may contain a personal name or abbreviation. The rest of the clear copy is transcribed at grade H.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. Henriette de Clèves to the duke of Nevers, Lyon, 16 Sept [1574], ff. 15-16 read in part The duchess tells her husband that Pignerol and Savillan have been handed to the Duke of Savoy, to the contentment of the King and the Queen Mother, so that Nevers is left without his government; her exchange with the Queen Mother (who first approves warning him, then says he does not lose his government) and her tears; a report to the King that Nevers had written of a league of four or five near the King; promises of the next vacant government (Picardy, Languedoc); his friends say he would harm himself by keeping the reduced government. Cipher continues on f. 16r (19 lines), then a clear closing: it is midnight, she would rather be in paradise. The letter reports the news, the duchess's audience with Catherine de Médicis (la Royne mere / la Royne), a rumour at court that Nevers had written to the King about a "ligue" of four or five, and his friends' advice about the remaining governorship. The two governorships "qui ne pouvoient faillir" are Picardie and Languedoc. Birago's letter of 28 Sept (f. 21) speaks of the same "governo". * 15r l.3: the group after "du" is not spelled out; it is glossed "Roy" (same sense as `SS` elsewhere). * 15r l.12: "et recevoir une conte…": signs `F4 TFCF687T 62F C824F..`; the end of the line is crossed by the gloss. * 15r l.17: "tiens": the sign group is partly struck; the gloss is "t[?]". * 15r l.21: "veid": signs `6Fb74`; the gloss reads "veit/veid". * 15v ll.1-5 (after "25 ans ceste couronne si fidellement"): the cipher is overwritten letter by letter by the decipherer and the gloss above is faded; only "ayant tant", "aviez", "la moitié", "elle a", "recompense" and "France" are carried. This is the main hole of the letter (about 70 words). * 15v l.7: `T1b879` after "chose que" does not resolve ("racontoit"?); `XXm` is glossed "24". * 15v l.9: "qu'il c'estoit faict" as written (`CF94874`), i.e. s'estoit. * 15v l.10: the group `XX` before "une ligue" is not spelled; left unread. * 16r l.1: `21 CF(99F` after "vous n'a…" does not resolve. * 16r l.14: `C824F2bTF` (glossed illegibly) left unread. * The f. 16r clear ending was re-read on the native image: "de Lion ce 16 [one word struck] septembre". The word after "je ne vous" (underlined with a flourish) is not read. * Ernest Lavisse, *Histoire de France* VI.1, prints an emotional appeal of Henri III to the duchess written before his departure for Poland. It is not this letter and was not used as a crib. Having learnt this, I went to the Queen's council and said to her: "Madame, my husband wrote to me in the last of his letters that on his way back here he would pass through his government; he was planning to stay a week to put things in order there, which he no longer needs to do, since he no longer has a government. Will you allow me to tell him so, so that he wastes no time [?and receives] a [?...]." She answered that I would do very well to do so; and then she corrected herself and said to me: "Why should he not go there? He does not lose his government because of this." I answered that, left as small as it was, I [?hold] it as good as lost, because you had too much heart to keep what a mere gentleman would refuse. She added that it was true that it was left very small indeed. When she had gone to bed she told me, because she saw me weeping, that I must not torment myself over this, and that the loss is not my husband's but entirely the King's. I told her that I was not weeping for the King's loss, but for your misfortune, that after serving ## f. 15v this crown so faithfully for 25 years, and having so much [?affection] [...] you had [...] [...] [...]. [...] and [?half] [...] she has [...] [...] and as a reward [...]. [... about twenty words unread ...] France. Besides, I [?wished] to tell her [...] a thing that [...] in the last 24 hours, which was that the King had been told that it was you who had written to him that a league [...] of four or five had been formed close to the King, and that she would do well to deal with it. What I [?thought] [...] in [?part] that he [...] [...]. [...] because since he came back he [...] [...] to speak of you as he had [...]. [...] [...] it was a thing about which [one] himself [?could] bear witness; then she told me that she thought not, for the King had not spoken to her of it at all, but that tomorrow she would speak to him about it and learn the truth; and [...] or the other that [...] it would be very strange to [...] such people against one who had done him so many services. For the rest, [...] that I first [...] government that should fall vacant, you [...]; in [?fact] there would be two that could not fail, such as Picardy and Languedoc. I ## f. 16r (cipher, lines 1-19) answered her that it was a thing you had [...] never [asked] anything but the offices of men still living, that one was too close a kinsman of yours and that the other had too much means of making his own settlement. That is how everything went, which I wished to tell you word for word so that you may decide what you have to do about it. But I cannot keep from telling you that all your friends and servants say that if you keep your said government in the state it is left in today, you would do yourself great harm; yet I cannot [...] you on these matters, because they are beyond my reach. I could not express to you the [...] and the satisfaction they have at the said surrender, and I advise you not to send them anything about it, for fear they take it badly. ## f. 16r (clear, in the duchess's hand) I beg you to excuse me if I do not write to you at greater length, for it is midnight and my eyes hurt me so much from weeping that I cannot [...] you so; I have nothing else to tell you for now, except that, seeing the way we are [?led], I would wish to be in paradise. I pray God, my good brother, to give you patience. From Lyon, this 16 September. Address: To Monsieur, Monsieur the duke of Nevers, peer of France. Renato Birago to the duke of Nevers, Lyon, 28 Sept 1574, f. 21 Birago had expected Nevers in Lyon for St Michael's day; the bearer's business comes at the worst moment, as the affairs of the kingdom make anything else more urgent; Birago will speak of Piedmont by mouth; Their Majesties are well disposed to give Nevers a government and whatever else he deserves. The decryption is the clear fair copy on the same recto; the cipher flap itself was not transcribed sign by sign. One doubtful phrase, `[?Salvato] suo` (written *saluato suo*: a name, or the participle "saved"). Italian. ## Translation Most illustrious and most excellent lord, I wrote to Your Excellency these past days what was needed for your [?Salvato], and I believed you would be here by the end of this month to keep the feast of Saint Michael; but since you have not come so far, I hope you will come soon, though it will not be as soon as I desire. For the rest, the occasion for which the present bearer has come here has been ill-timed and out of season, more than could be, because the affairs of this kingdom are today in such a state that one would sooner think of anything else in the world than of that. And so he returns with such a despatch as Your Excellency will learn, on which I have nothing more to tell you. And as to the affairs of Piedmont, you will likewise learn how they have passed, on which it does not seem to me fit to enter into any other discourse with Your Excellency for now, leaving it to speak to you of it more minutely by mouth, when God grants me the grace of seeing you. Only I will tell you that Their Majesties are of very good will to provide Your Excellency with a government, and with every other thing, as you deserve. In which (although I know it is not necessary) I have not failed, nor shall I fail, to do for you every good office that a true servant and friend of yours should do. And with this, after humbly commending myself to Your Excellency's good grace, I pray Our Lord God to grant you a long and happy life. From Lyon, the 28th of September 1574. Your Excellency's most affectionate servant, Renato Birago Key: f15_key.md

A Venetian ambassador’s despatch from the court of Paul IV (ASVe Busta 30, DECODE R1873), catalogued with a neighbour’s 1555 English metadata. Its four passages in a nomenclator of letters with superscript letters (176 signs) were transcribed and deciphered by Paolo Bonavoglia; the text is taken from his published decipherment, and the key was not rebuilt. Mocenigo found the Pope cold and suspected the Carafa nephews of keeping him from an audience over the bishopric of Brescia. ee Ey ts ao Lo ac ft ca eo Lu nx … (base letter + superscript letter) Sua Santità quando principiai parlare di questo… Rome → Doge of Venice · letter-and-superscript nomenclator, Italian · 25 April 1558 · existing decipherment Alvise Mocenigo to the Doge, Rome 1558 from Alvise Mocenigo → to Doge Lorenzo Priuli Go to the full text ↓ A Venetian ambassador’s report from the court of Paul IV, with four passages in a nomenclator of letters carrying superscript letters; the text comes from Paolo Bonavoglia’s published decipherment. A signed duplicate of his despatch. Where Archivio di Stato di Venezia, IT ASVe 0045 010 Busta 30 ff. 4–6; DECODE R1873. Catalogued under catalogue 264 together with R1871, a Paris despatch of 1680 in another cipher. The cipher Each sign is a base letter with a superscript letter; signs stand for letters, syllables and words. 176 signs, 89 distinct. How it was deciphered Paolo Bonavoglia transcribed and deciphered the four passages on crittologia.eu. His text is taken unchanged; the key was not rebuilt here. What it says The Pope cooled when Mocenigo raised his business, and the Carafa nephews, chasing the bishopric of Brescia, seemed to want him kept from an audience. Still open The key, sign by sign. The text itself is complete. Credit Paolo Bonavoglia (decipherment); Satoshi Tomokiyo (pointer on DECODE R1872). Until 14 October 2026 this despatch shared an entry with R1871, Sebastiano Foscarini’s Paris despatch of 1680: a different cipher, with its own page .

The six images of R1873 (folios 4–6) show a despatch headed “Duplicato”, dated “Di Roma alli 25 d’April 1558” and signed by Alvise Mocenigo, knight, Venetian ambassador to Paul IV. The clear Italian deals with Cardinal Carlo Carafa, the bishoprics of Cyprus and Brescia (Bernardo Navagero, “mio precessor”), and the envoy of the Duke of Urbino. Four passages on pages 3, 4 and 5 are in cipher. DECODE lists the record with an unnamed sender and an unknown recipient; catalogue 264 gave the pair “England?” and 1555, metadata that seems to come from the neighbouring record R1872 (Giovanni Michiel, Brussels, 1555). The despatch is not calendared in CSP Venice vi, which for April 1558 prints only despatches touching England. The DECODE images are not in the public domain and may be published only with the archive’s permission, so none are reproduced here. The line in the strip above is the opening of Bonavoglia’s transcription.

Every cipher sign is a letter with a second letter written above it (Bonavoglia writes them as pairs: ee Ey ts ao Lo… ). The four passages hold 176 signs, 89 of them different; the commonest are nx (9 times) and ca (7). The table covers single letters, syllables and a list of words. Bonavoglia places it in the family of the Venetian “Cifra n. 3” of 1577, and compares it with the cipher Michel Surian used in England in 1557.

Bonavoglia’s decipherment opens: Sua Santità quando principiai parlare di questo lo uidi alquanto mutare nella facia et nelli ochi… In English: when Mocenigo began to speak of the matter, the Pope’s face changed and he answered coldly, so Mocenigo expected no good office from “sua signoria”. It was common talk that this lord would do anything to obtain the bishopric of Brescia (“il uescouado di Bressa”), and that the will of Cardinal Carafa would prevail. Mocenigo suspected that the Carafa nephews, because of these bishoprics, did not want him heard by the Pope so soon. The text is Bonavoglia’s, saved from the Wayback Machine’s copy of his page (22 June 2025; the live page returned an error in September 2026). It was not re-checked here against the images sign by sign.
The key. Bonavoglia’s transcription and decipherment have not been aligned sign by sign here, so no table of values is published with this page.

DECODE R8356, catalogued as a ciphered letter of Elizabeth, is Walsingham’s Paris letter-book: the Queen’s letter is in clear, and the cipher is a nine-symbol run and two code groups in Walsingham to Burghley of 25 June 1571. Transcribed but not deciphered: no key survives and the run is too short to recover one. The [12] 6 1 7 4 a H 6 H H shewed me his M[aste]rs letters … come from [E4] Paris → London · name code with a short cipher run · June 1571 Walsingham’s letter-book, June 1571 from Francis Walsingham → to William Cecil BL Harley MS 260 ff. 112v–113r, DECODE R8356, catalogued as a ciphered letter of Elizabeth to an unknown recipient. It is a letter-book copy of Walsingham to Burghley, 25 June 1571, with one cipher run and two code groups, followed by the Queen’s letter to Walsingham in clear. The cipher was transcribed and not deciphered: no key survives and the run is too short to recover one. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained · On the map not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letter Walsingham to Burghley, 25 June 1571, copied in the fair-copy letter-book of Walsingham’s Paris embassy. The Queen’s clear letter that follows it gives the record its “Elizabeth R.” heading. Where British Library, Harley MS 260 ff. 112v–113r; DECODE R8356, two pages, the same volume as R8361. The cipher Two boxed codes, [12] and [E4], and a nine-symbol run whose pattern (first = seventh, sixth = eighth = ninth) fits no English word under simple substitution. How it was tried Digges printed the letter in The Compleat Ambassador (1655) with the cipher as figures and no decipherment. CSP Foreign gives none, and no Walsingham key of 1570–73 is known. What it says In context, [12] with the run names a man who showed Walsingham his master’s letters, warning of a practice to steal away the Queen of Scots; [E4] is the informant. Still open The nine-symbol run is too short to attack without a key, and [12] and [E4] each occur once. Sender, recipient, date and context are identified; the cipher is not.

Image P1 (f. 112v) ends Leicester’s letter to Walsingham (“Yo r assured frend R. Leicester”) and begins Walsingham to Burghley. Image P2 (f. 113r) ends that letter, “the xxv th of June 1571”, and begins “Elizabeth R. … To the right trustie and welbeloved Frauncis Walsingham Esq r o r Amba: resident w th o r good brother the Frenche Kinge”. The Queen’s letter concerns the French ambassador, M. de L’Archant, captain of the guard of the Duke of Anjou, and the coming of the Marshal Montmorency. It is written entirely in clear. f. 112v: the cipher run in line 1, and [E4] in line 12 (“come from [E4] who discovereth it to his M.”). Image: British Library, Harley MS 260 f. 112v, via DECODE R8356 (image P1).

“The [12] 6 1 7 4 a H 6 H H shewed me his M rs letters dated the ix th of this moneth”. Image: British Library, Harley MS 260 f. 112v, via DECODE R8356 (image P1). In context, [12] with the run names the man who showed Walsingham his master’s letters, which asked him to warn “A.” of a practice to steal away the Queen of Scots. [E4] is the informant “who discovereth it to his Master”. Digges (p. 106) prints the run as “1627 40q0n 6> nu” and [E4] as “54”. Both are the compositor’s guesses at the symbols and carry no decipherment.

Print: the letter is in Digges 1655 with the cipher as figures. CSP Foreign 1569–71 gives no decipherment. Pattern: A B C D E F A F F fits no English word or name under one-to-one substitution. The cipher is homophonic, uses code symbols, or is several codes. Siblings: the letter run in R8361 ( 7 7 6 + w 5 ‡ 6 3 ∩ 6 , Nov 1572) shares signs but gives no crib. Keys: no Walsingham–Burghley key of 1570–73 is on DECODE or in Tomokiyo’s Elizabethan tables.
The nine-symbol run: too short, with no key. Codes [12] and [E4]: each is used once, and no key material exists.

Its only marks are two boxed 9s that flag the cover-names Lyons and Roome. Not a cipher; nothing to decipher. Baurleighs? to unknown recipient, 27 Jan 1572”. The page is a fair copy of a letter from William Cecil, Lord Burghley, to Sir Francis Walsingham, ambassador in France. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 22 September 2026 · updated 26 October 2026 Method: not a cipher · On the map closed At a glance Not a cipher The letter Burghley to Walsingham, Westminster, 24 January 1572 (1573 in modern reckoning), copied in a fair-copy letter-book. He regrets he cannot yet settle Walsingham’s recall from France. Where British Library, Harley MS 260 f. 395r; DECODE R8362 lists it as a ciphered letter of “W. Baurleighs?” dated 27 January 1572. The day is 24, and the recipient is Walsingham. The cipher There is none to solve. The page holds no letter cipher or code numbers, only two boxed 9s after “Lyons” and “Roome”, which in this volume mark cover-names. What it says Printed by Digges (1655). The cover-names concern a ship that waited “the space of 23 daies”; the whole letter is cleartext. Still open Who “Lyons” and “Roome” stand for is not stated in the letter-book, Digges or the Calendars. Whether the boxed 9 carries a value is not established.

The page carries the running head “Januarie 1572”. The letter is copied in the same hand as the rest of the register, so this is the letter-book copy, not the letter as sent. DECODE made two misreadings. It read the day as 27 when the page has “24th”, and it left the recipient unknown although the register belongs to Walsingham. The address at the foot of the page, “To my verie …”, is cut off at the page end. Harley MS 260 f. 395r: “Glascoe Davison longeth to heare from Lyons [9] for that by your last tickett … one should come from Roome [9]”. Image: British Library, Harley MS 260 f. 395r, via DECODE R8362.

Burghley writes that he is “sorie and ashamed” that he cannot yet send anything that settles Walsingham’s own case, his recall from France. He promises to keep working for it. He leaves news of Lord Worcester’s journey to the Secretary. Then he comes to the business of the cover-names: Glascoe Davison longeth to heare from Lyons [9] for that by your last tickett, I understand that Steward tould you that one should come from Roome [9], the shipp abode in the place appointed the space of 23 daies. And soe I end, trusting to see you here amongst your frinds within this sixe weekes at the leaste to bee revoked by that tyme. From Westm the 24th of Januarie 1572. Your assured frind William Baurleighe. “Tickett” is the separate slip on which Walsingham sent his secret news. The same plot about a ship runs through the letters of November 1572 and January 1573 in this volume ( R8361 , R8364 ). Added 1 October 2026: the ship that stayed “the space of 23 daies” is the one sent for the Duke of Alençon; a Folger chronology says it waited in vain off the French coast for 23 days. “Davison” is his agent Maisonfleur (see R8364 ).

In the Harley 260 letters that Digges printed, boxed digits appear directly after a place name: Florence [9], Rome [9], Glasgow [7], and in February 1573 both “Glasco [9]” and “Glasco [g]”. The same cover-word takes different digits, so the digit does not encode a value. The box flags the word before it as a cover-name for a person. In R8362 both boxes follow place names, Lyons and Roome, and the sentence makes sense without them. That accounts for both marks; the page has no others. Caution, 1 October 2026: in R8364 the boxed 9 reads as the Duke of Alençon in context, so it may carry a value. That the box means nothing is not established.

Who is meant by “Lyons” and “Roome”. “Glascoe” is a cover-name for the Duke of Alençon, not the Archbishop of Glasgow as first thought (see R8364 ). The other two cover-names are never glossed. This is a question of historical identification, not of cipher.

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 Method: not solved · Extent: text not obtained not solved At a glance Not solved · text not obtained The letters Two undated letters signed by Fabrizio Ruffo, principe di Castelcicala, Neapolitan ambassador in London and Paris, to Naples; no number, address or date survives on either. Where Archivio di Stato di Napoli, Ministero degli affari esteri, busta 2337; DECODE R9586 (catalogue item 167) and R9588 (catalogue item 166). The cipher A numeric code with groups mostly from 100 to 1100 and a few higher ones (1405, 1698, 1858, 1930); many groups carry short overbars. Castelcicala’s other despatches use the Segreteria di Stato code, whose groups run mostly from 1350 to 2450. How far it got Both letters were transcribed (537 and 432 groups) with the rest of the busta and recognised as a separate system. No key has been tried and no attack run. What might finish it Faint pencil syllabic glosses over a few runs (“ba li, che non effett in o la sol tan za”) are a possible crib; aligning them with their groups is the next step. Other ciphers Castelcicala’s despatches in the Segreteria di Stato code are deciphered in part on their own page .

R9586 : three pages, no number, address or date visible, signed “Castelcicala”; 537 groups, 240 distinct. R9588 : two pages, no number, Eccellenza or date, signed “Il Principe di Castelcicala”; 432 groups, 220 distinct; the top four lines of the second page were photographed blurred. The two letters share their frequent groups (224, 1043, 1698, 294, 319) and almost none of the 1400–2450 groups that dominate the Segreteria di Stato code of the other twenty-five letters in the busta, so they are one system and a different one. The images carry the archive’s notice on DECODE that publishing them needs its permission, so no crop is shown here.

A later hand wrote a few syllables in faint pencil over some runs. Transcribed so far: on R9586 p. 2, “se dell … cam bia … an … cut … ver” over eight groups, “ba li, che non effett in o la sol tan za”, “tta con … si … ri … chi … ed ella” and “ei di san”; on R9588, “tal … in che stato”. Their placement over the groups is not yet fixed, so no value is claimed.

Aligning the glosses with their groups on the images, extending the values through repeats in the two letters, and trying the other codes of busta 2337 and of the Neapolitan legations. The work is in progress; for now the letters are attempted, not solved.

The letter opens in clear. Sessa had seen a letter of the Bishop of Veroli from Constance and sent to the Pope for particulars. Felice, the papal secretary, told him the bishop’s letters of the 6th and 7th reported that the Swiss diet was over and that Lucerne had not agreed to help the French. Bern, Fribourg and Solothurn, the letter goes on, were spreading word that the Swiss in Lombardy were surrounded, so as to raise eight thousand men. The bishop’s friends in Switzerland wanted him to urge the Pope towards some form of peace. Esto es lo que me ha referido. Then nine lines of cipher. Code groups are resolved; a hyphen joins letters spelled sign by sign; brackets mark what is not deciphered; bold is clear text written between the cipher runs. las dichas [—]s no le las mostraron, que le ponen sospecha que desea aver algo que refiera de lo susodicho, aunque no / me parece que concuerda mucho con lo primero y postrero que el dicho obispo dize al maestro de postas / hablé en la ora a Su Santidad a pedirle que haya provisión de [—]-r-a los casos de suyços, persuadiéndole los m-re que r-ido los que no m-r-e-van / pues tiene color para ello, aviendo començado la plática de la paz y tregua … entender lo que mas podré. Al visorrey escrivo en el mismo punto. In English: The said [letters] they did not show him, for they make him suspect a wish to get something out of them that he might report of the aforesaid, although not; it seems to me that it agrees closely with the first and last of what the said bishop writes to the postmaster. I spoke at once to His Holiness to ask him to make provision [of money] for the Swiss business, persuading him … since he has a pretext for it, having begun the negotiation of the peace and truce … to learn what more I can. I write to the Viceroy at the same moment. Bergenroth’s abstract of the 22 April letter (CSP Spain 2, no. 643) continues the story: the Pope and the Swiss disapprove of the disbanding of the army, and there is “no provision of money from His Holiness or the Florentines beyond what I wrote”.

A holograph of eight leaves (A-31 ff. 79–86), clear with cipher runs on ff. 80v–84r and a postscript wholly in cipher on f. 86r, dated in clear A xiiij de Abril 1524 . No decipherment is bound with it. Bergenroth calendars it as no. 637, “deciphered by Don Manuel de Goicoechea” for him in the nineteenth century; no. 636 is the triplicate of the same despatch with a contemporary deciphering, and no. 638 a court abstract. Those English abstracts were used for the order of topics only: no group value was taken from them without a second Spanish context. The whole letter was transcribed on 2 October 2026 and read with the pass-16 key. 2,165 of 2,473 cipher tokens read as sense (87.5%) , each assembled word scored on a Golden Age Spanish model; 256 tokens are in open code groups and 52 spelled letters make no word. Pass 17 (3 October 2026) pooled the open groups of R9873, R9898 and R9660 (Sessa’s letter of 1523): 84 groups occur in two or more letters, and a value was taken only where it reads in every occurrence, for example cas = tiene , var = agora , rac = dize , pam = paga , xoc = socorr- , sur = parte , yer = Florencia . All are tentative: none has a deciphered occurrence. With them, 2,295 of 2,474 tokens read as sense (92.8%) ; counting them as open, 87.8%. About 100 groups (145 tokens) and 34 spelled letters remain without sense; the non-words were re-checked at full zoom and stand as written, apart from one sign (f. 83r, pudiesse ). Written out, 23 October 2026. The reading audit of 22 October 2026 set R9873 back to decoded, not read: the working file was a line-by-line decode with an open group or a non-word in most sentences. It was then written out as continuous Spanish in its 1524 spelling, every word aligned with the decode or the clear text ( r9873_reading.md , English r9873_en.md ), with further values pooled from R9898, R9660 and a new sibling, R9899 (A-34 ff. 194–195, March 1525), whose one marginal decipherment gives hog = querria . Adopted: gal embia- , hog querria , kaz -mente , and, from sense only and flagged, reb dezi- , dis servido , sur / luc parte , gom quatro and others. The sentences hold through ff. 80v–82v, 83v–84r and the postscript, and agree topic by topic with CSP Spain 2 no. 636; f. 83r ll. 19–25 still do not hold. Counting every sense-only value and every look-alike letter as a hole, the letter stays just over the reading bar, so it reads (grade B); the flagged values await the triplicate’s contemporary decipherment (Gayangos papers) or Kolosova’s key. R9898 was written out the same way ( r9898_reading.md ) but stays decoded, not read: about 140 code groups occur once, and its bleed-through pages do not resolve. ff. 80v–81r. The disbanding of the army in Navarre was known in Rome; the Emperor is said to be holding cortes in Burgos, then in Aragon and Catalonia, and coming to Italy with the grant, which does not please this court. The Archbishop of Capua left Blois on the 7th with the truce articles. Sessa proposed two things: that the archbishop go from France to England first, para satisfazer a la autoridad del rey , and that the King of France pay the King of England his old pension for the length of the truce. ff. 81v–82r. The 4,000 ducats the Lodi men took at the Stradella, sent by the Pope under another name; the Pope at first muy bravo , then cooled. He will write to the Cardinal of Cortona that his nephew Ippolito is to assist at the government of Florence, has made good the 4,000 ducats and sends 4,000 more; Su Sd. ha estado en grandissimo conflito , not willing to disdain the enemies; those around him keep him irresolute, si no Micer Agostino Foyeta (Foglietta). ff. 82v–83v. Money found on exchange for the viceroy’s army; the nuncio’s letters of 26 March from England: the King has no heart for the war; Wolsey would hear of a truce if the Pope got the King of France to send someone debaxo de alguna onesta color ; the English will not contribute in Italy por ninguna via . Advice on the Emperor’s standing with friends and enemies, his nephews’ marriages, Alberto Pio, Count of Carpi. f. 86r, the postscript. The Pope and his ministers are grieved beyond measure at the disbanding; he will not declare himself en liga defensiva ni ofensiva , though there was never a time so fit para acabar de ronper las alas a franceses ; what holds him back is fear. The order and substance match Bergenroth’s no. 636 point for point (the cortes, Capua from Blois, the two proposals, the pension, the 4,000 ducats, the nuncio’s letters of 26 March, the English refusal, Madame Margaret). That agreement is the check on the reading.

A long despatch in a secretary’s hand (A-34 ff. 150–156), dated in clear De Roma a xxiiij de hebrero 1525 , the day of the battle of Pavia and so written before the news. It is not calendared in CSP Spain iii.1. An earlier pass here said it carried no decipherment despite DECODE’s status; that was wrong. Six cipher runs have a contemporary marginal decipherment in a second hand (ff. 150r, 152r, 153v, 154r, 154v three times, 156r), and they were the cribs of pass 16: v em cierto , li mi , le me , net halla , sud datario , yol aqui , kun duque , and the name Micer Agostino Foyeta . 2,361 of 3,059 cipher tokens read as sense (77.2%) after pass 16; 300 tokens are in open groups, and 398 spelled letters make no word, most of them on ff. 150v–151r and 155v, where bleed-through on the images hides the difference between the cursive r, u and n. With the pass-17 tentative values, 2,441 (79.8%) , or 77.9% counting them as open; 237 tokens in about 140 groups and 381 letters on the bleed-through pages remain. Re-cut at 1.5 times, those pages do not resolve further, and no other image of A-34 could be found. ff. 150r–152r. The Pope did not answer the Emperor’s letters of 15 November and 15 December; the Datary’s French partisanship que abiertamente se conoce ; the French have tried the English ambassador; the Pope offered to secure his master’s pension during the truce. In the margin: aqui ninguna cosa nos comunican, sabiendo que las entendemos y conocemos; por conjeturas sabemos lo que ocurre . ff. 152v–154r. Albany’s march on the Kingdom of Naples; lo de Inglaterra se va calentando ; the Archbishop of Capua kept at Piacenza con color de la platica de la paz ; in the margin, se de buena parte que el datario ha tentado de reduzir al duque a franceses . f. 154v. Sessa sent to San Germano by the viceroy; in the margin, y cierto si mi obligacion no me forçara … y viendo la malissima providencia que ha avido, dueleme grandemente hallarme a lo que por razon y no por caso temo que suceda . ff. 155v–156r. Pavia expects relief; attacking the French in their strong position would be a manifest disadvantage. Postscript: the Duke of Ferrara has lent the King of France another 50,000 ducats, and (margin) no le plaze mucho al papa, aunque no quiere confessar, es en su menosprecio y que franceses le ayan tomado en su protecion .

No key for this cipher survives, and none is in print. What survives is Sessa’s correspondence, and in a number of his letters the court wrote the decipherment on a separate leaf marked A Claro , B Claro . Each of those gives cipher and clear side by side. The work went through eight of them. Three letters of April and May 1524 gave the first 60 groups: f. 138 against f. 140 (17 April), ff. 168v–171 against ff. 172–173 (22 April), f. 322 against ff. 324–325 (19 May). Every cipher line was cut into images of single tokens by a script that splits the line at gaps in the ink, and each token was transcribed and aligned from its image. That separated look-alike signs the eye had merged: two p-loops (plural -s and b ), two three-shapes ( r and i ), two hooked signs ( d and u ). Six more letters were fetched from DECODE: January and February 1525, 24 and 29 July 1524, and seven of 1523. The January 1525 letter gave dicha ; 24 July gave mostrar , quiere and hay . The February 1525 letter was at first taken to carry no decipherment; on 2 October 2026 six marginal decipherments were found on it (section 05). Template matching then searched every downloaded page, about 110, for the target’s groups still without a value, at five scales. The September 1523 letter gave -on , twice, in dilataron and concedieron .

The coming of the Archbishop of Capua (he left Blois on the 7th with the truce articles; the Pope had a copy given to Sessa) would settle *estas alteraciones*. Sessa proposed two things: that the archbishop go from France to England first, *para satisfazer a la autoridad del rey*, and that the King of France pay the King of England the pension he used to pay before the war, for the length of the truce. Starting from the Pope it would have been easier; it was not done, *no se si del poco aparejo que saben* there is for carrying the war on; they try to settle things with less difficult conditions. Couriers by sea and by land (Rodrigo de Mayorga); the coming, quality and nature of *el dicho duque*. - **f. 81v.** The Emperor's estimation; the 4,000 ducats the Lodi men took at the Stradella, sent by the Pope *con nombre que yva al [kam] de su casa*. - **f. 82r.** The Pope at first *muy bravo*, then cooled; his difficulty in contributing to the army; the Florentines have given nothing; he has told Sessa he will write this week to the Cardinal of Cortona that Ippolito, his nephew, is to assist at the government (of Florence); he has made good the said 4,000 ducats lost and is sending another 4,000 this week; he is *en grandissimo conflicto*, temporising, not willing to disdain the enemies; nothing hoped for has come from England; those near him conform him in this irresolution and draw him away, *si no Micer Agostino Foyeta* (Foglietta); Sessa declares himself *mas aficionado* (to the Pope's service). - **f. 82v.** Sessa has found a sum of ducats on exchange for the viceroy's need to keep the army (with the bishops of Salamanca and Ávila). England: the nuncio's letters of 26 March say the King takes no great heart to undertake the war and waits for the Emperor's resolution; the Cardinal (Wolsey) said lately that if the Pope got the King of France to send a person *debaxo de alguna onesta color*, the truce or peace would be heard, so as not to seem to incline to it himself, *que seria perder de reputacion*; the English will not contribute to the war in Italy *por ninguna via*; Madama (Margaret) writes the same. - **f. 83r.** Advice: the Emperor's estimation, in peace or in war, must grow and be kept, more with friends than with enemies; the confederates; to treat with the Pope; marriages and the advancement of his nephews; the Emperor's coming to Italy, *sin hablarlo con Su Sd.*; *no fiandose V.Md. en la que hizo con la buena memoria del papa Leon*. - **f. 83v.** If the Emperor came to Italy with great power ...; the pontificate; Alberto Pio, Count of Carpi *(que da al B-e-r-t-o del C-a-r-p-i-o)* and his credit with the Datary. - **f. 86r (postscript).** The Pope and his ministers are grieved beyond measure at the disbanding; those who advised his irresolution think they have won; he will not declare himself in a defensive or offensive league, although they judge there was never a time so fit to break the wings of the French; if on that frontier and in Picardy something were done, the Pope would decide, though Sessa has always known him inclined to abase the French; what holds him back is fear; they wait for what the Archbishop of Capua brings. A slip of eleven lines, 496 signs in 65 words divided by points, all in cipher. Its 22 signs are built on a running horizontal stroke: uprights with one, two or three bars, crosses, a Greek-looking π. The transcription was made from the DECODE photograph; a staged annealing search over the words with an Italian language model gave the key with no crib, and a check of every doubtful word on the image separated two look-alike signs (a plain y is m , a hooked χ is r ). 477 of the 496 signs (96.2%) fall in words that make Italian sense ; 18 are in two words not yet understood and one sign, standing alone, is unread. So we remind your lordship to have bread, fodder and victuals laid in at those places as you think fit.” The envoys write from the Volterra side, on the road that enters the Sienese state at Radicondoli and Casole. SUMMARY Sienese envoys (writing "noi") warn the Signoria that a lord ("questo signiore") will not ride the way "those here" would like: he has decided, without stopping(?) here, to leave and go to Siena's territory ("d'esare chostà"). They expect him on Saturday next, by way of Laiatico (Volterra country), then Radicondoli and Casole (Sienese Val d'Elsa / Colline Metallifere) and so towards Siena. They ask the Signoria to have bread, fodder (biada) and victuals made ready in those places as it sees fit, and promise to report further by a messenger of their own ("per fante propio"). Undated; the route Laiatico -> Radicondoli -> Casole suggests a lord and his escort passing from Pisan/Volterran territory into the Sienese state. No names except places; the lord is probably behind the TH sign or unnamed on purpose. Where Archiwum Narodowe w Krakowie, Zbiór Dzieduszyckich 26/32 nr 13 and nr 5 (DECODE R7468–R7474, R7477–R7480, R7483), status N/A, no decipherment attached. The cipher Two-digit numbers for letters (a = 19, e = 9, i = 29, n = 72 …), dot-separated or run together, with a few code numbers (900 = August). How it was deciphered M. W. Kaczka printed all twelve from these originals in 2012, with the key. Ten lines of R7473, decoded with his key here, agree with the decipherment written between the lines and with his text. Still open Nothing in these letters; they were not transcribed here beyond the check. Credit Kaczka’s edition and key (after A. Mareș 1987); the contemporary interlinear decipherments. DECODE catalogues these records in one range (R7468–R7500, catalogue entry 333) with letters in four other keys, which have their own pages (a different cipher in each): fifteen German letters from a Vienna agent to Baron Schenck ( schenck1706 ), news from Bender in 1709 ( turculet1709 ), an adviser’s letter of about 1707 ( r7475 ) and Chomentowski’s letters from the Porte ( chomentowski1713 ).

Mariusz Kaczka printed the Polish letters of Constantin Brâncoveanu and Constantin Cantacuzino to Sieniawski from these originals in Danubius XXX (2012), with the Wallachian chancellery’s key in his note 21, after Andrei Mareș (1987). The DECODE records match his numbers as follows: DECODE Kaczka Letter R7468–R7469 V Brâncoveanu, 28 June 1709, with postscript R7470 VIII postscript of 30 August 1709 R7471 IV Brâncoveanu, 15 June 1709 R7472 XXIII Cantacuzino, 15 June 1709 R7473 XIII Brâncoveanu, 25 August 1712 R7474 XXVI Cantacuzino, 8 September 1714 R7477 XXV Cantacuzino, 7 May 1714 R7478 XVII Brâncoveanu, 10 August 1713 R7479 XIX Brâncoveanu, 24 January 1714 R7480 XX Brâncoveanu, 29 March 1714 R7483 XXI postscript, 1714 (nr 5, now pp. 9–10) Kaczka names the collection Zbiór Dzieduszyckich; DECODE’s short names read “ADzied”.

R7473 p. 17, the head of Brâncoveanu’s letter of 25 August 1712: Jasnie wielmozny M. P. Kasztela[nie krakowski] hetmanie written letter by letter over the numbers. Image: Archiwum Narodowe w Krakowie, Zbiór Dzieduszyckich 26/32 nr 13 p. 17, via DECODE R7473. R7473 is written with a dot after each number and deciphered letter by letter between the lines: Jaśnie wielmożny M. P. Kasztelanie krakowski hetmanie w. k. … with J/i = 29, a = 19, s = 73, n = 72, e = 9, w = 65, l = 74, m = 76, o = 39, z = 69, y = 59, P = 62, k = 67, t = 77. The same numbers, run together without dots, fill R7468–R7472, with the clear words “WM Pana” between them. Ten lines of p. 17, decoded with Kaczka’s key, give the interlinear text and his printed text, with two slips of the encipherer (69 for 67 in krakowski , prszez ). The letters were not transcribed in full here: their text is Kaczka’s. What this entry adds is the identification of twelve DECODE records, listed with no decipherment, with his edition.

George Lasry reconstructed the key (SP106-2) and deciphered it on DECODE in 2020; his key, applied here group by group, gives back his text.
