Lasry suggests it may be Dr Stephen Goffe’s letter from Holland, forwarded unchanged to the King. Where The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 ff. 216–217; DECODE R787. It was part of catalogue item 59, which grouped six letters in four different keys. The cipher Numbers from 1 to 60 for letters, two for most letters and nine for I, separated by commas. Numbers above 60 stand for names and titles. How it was deciphered George Lasry reconstructed the key (“TNA SP106-2”) and deciphered the letter on DECODE in October 2020. His plaintext is the text; it stays on DECODE as his work and is not in this repository, so the reading audit of 22 October 2026 counted the letter as decoded, not read. On 23 October his files were fetched and the letter decoded again group by group; it still counts as decoded, not read, because the nomenclator numbers his key leaves open fall in most sentences. Applied here group by group, his key gives exactly his text. What it says The Parlement de Paris and the duc d’Épernon, an envoy who will be heard only as an ambassador, and the war news of summer 1645: Enghien, Piccolomini, the fort of Linck, Montrose. Still open 19 numbers above 60 that the key does not cover, 31 occurrences in all, including the signature. Other keys The five other letters once filed with it are in different ciphers: R785, R790, R923 (TNA SP 106), R924 (SP106-8), R929 (SP106-5).

Catalogue item 59 grouped six cipher letters of SP 106/10 from Henrietta Maria’s household in France to Charles I. George Lasry reconstructed four keys for the run, and on 14 October 2026 the entry was split so that each page presents one key. This letter is the only one of the six in his “SP106-2” key, which he dates to July and August 1645. In his files the same key also covers f. 219, a letter of 30 August 1645 bound inside the next record (R788, ff. 218–221), whose other leaves are in another key. Lasry’s note on the letter reads: “In French but not from the King. Might be Goffe from Holland to the Queen, the letter being forwarded without change from France to the King.” DECODE gives the writer as an assistant of the Queen and the receivers as the Queen and the King. Neither is settled; the letter is signed only with the numbers 103 62 A 104. The key has letter values on the numbers 1 to 60: two for most letters, four for A, E and O, and nine for I. Lasry calls it “homophonic cipher with nomenclature” and says it has no nulls, but his file lists no nomenclator values. F. 216, the head of the letter (written sideways on the leaf; shown turned). The indented first line, 103, 71, 8, 104, … , opens with the writer’s numbers; above it, “19/29” is the date, written in figures. Image: The National Archives, SP 106/10 f. 216, via DECODE R787.

The plaintext is Lasry’s and is on the DECODE record. It is quoted here with punctuation and apostrophes added, and two spellings normalised here (his “LU(LE?)” as LE, “ORLERNS” as ORLÉANS). It opens: <103> <71> A <104> DUPLICATA ENVOIE LE 19/29 JUILLET PAR AUTRE VOIE. IL Y A <9> <121>S QUE J’AI RECEU L’AUTRE DU 1 & LES DEUX JOINTES … and ends with the war news: LE DUC D’ENGUIEN A PRIS HEILDEBERG, POURSUIT LES BAVAROIS POUR LEUR DONNER BATAILLE. LE DUC D’ORLÉANS A PRIS ENCOR LE FORT DE LINCK. PICOLOMINI EST RETRANCHÉ AUTOUR DE DUNCKERQUE … JE SUIS VOTRE SERVITEUR <103> <62> A <104>, 19/29 JUILLET

Lasry’s interlinear file pairs each line of Sofia Pettersson’s transcription with his plaintext. His key was applied group by group to the cipher lines, without his plaintext. Of 1569 groups, 1538 (98.0%) get a value, and all 1538 equal his plaintext; every line’s columns line up. The other 31 are the numbers above 60 (64 five times, 103, 61 and 62 three times each, 104 and 116 twice, and single 63, 71–75, 83, 97, 102, 105, 121) and two stray figures, 9 and 06, which his plaintext also leaves open. The replay in section 02 shows the first 120 groups of that run.

The nomenclator numbers above 60. 64 looks like a party or a person (“l’estat du 64”). 103 62 A 104 is the signature. Who wrote the letter and to whom. Lasry’s suggestion, Goffe in Holland, is not tested here. Tomokiyo’s list of ciphers with no known decipherment still carries the SP 106 letters. Re-reading, 23 October 2026. Lasry’s files were fetched with the project’s DECODE login (kept out of the repository), his plaintext checked group by group on the images, and a partial reading written ( R787_reading.md , English R787_en.md ). It found something no transcription had: a covering note in cipher in the margins of f. 217 , four dot-separated lines, which reads “Celle ici est un duplicata, auquel je joins le pacquet ci-enclos que j’ai receu de la cour.” Number 116 is lettre by sense (five occurrences). The 18 other nomenclator numbers carry the names and fall in most sentences, so the letter stays decoded, not read; f. 219, the only other letter in this key, gives none of them.

A one-page cipher letter from the queen’s circle at Paris (TNA SP 106/10 f. 247, DECODE R929) on the King’s desperate affairs and the Prince’s marriage, in the key of the King’s own letters to the Queen. George Lasry’s reconstructed key (SP106-5), applied here to the transcription, gives 293 of 348 groups a value, all equal to his decipherment. 34 : 14 : 66 : 33 : 57 … n3 : 334 : e2 : n4 … P A R I S … THE <334> HAS THIS … Paris → “Sir” at the King’s side · homophonic numerical cipher with a letter-and-digit nomenclator, Lasry’s “SP106-5” key · 26 January 1646 · known key applied Henrietta Maria’s household to “Sir”, Paris, 26 January 1646 Go to the full text ↓ A one-page letter from the queen’s circle in Paris on the King’s desperate affairs and Prince Charles’s marriage, deciphered here with George Lasry’s key, which reproduces his own decipherment group for group. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 15 October 2026 · updated 23 October 2026 Method: read with known key · Extent: complete Credits · George Lasry (key or decipherment used) · Sofia Pettersson (transcription) known key At a glance Known key applied · complete The letter A writer in Henrietta Maria’s household at Paris to “Sir”, who sends weekly news of the King’s affairs, 26 January [1646]. Signed with the numbers 316 440. Where The National Archives, Kew, SP 106/10 f. 247; DECODE R929. It was part of catalogue item 59, which grouped six letters in four different keys. The cipher One- and two-digit numbers for letters, up to five for E, and a nomenclator written as a letter and a digit (n3 the , k1 of , a1 and ). This is the key of the King’s own letters to the Queen. How it was deciphered George Lasry reconstructed the key (“TNA SP106-5”) and deciphered the letter on DECODE in 2020. His key was applied here to Sofia Pettersson’s transcription without his plaintext. All 293 groups it gives a value agree with his text. The reading audit of 22 October 2026 counted the letter as decoded, not read, because his plaintext was not in this repository. On 23 October the image was transcribed line by line at full size, ten groups of the transcription corrected, and the letter built from the figures with his key and checked against his plaintext (compared, not copied): it reads. What it says Thanks for the weekly news. The King’s affairs are bad, but the writer hopes they can hold out without further losses until help arrives. Then a word on the embassy and the marriage. Still open Three code groups (566, 554, 620) and the three-group signature (316 440 236), each seen once; 199 is give or send . The other nomenclator numbers were valued from context on 23 October 2026, and the figures 81–90 turn out to be word dividers. With the open and context-valued codes as holes, the reading builds coherent sentences but reads at 89.3% of its words (measured 24 October 2026), under the 95% a complete reading needs. Other keys The five other letters once filed with it are in different ciphers: R785, R790, R923 (TNA SP 106), R787 (SP106-2), R924 (SP106-8).

Catalogue item 59 grouped six cipher letters of SP 106/10 written from Henrietta Maria’s household in France. George Lasry reconstructed four keys for the run, one for each period of the correspondence, and on 14 October 2026 the entry was split so that each page presents one key. This letter is the only one of the six in his “SP106-5” key, dated January 1646. The same key, in his files, also reads the long letter on ff. 245–246 (R928, Dr Stephen Goffe at The Hague), and it is the key of Charles I’s own letters to the Queen read on the Rupert 1645 page. The key has one- and two-digit homophones (A 14, 15, 16, 17; E 1 to 5) and a nomenclator written as a letter and a digit: a1 and , a2 are , d5 his , e5 in , k1 of , n1 to , n3 the , n4 this , p5 with . A few three-digit numbers stand for names. Lasry’s key file says there are no nulls. F. 247, the first five lines (written sideways on the leaf; shown turned). Line 1 reads 34:14:66:33:57 P-A-R-I-S; the groups n3 the and k1 of are the letter-and-digit nomenclator. Image: The National Archives, SP 106/10 f. 247, via DECODE R929.

Sr, the [?Queen] has this weke received {your}s of the 26 of Decemb and of the 4 of Ianuary, and [?give]s {you} thankes in the continuation of {your} care in [?giv]ing {her} wekly aduertisements of [566] the estate of the {King}s affaires. How bad so euer it be, I hope it is not so desperate as not to be able to subsist withovt farether losses till our endeauours {her}e for his [?Majesty]s releif may be brovght to effect. For which, as likewise concerning the embassage and mareriage of [?Port]ugall, I refer {you} to the {King} his [?letter]s, and remain, Sr, {your} most [554] [620] hvmble seruant, [316] [440] [236]. The image, read line by line at full size, corrected ten groups of Pettersson’s transcription: 810 is o2 = WE ( weke , wekly ), 993 is g3 MAY, e5 106 is c5 p6 FOR WHICH. The figures 81–90 fall only between words: they are dividers. Code values from context: 425 your , 429 you , e3 her and 241 King (two or more contexts each); 334 Queen , 208 Majesty , 319 Port ( ugall ) and 259 letter (one context or sense). Lasry’s plaintext, in his spelling, with the nomenclator numbers he left open: PARIS JAN 26 SR. THE <334> HAS THIS WEKE RECEIVED <425>S OF THE 26 OF DECEMB AND OF THE 4 OF JANUARY AND <199>S <429> THANKES IN THE CONTINUATION OF <425> CARE IN <199>ING <e3> WEKLY ADVERTISEMENTS OF <566> THEE STATE OF THE <241>S AFFAIRES. HOW BAD SO EVER IT BE I HOPE IT IS NOT SO DESPERATE AS NOT TO BE ABLE TO SUBSIST WITHOUT FARETHER LOSSES TILL OUR ENDEAVOURS <e3>E IN HIS <208>S RELEIF MAY BE BROUGHT TO EFFECT … AS LIKEWISE CONCERNING THE EMBASSAGE AND MARRIAGE The margin closes the letter: “of <319>ug all I refer <429> to the <241> his <259>s and remain, Sr, <425> most <554> <620> humble servant <316> <440> <236>”. The “embassage and marriage” are the embassy and the treaty for the Prince of Wales’s marriage, which also appear in Charles’s letter to the Queen of 22 January 1646. Lasry uses that letter to date this one to 1646.

On 19 September 2026 Lasry’s alphabet was applied by hand to Pettersson’s raw transcription, without his plaintext file. It gave “…ARIS … IAN … SR … RECEIVED <425>S … DECEMB … IANVARY … THANKES … WEKLY ADVERTISEMENTS … AFFAIRES HOW BAD … EVER … DESPERATE … LIKEWISE CONCERNING THE EMBASSAGE AND MARRIAGE”. On 14 October 2026 the whole letter was run through the key group by group. Of 348 groups, 293 (84.2%) get a value, and every one of them equals Lasry’s plaintext. The other 55 are 17 three-digit numbers (23 occurrences), the group e3 twice, and the figures 81–90 (30 occurrences). The replay in section 02 shows the first 120 groups of that run.

The three-digit nomenclator numbers: <425> (three times), <199>, <429>, <810>, <241> and others. 241 is probably the King (“the <241>s affaires”). Most of the rest look like persons. The figures 81–90 have no value in the key. They fall between words (“HOW _ BAD _ SO EUER”), so they look like word dividers or nulls, although Lasry’s key file says there are none. This is not settled here. Who 316 440 is, and who “Sir” is. DECODE gives the Queen and the King as receivers, but the letter is written from Paris, where the Queen was, to someone who sends news of the King’s affairs.

Charles XII’s letter from Bender to the Swedish Council of the Realm, with a second copy for his envoys in London and The Hague, in a Swedish nomenclator of about 1,100 numbers in alphabetical order (NLA Stade Rep. 5a Nr. 670). Brice Dudout rebuilt the key from a ciphered troop list and its clear draft in the same file, tested it on letters not used to build it, and deciphered both copies: 639 of 640 groups. After the Danish defeat at Helsingborg the King offers Denmark peace under the mediation of the Maritime Powers and gives the Council a free hand to agree an armistice, even for a whole year. G. von Müllern. A second copy went, with the necessary changes, to his envoys in London and The Hague. Where Niedersächsisches Landesarchiv, Abt. Stade, Rep. 5a Nr. 670 (old Fach 76 Nr. 38), fols. 83r–84r (copy for the Rådet) and 85r–v (copy for the envoys): the copies received by the Swedish government of Bremen-Verden. Images on Archivportal-D. Catalogue no. 599. The cipher A Swedish nomenclator of about 1,100 numbers in alphabetical order: letters in two series, syllables, numbers, endings, then words and names. Denmark, England and Holland are written in clear as sigla (B.B., LL, ddd). How it was deciphered Brice Dudout rebuilt the key from a ciphered troop list in the same file whose clear draft survives, froze it, and tested it on letters not used to build it (93% and 96% of words recognised, controls at most 80%). The two copies of the letter, which encipher partly different words, check each other. What it says The Danish army has been routed in Scania. Charles is ready for “en billig fred under Sjömakternas mediation” and gives the Council leave to negotiate and to agree an armistice, for as long as a whole year. Still open One group (212) in the Rådet copy; ten word values set from the table’s order and the sense; five clerk’s slips. The Council’s clear copy, probably in the Riksarkivet, has not been consulted. Credit Brice Dudout (Europe chiffrée), working with Claude Opus 5.5: transcription, key, decipherment, Swedish text and English translation; he checked the doubtful numbers blind on the image. His write-up .

Rep. 5a Nr. 670 of the Stade branch of the Lower Saxony state archives is a file of Diverse chiffrierte Schreiben von und an Generalgouverneur Baron Nils Gyllenstierna , 1700–1711: ciphered letters received and sent by the Swedish government of Bremen-Verden, then a Swedish possession on the lower Elbe. It is digitised in 135 images under the Public Domain Mark. Fols. 83–85 hold two ciphered copies of one letter of Charles XII, dated Bender d. 26 April 1710 in the Swedish calendar, signed Carolus and countersigned by H. G. von Müllern of the King’s field chancery. The copy headed Copia till hela Rådet i Stockholm (fols. 83r–84r) is for the Council of the Realm, which governed Sweden while the King was abroad. The copy headed Copia till Envoyerne Leijoncrona och Palmqvist mut. mutand. (fol. 85r–v) is the version for the envoys Christoffer Leijoncrona in London and Johan Palmquist at The Hague. Both are written the same way: the narrative in clear Swedish, the sensitive passages in number groups separated by points. Gyllenstierna’s chancery at Stade received them; no key or decipherment is filed with them. Fol. 85r, the copy for the envoys. The account of the Danish defeat is in clear down to så att ; then the numbers begin: 180 392 59 236 319 137 47 149 121 48 163 82 53 110 984 52 365 365 , wi billigt deraf kunne giöra oss de tankar, att att . Image: Niedersächsisches Landesarchiv, Abt. Stade, Rep. 5a Nr. 670 fol. 85r (image 0086), via Archivportal-D. The two copies do not encipher the same words. The envoys’ copy has 287 cipher groups and the Rådet copy 353, 640 in all. A word left in clear in one is often in cipher in the other ( sidan is 170 231 in the envoys’ copy and clear in the Rådet copy), and the Rådet copy adds a long passage the envoys did not need: the Council’s authority to negotiate and to agree an armistice. Where the copies overlap, each is a check on the other.

A one-part nomenclator in Swedish: about 1,100 numbers in alphabetical order. No table of it survives in the file, and its layout was worked out from the recovered values: numbers content examples 31–64 letters, first series: a ä å b c ch ck d e f g h i k l m n o p q r s sk sch sp st t u w x y z 31 a, 47 n, 52 r, 59 t 65–98 letters, second series: the first plus 34 65 a, 81 n, 87 s, 93 t 99–182 syllables, consonant and vowel, from ba to wu 100 be, 149 ne, 163 ra, 180 wi 183–211 numbers 183 en (1), 210 hundra, 211 tusen 212–304 endings 245 en, 267 ing, 304 tion 310–1102 words and names, from af to Wismar 552 fred, 653 Konung, 956 stille, 1033 wapen Each letter has two numbers, one in each series; each syllable, ending and word has one. A word that is not in the table is spelled out from syllables, letters and endings: Sjömakternas is 913 692 312 47 65 53 , Sjö-makt-er-n-a-s, and kunne is 137 47 149 , ku-n-ne. The three powers are not enciphered at all: they stand in clear inside the number runs as sigla, B.B. for Denmark, LL for England and ddd for Holland, the United Provinces. The recovered word values follow alphabetical order almost without exception (99.7% by the contributor’s count), and that order is what let values occurring only once be placed. The two copies use 178 different numbers for 638 occurrences, about 3.6 occurrences per number. Most numbers stand for a syllable or a whole word and occur once or twice. That matters for the statistical check in section 04.

A crib from the same file. The file also holds a ciphered troop list (fols. 73 and 82) whose clear draft survives (fol. 74). Aligning the two, Brice Dudout fixed the number groups from the totals and the officers’ names, then the first letter and syllable values, and from them the alphabetical layout of the whole table. Frozen, then tested. The key, K1710, was frozen with its SHA-256 fingerprint recorded, and applied to pages not opened before: a German letter to von Müllern (fol. 100), in which 93% of the words were recognised, and two pages of a letter to the King (fols. 78v–79r), with 96%. Control keys with permuted values or shuffled groups reached at most 77–80% on the same measure. The letter of 26 April. Both copies were then deciphered and compared word by word. Values that occur only in this letter were set from their place between neighbours in the table and from the sense: 345 andra lies between 337 allt and 357 Arme , 1049 wilkor just before 1054 Winter . Brice Dudout then checked the doubtful numbers on the image without being told the expected value, sixteen points in all. The key file in the repository holds 334 values.

The project’s statistical check ( docs/_validate.py ) scores the deciphered letters with a Swedish letter model and compares the score with two kinds of rival key. Random keys score far below the reading: −3.54 per letter on average against −2.59, 7.6 standard deviations lower. A key fitted by the annealer to the same numbers shuffled into random order, though, scores better than the reading (−2.35 on average, −2.33 at best). The verdict is underdetermined : on this text the letter model cannot tell the reading from a fitted key. That follows from the cipher. With 178 different numbers for 638 occurrences, a free key can give each number whatever syllable makes the letters look Swedish, so almost any sequence can be fitted. The model is also built on modern Swedish, and the letter is spelt as in 1710 ( wij , hwilken , giöra ). The evidence for this key is of another kind: the crib, the letters held out from building it, the alphabetical order of the table, the agreement of the two copies, and the checks on the image.

From the third line: 53 982 224 77 212 59 with the unread 212, then och imedlertid 365 60 49 52 32 59 93 31 705 b.b. 73 93 956 950 508 1033 , att uprätta med [Denmark] ett stillestånd eller wapen… ; the struck group is in the fourth line from the bottom. Image: Niedersächsisches Landesarchiv, Abt. Stade, Rep. 5a Nr. 670 fol. 83v (image 0085), via Archivportal-D. English The news. Charles has learnt that the King of Denmark’s army, shipped into Scania the previous autumn, has been beaten and scattered. He takes it as God’s punishment of the Danish King’s faithlessness and breach of his word and seal, and expects him to change his designs and seek terms. The offer. He has reason enough to press his advantage, and the States General have let themselves be drawn onto the Danish side “by others”; even so he is inclined to an equitable peace with Denmark under the mediation of the Maritime Powers, England and the United Provinces, provided he is asked and assured beforehand of satisfaction for the wrong and damage that he and his subjects have suffered from “so unjust a breach of the peace”. To the envoys. The longer the King of Denmark draws out the war, the harder he will find it to satisfy Sweden. The envoys are to declare, as of themselves and without any order, the King’s wish for peace and his trust in Queen Anne’s friendship and readiness to procure an honourable and secure peace with Denmark. To the Council. The Rådet may hear and accept equitable peace proposals under the mediation of the Maritime Powers, if the Danes ask for it willingly and without further delay. It has leave and a free hand to open a peace negotiation with Denmark under English and Dutch mediation on the conditions stated, and meanwhile to agree an armistice or suspension of arms for as long as both sides accept: the King is content with any term, even a whole year. His ministers in England and Holland are told to say the same as of themselves; the Council is to settle the rest as it thinks best.

Charles XII had been at Bender, on Ottoman soil, since the destruction of his army at Poltava in July 1709. Denmark re-entered the war that autumn and landed an army in Scania; Magnus Stenbock beat it at Helsingborg on 28 February 1710 (Swedish calendar), and it re-embarked. That is the action of the first sentence, which the letter presents as divine punishment. The sentence on the Staterherrorna , the States General, has no verb in either copy, left out by the clerk or already missing in the draft. It probably refers to the negotiations of winter 1709–10 that led to the Hague convention of neutrality of 31 March 1710 (New Style), which in effect shielded Denmark from the Swedish troops in Germany; news of its signature could hardly have reached Bender by 26 April. The mediation of the Maritime Powers brought no Danish–Swedish peace. The war went on in northern Germany, where Stenbock beat the Danes again at Gadebusch in December 1712. The same key deciphers other pieces of the file: the troop list used as the crib and a long German letter to the King of autumn 1710 (plague and famine in Sweden, the neutrality of northern Germany, Poniatowski, the Porte and the Tsar). Those are not published here.

Group 212 , in the Rådet copy only (fol. 83v, bo‹s‑tag‑are‑i‑212›t after som wid ett slikt wärk ): not deciphered. It is the first number of the endings; the clear text before it is itself poorly made out, and the envoys’ copy lacks the passage. The sense of the clause around it is not established. Values set from the table’s order and the sense (grade I): 238 det (twice; between 236 der and 239 dig , taken as the conjunction “that”, a use found in clear in the same letter), 473 Dansk (three times; between 444 Condition and 477 dem ), 345 andra , 337 allt , 1049 wilkor , 25 ak in nöjaktig (Brice Dudout confirmed the number on the image, but it lies below the known letter series), and the word values 512 emot , 548 fort , 572 gärna and 934 slut . In the key file 1049 is still listed as wis? . Clerk’s slips , checked on the image by Brice Dudout (grade M for the corrections made from sense): Konung‹169›en , a superfluous se ; förlika 108 med oss , 108 cu for 908 sig , which the other copy has; satisfa-31-tion , a for c ; Stat-ä-58 for r , which the other copy enciphers as 52; and ‹slores› , garbled for a verb whose sense is clear (“were it concluded”), followed by a struck group and ra . Both copies spell ge-na for gärna , so that slip was probably in the draft. The clear text is in a fast cursive, and its reading is a working one: the gaps marked (…) and [?] are in the clear, not in the numbers. Prior work. No edition of the letter was found: it is not in Carlson’s Konung Karl XII:s egenhändiga bref (1893, autograph letters only) or in the Handlingar rörande Skandinaviens historia , and web searches in Swedish, English and German found nothing (27 October 2026). The Historiska handlingar volumes and the Riksarkivet registers are not searchable online. The Council’s clear copy is probably in the Riksarkivet, Stockholm, and its content may be known to historians from there; it has not been consulted. The rest of Rep. 5a Nr. 670 and the other Stade files of catalogue no. 599 are not covered by this page.

The transcription and the decryption of every document on this page, so that the reading can be used and checked. Short files are shown here; all are in the repository. Charles XII, Bender, 26 April 1710: copies for the envoys (fol. 85) and for the Rådet (fols. 83-84) A refugee at Bender, on Ottoman soil, since Poltava, Charles XII learns of the rout of the Danish army at Helsingborg. In a chancery letter whose sensitive passages are in cipher, he declares himself ready to make peace with Denmark under the mediation of England and the United Provinces, and gives the Council a “free hand” to negotiate and to conclude an armistice, “even for a whole year”. Two ciphered copies, received by the Swedish government of Bremen-Verden, are kept at Stade. G. von Müllern] Translation translation.md # English translation ## Copy for the envoys (fol. 85r–v) Charles. Since we have lately learnt that the King of Denmark’s army, which last autumn was shipped over into Scania, has a short while ago, in an action, been utterly overcome, beaten and scattered, we may rightly conclude that the said King — inasmuch as the just God has thus punished his faithlessness and his wrongful dealing against his given word and seal — will change his evil designs and willingly seek to come to terms with us. Therefore, although we have reason enough to pursue the happy success of our arms against him and to bring him into such straits that he can no longer harm us, while we have our other enemies to deal with, nevertheless, as we find that the Lords States, out of hasty thoughtlessness, [have placed themselves] on the Danish side, to which they have let themselves be led by others, we are inclined to enter into an equitable peace with the King of Denmark under the mediation of the Maritime Powers, provided that we are requested to do so and assured beforehand of a sufficient satisfaction for all the wrong, damage and prejudice that we and our subjects have had to suffer from so unjust a breach of the peace. [You shall give to understand] that the longer the King of Denmark draws out the war and continues hostilities against us, the harder it will be for him to satisfy us in future and to make the amends [we can demand of him]. You shall, as of yourselves and without any order from us, declare not only our peace-loving disposition but also the trust we place in the friendship of the Queen of England and in her readiness to procure us an honourable and secure peace with Denmark. Herewith etc. Bender, 26 April 1710. Carolus. H. G. von Müllern. ## What the copy for the Rådet adds … we wish to show ourselves inclined to hear and accept equitable peace proposals under the mediation of the Maritime Powers, provided that the Danes request it willingly, without further delay, and assure us beforehand of an equitable amends for the damage and inconvenience that we and our subjects have suffered from this breach of the peace and from the hostilities committed in one way or another. We therefore hereby leave you permission and a free hand to open, under the mediation of England and Holland, a peace negotiation with Denmark on the conditions named above […], and meanwhile to conclude with Denmark an armistice or suspension of arms for as long as can be agreed on both sides; and we are content with whatever term such an armistice is concluded for, even if it be for a whole year. We are letting our ministers in England and Holland know that they should declare our peace-loving disposition there as of themselves, as may be seen more fully in the enclosure. Relying on your known dexterity and proven zeal for our service and interest, [we leave you] to settle all this as you think best. Key: key.tsv

Daniel Bourdeau · posted 23 October 2026 Method: read from existing decipherment · Extent: complete Credits · Satoshi Tomokiyo (identification) · Contemporary key or decipherment (earlier solution) deciphered copy At a glance Existing decipherment · complete The letter Francisco de Vargas, Charles V's ambassador at Venice, to the Emperor, 25 August 1552: fourteen pages, most of them in cipher, with a postscript of the same day. Where Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1320 ff. 35–38; DECODE R9967 (16 images), listed with no decryption attached; catalogue item 197. The cipher The Imperial Cipher of 1544–1554 (Tomokiyo): letter symbols and code groups such as ager cardenal and pollo papa, with some clear words left in the cipher lines. How it was deciphered At the time: a second hand wrote the decipherment in the left margins, at the page feet and between the lines, as one continuous text. It was transcribed from the DECODE images on 23 Oct 2026 and checked against the clear words in the cipher lines (ten places agree) and five recurring code groups. What it says Cardinal Sant'Angelo coming to Venice on French business; the Pope no anda limpio over Siena and his legate there may be a cover for taking the city; the Duke of Florence at risk of being deceived; the Duke of Urbino's request to Venice. Still open Eight words of the marginal hand, among them the legate's name (Mignanelli?), not made out at DECODE's resolution; the spelled cipher runs were not checked symbol by symbol, since the key is not in the repository. Credit Satoshi Tomokiyo (cryptiana) recorded the marginal decipherment and identified the cipher as the Imperial Cipher of 1544–1554. Archive image 0002: the cipher block, struck through after deciphering, and the decipherment in the left margin ( Con esto ay q la neutralidad suya en q dize quiere estar podria ser fuesse, y assi es de presumir por lo dicho ). The clear words podria ser fuese, y assi es de presumir also stand in the cipher lines. Image: Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1320 ff. 35-38, image 0002, via DECODE R9967.

DECODE imaged the four leaves as sixteen pictures whose own numbers are out of order; the archive's numbers in the image headers (0001–0016) give the order of the pages. The letter opens in clear (“En xvij del presente screvi a vuestra magestad”), runs in cipher from page 0001 to page 0011, each block struck through with a saltire once deciphered, returns to clear for the conde de Pitigliano's business, Piedmont and don Fernando de Gonzaga with three shorter cipher runs, and ends De Venecia xxv de Agosto MDLij , a postscript and the signature Fran.co de Vargas . The decipherment is in a second hand, written beside and under the cipher it renders, so that the foot of one page and the top of the next carry the text of the cipher lines that follow. It was transcribed in full, marked margin, foot, top, interlinear and clear ( R9967_decipherment.txt ), and the letter was written out from it with the clear paragraphs from the original ( R9967_reading.md , English R9967_en.md ).

The key is not in the repository, so the cipher was not decoded symbol by symbol. Two checks were made instead ( R9967_code_check.tsv ): Clear words in the cipher lines. Vargas left short phrases in clear inside his cipher, and they agree with the decipherment word for word at every place they occur, ten in all: Tengo aviso de buen lugar que (0001), dixo en secreto aun confidente suyo (de do lo he entendido) que (0002), De aqui vengo a concluir (sino me engaño) que (0006) and others. Code groups. ager is rendered cardenal three times, pollo papa five times, and the short groups s-o , x-o , n-o el , del , al ; once (0005) the decipherer wrote su Santidad for s-o pollo . Every unbracketed word of the reading is in the decipherment or in the clear text; one word, [parte] , is supplied where the margin breaks off.

Tengo aviso de buen lugar que el cardenal Santangel, hermano de Fernesio, so color de lo que aqui tiene, se viene a esta ciudad para tratar negocios del Rey de Francia ... el papa no anda limpio en estas materias. “I have word from a good source that Cardinal Sant'Angelo, Farnese's brother, under colour of what he holds here, is coming to this city to deal in the King of France's business ... the Pope is not acting cleanly in these matters.” A secretary of the Pope close to the nuncio told him so, and a member of the Pregadi had heard from the Venetian ambassador in Rome that the Pope told the French ambassador he would be glad to see the King set foot in Italy over Siena. Vargas recalls a letter of Cardinal Ridolfi to the Bishop of Fiesole at the first session of Trent, which he saw in the original. He suspects that the legate sent to Siena is a cover for taking the city, as the Popes took Bologna under the name of protection; that the Duke of Florence may be deceived a second time; and that any settlement over Siena with France or the Pope would harm the Emperor, so that both must be kept out. The Duke of Urbino's request to Venice to be named captain general or released, and his ambassador's instructions not to press for an answer, he reads as a plan concerted with the French against the kingdom of Naples.

Eight words of the marginal hand, marked [?word] or […] in the reading, and the legate's name, [?Mignanelo] : the small hand at DECODE's 1850 × 2600 pixels; only the originals at Simancas would settle them (blocker: illegible). A symbol-by-symbol check of the spelled cipher runs, which needs the key (Tomokiyo's reconstruction of the Imperial Cipher of 1544–1554 is not in the repository; blocker: no key material here).

Mag.d he scripto interlinear del Embax.or de Urbino / tan frances clear frame agrees Transcription: 9967 Decryption: R9967_reading.md Reading: R9967_reading.md Translation R9967_en.md # R9967: Francisco de Vargas to Charles V, Venice, 25 August 1552, English Translation of `R9967_reading.md` (23 Oct 2026, Claude Opus 5.5, batch b36), modern English, same holes. ## Reading On the 17th of this month I wrote to Your Majesty. In this I will say what is happening and some things that occur to me, which seem important in the present state of affairs. I have word from a good source that Cardinal Sant'Angelo, Farnese's brother, under colour of what he holds here, is coming to this city to deal in the King of France's business, and that he will leave Rome soon unless the Farnese change their mind or something happens to prevent it. Talking with me, the man who gave me this news, who is a secretary of the Pope and a close confidant of the nuncio resident here, told me what I have in some measure understood by other ways: that the Pope is not acting cleanly in these matters, so that this coming of the cardinal and other things being done may be with some intention of his. With this agrees that a gentleman of the Council of the Pregadi told a confidant of his in secret, from whom I learned it, that this Signory had word from its ambassador in Rome that the Pope, speaking with the French ambassador about this business of Siena, told him he would be glad if the King set foot in Italy in this way, and that he would be ready to help him as far as he reasonably could so that he should hold as much in it as Your Majesty. This is not very hard to believe, given his nature, his little vigour and inconstancy, and what is known of his mind in many past and present matters. With this, the neutrality in which he says he wishes to stay may be what it was, and so it is to be presumed from what has been said, like that of some of his predecessors, who we know took great pains, under colour of reconciling princes and the affairs of Italy, to set them at odds so that things should come to such a pass that they could step in and take what they could, always seeking to extend their temporal lordship in Italy, unable to bear the name of emperor or the Spaniards, and trying by many ways to throw them out of it; on which much could be said were it not so well known, for it is the old aim. On this point I remember that when I was at Trent for the first session of the Council, Cardinal Ridolfi, who died at the last election, wrote a letter to the Bishop of Fiesole, an honourable prelate who always voted with great freedom and Christian spirit, in which, as regards the Pope, perhaps with his approval, wanting to frighten him and draw him back from the good zeal and freedom that all the fathers ought to have, he rebuked him severely, saying quite unworthy things against Your Majesty, concluding in effect that what Your Majesty was doing came from not being able to bear the majesty and power of His Holiness in Italy, being very envious of it. I saw that letter in the original, because the bishop showed it to me, much distressed and weighing how the affairs of the Church stood and [?what] was going on in Rome; I gave word of it at the time to the proper person, and I believe it was written to Your Majesty. From these things I have come to suspect, and I believe I am not much mistaken, that the Pope's sending Cardinal [?Mignanelli] as legate to Siena, he being a native of it and so astute and so close to him, named in camera outside the consistory and outside the custom observed in such cases, has been with another intention than the one announced: to weave something under cover, so that, seeming to mediate and to make some agreement, he may divert Your Majesty and the King of France from Siena and take hold of it as best he can, under colour of taking up the protection the Sienese sent to beg of him, and so go on gaining ground this way, which is the very way by which the popes have seized some lands in Italy, among them Bologna, where, under title of the commendation and protection they had, saying that they left the Bolognese their liberty, they have for some time now made themselves masters and lords of it, as is known, leaving the citizens nothing but the name and some traces of the liberty they claimed. It may also be that he has been persuaded, like Pope Paul in the matter of Parma and Piacenza, to want to make his house in this business of Siena, for however far-fetched it is, flatterers are never lacking, and seeing himself so exalted one sometimes persuades oneself one can carry such things off, unless holiness and zeal for the common good hold one back; and finally the French and the Farnese may have put some such idea into his head to do their own business, for they will not lack tricks and plots, as they attend to nothing else. And since it is true, as he says, that His Holiness is raising troops in Bologna, it can be presumed to be for the said purpose. This being so, one may fear with reason, in my judgement, that the Duke of Florence will easily be deceived again in this business of Siena, to his great loss and Your Majesty's disservice, because, the Pope having the said intention and the Duke trusting him so much, as is well known, he will think he is ridding himself of the French and that his state is safe by taking some settlement His Holiness makes; and perhaps the second error will be worse than the first, though that was so great and done with such haste as was seen [?at once]; and now much more so, granted that the Duke's intention is to be believed good, which, with everything else touching the Duke, I always defend in public and [anywhere] anyone speaks to me, for the sake of Your Majesty's service and because of the French effort to separate him from Your Majesty and make him distrustful. In this, and in all the talks touching the said Duke or other powers, I am not [?careless], nor will they [?trust] me, according to [...]. From this I conclude, unless I am mistaken, that any course taken in this business of Siena with the French or with the Pope will be extremely harmful and a great disservice to Your Majesty, unless it were so evidently good that it could not be denied; but I do not see at present how that [?can be done]. So what matters is to exclude the Pope from there entirely, as well as the French, and that if he wants to and does intervene, it be to this end, without leaving a legate there; for he could certainly go on day by day doing what has been said, in which the Sienese would easily be deceived, or, even if they understood it, they would soon let themselves be led to be free of Your Majesty and of the King's tyranny, seeing that this would leave them more liberty. Of this Signory I say what I have said before: it is prudent and knows very well how to govern itself, and all the more for that it will know how to do what suits it when it sees the occasion, and times and things come to be very troubled, without seeming to depart from the friendship and regard it has for Your Majesty or to ally with the French. On this, and on the Duke of Urbino's going, I refer to what I wrote to Your Majesty some days ago, in which I am confirmed more every day; and lately there is a strong argument: not many days ago the Duke sent word to this Signory by his ambassador asking them to do him the favour of naming him their captain general on this occasion or to give him leave, saying it was against his honour to remain as he was. The Signory answered that it would consider it and give the answer later; after which the said ambassador, discussing the matter with a confidant of his who was blaming the Duke for wanting to leave this Signory so lightly, told him by way of excuse that the Duke had written to him not to press or hurry for the answer but to keep the matter in hand until he wrote again. From all this one may well infer the following: first, that the Duke's going, as they say, has been with the intention of these lords, and if not of all, of those who matter, to keep the business more secret, which must have been discussed and agreed when the Duke was here in April; next, that if it were not so, the times being what they are and things so unsettled, this Signory would not have overlooked so long an absence of the Duke, knowing he is not ill, nor ever [...] to be absent; next, that if it were not so, the Signory would not have suffered the Duke to send it the threat I have described, nor afterwards have overlooked it, nor would it have been left to the said ambassador whether the Signory answered or not. Given which, and putting together everything in this article, one may presume what I have said: that the request for the generalship or else leave, about having to [...] under cover and to temporise, presupposed giving him leave when they saw the affairs of the Kingdom [of Naples] so unsettled that they thought they could get the places and strongholds they claim in the Kingdom. Thus the Duke, who is as French as is understood, publicly disgruntled, would join the King on his own and not as a matter of this Signory to carry out the plan, without this Signory committing itself to him or seeming to act against Your Majesty, and whether the thing were concluded or not, they would take him back afterwards, not having left him out of the secret. And if the Duke asked for leave, it was, I believe, because at that moment the enterprise of the Kingdom was well under way by the French; and if the Signory has not given it him so far, and he has held back, ordering his ambassador not to press for it, it is because of their doubt about the enterprise, the season being so far advanced, and because of what is thought of the Turkish fleet, that it is heading back towards the Levant as usual, this business of Siena and the other difficulties that arise; and until one sees what the French and the outlaws are planning to do, and so from what the Duke of Urbino does, and from his staying away or coming back here, there will be a conjecture, and no small one, in my view, of what the French intend about making the enterprise of the Kingdom or leaving it; for it seems to me that this Signory will always want to remain in the regard and friendship it has with Your Majesty, as it has declared, while aiming [?at the gains] when such an occasion came, to keep what is its own, by itself and by the means it would think to have with Your Majesty and with the King, for this is the neutrality practised in Italy. Although I am sure that in all this I tell Your Majesty nothing new, who knows so well and sees so deeply into everyone's minds and doings, it has seemed right to me to set these things before Your Majesty, to do my duty and what Your Majesty has commanded me, and because it seems to me that things are coming to a head and have reached such a point that there is danger in many ways unless provision is made at once; and there can be no rashness in judging this outcome, especially with so many reasons; and so I hope Your Majesty will have ordered provision to be made and will apply the remedy in everything as is fitting. On the matter of the Count of Pitigliano, I have already written to Your Majesty and await an answer. He thought fit afterwards that I should send Your Majesty the original letters of Farnese and the others, and so I do. He sent me word at the same time of his grief that Orso, his second son, the one he kept with him and for whom he wants the succession, had been drawn away by the Farnese and had gone to serve the King of France on promises they must have made him; and that he was firmer than ever in what he had offered, to serve Your Majesty, both because of the impiety of his son Niccolò and because the King had abandoned him in exchange for him, and from understanding the mind of those who wrote to him, and because this was his wish. Whether this business of the son is only his youth or a device of the father on the advice of the ambassador of Urbino, his friend, who makes a great profession of such things, according to the Italian custom of dividing themselves so that the son goes to the King and he himself serves Your Majesty, I do not know. It is true that the father laments it greatly, saying they have deceived him and that he thinks they will kill him. He has written me another letter, which I send Your Majesty, showing how he presses for the answer and that he wants no one but himself to learn of it. And if he wishes to beware of the ambassador of Urbino, so French, he would not be much wrong, he being as French as I have written to Your Majesty; and so I believe that it was through the information he gave the French that the Farnese and the others wrote to the Count so insistently. From what happens every day in Piedmont, the continual reinforcing of the French army, what is seen at Siena and what is stirring everywhere, there is cause for fear in all those places, and that they may want to attempt something here beyond what they let be understood. They tell those they trust that within a very few days something great will be seen in Italy, greater than Siena. I never fail to inform the ministers of everything that comes to me, and what I think of this I wrote to Your Majesty days ago. I have written today in haste to Don Ferrante Gonzaga to try to lay hands on Serri, secretary of the King of France, who was commissary of munitions in the Parma affair, who is to go now from Ferrara with important despatches from M. de Termes to M. de Brissac, disguised as the servant of two Ferrarese, servants of the Duke of Ferrara's eldest son, who wants to go to France through the Milanese, through Alfonso Trotti, the said Duke's ambassador with Don Ferrante. This secretary left here yesterday for Ferrara for that purpose; I had word of it that same night, and of the [?doings], from a person who goes about with these Frenchmen and is well placed to know. And I certainly believe that if this secretary and the others with him are taken, it will be of great importance and much will be learned from them. They tell me that Cardinal de Tournon, after leaving Este for France, has gone back there to speak again with the Cardinal of Ferrara. May Our Lord guard and prosper Your Majesty's imperial person and state for long years with the increase of more kingdoms and lordships. From Venice, 25 August 1552. Today, the 25th, some gentlemen have made it public that this Signory has letters from Rome of the 22nd, by a courier who came last night, saying that the Prince of Salerno had arrived at Porto Ercole with 26 French galleys, 12 of Salah Rais and 20 ships with 2,000 Gascons and other troops, and that he was taking the troops the French had raised in Siena to go on the enterprise of the Kingdom, and that they had sent some frigates to summon the Turkish fleet. I do not affirm this beyond what I have said; the truth will soon be known. The news I had yesterday from Rome of the 20th says that the enterprise of the Kingdom was given up for this year, it being late and the fleet having gone off towards the Levant. We shall soon see what it is, and whether it is for another purpose, as is also suspected, and how the Siena business will end; where, it seems to me, according to what the Duke of Florence writes to his secretary here, 2,000 soldiers were staying in the city for the French, after the rest had gone against Orbetello and other garrisons, and the legate was working on a way for them all to leave, an Italian garrison remaining in the city for the city and with a commander of their own; which increases the suspicion mentioned above. I may be mistaken in this and in the rest. Sacred Caesarean Catholic Majesty, Your Majesty's servant who kisses your royal feet and hands, Francisco de Vargas.

Pierre de Rigaud de Vaudreuil de Cavagnial was the last governor of New France. By the middle of August 1760 the colony had one town left: Montréal, with the British closing on it from the lake, the river and below Québec. On 13 August he sent the minister two kinds of letter. The clear ones, in the same volume, report the movements of the enemy on lake Champlain. This one is in number groups, because, he says, it holds “des particuliarités dont il seroit dangereux que les ennemis fussent instruits dans ce moment critique”. The catalogue describers had left it as a title only: “Lettre chiffrée … au ministre”. The ciphertext runs from f.147r to f.152r and ends with the clear formula “Je suis avec un très profond respect, Monsieur, votre très humble et très obéissant serviteur, Vaudreuil”. The scans are microfilm images 1125 pixels wide, and the last group of every line on a left-hand page is cut off by the binding. f.150v, lines 9–13. A line of small groups is written between lines 9 and 10 and belongs where the caret stands after “de” in the line below: “ces derniers se lassent de <notre extrême indigence, il ne fau>t rien moins que mes soins”. Image: Archives nationales d’outre-mer, COL C11A 105 f.150v, via New France Archives (Library and Archives Canada, e000875757).

Two thousand four hundred and twenty-four groups, of 395 distinct numbers, with 35 words in clear (names, titles, “Monseigneur”, the date and the closing formula). The numbers run from 1 to 700, so the table is a nomenclator: whole words ( pour , les , poudre ), names of places and ships, syllables and single letters for what is not in the table. The commonest items have several numbers ( de 309 and 642, t 51, i 661, s 235). Spelling is phonetic: “vi-t-ma-it-res” for maîtres . The key was in the volume that the catalogue entry pointed to. COL C11E 10 ff.285–290v, “Chiffre ou code de Montcalm et de Vaudreuil” (New France Archives 15213, ten images), holds three tables, each as an alphabetical sheet and a numerical sheet: two for Vaudreuil and the Marine in 1757, one for Montcalm in 1758. The numerical sheet that reads this letter is the second of Vaudreuil’s, e001295274, labelled Déchiffrant . The first, e001295272, gives nonsense. All 700 entries of e001295274 were transcribed from enlarged crops of the cells. The same table reads Vaudreuil’s three cipher letters of April 1759 in COL C11A 104 (catalogue items 1388–1390: whole letters of 3,637, 1,225 and 354 groups), which were transcribed and decoded here as French with it, so it was his working table from 1757 to August 1760. Those letters are not part of this write-up; they are decoded, and no one has yet built their text into sentences. A fourth cipher letter of that volume, by Trémais (6 November 1759), does not use the table and is a different code.

The whole French reading is under Full texts below, with an English translation. In outline: The ships at Restigouche. Three French ships with effects and troops are bound for Restigouche under M. Danjac (François-Gabriel d’Angeac), and the British have overwhelming force at that post. Vaudreuil hopes Danjac will send the frigate Machault , under the Sieur de La Giraudais, past the blockade by night with his despatches; the schooner l’Extravagante , wintering in the baie des Chaleurs, carries the duplicates. M. de Villemont, who had leave to carry the first news, has been sent back by Danjac to report. The war on the river. “Nous sommes sans marine ni même rien d’approchant.” The British fleet has passed lake Saint-François; twenty-two British ships have passed Jacques-Cartier, and it is announced that ships laden with the rest of the troops of Louisbourg are already at Cap Rouge. In the north the British pay the Canadians for what they take, make speeches, and warn that the houses of absent men will be burned. Vaudreuil has no food to gather the militia, and the French vessels on lakes Champlain and Ontario cannot match the enemy’s. No powder, no food, no money. The allies tire of the colony’s want. The English will have some forty thousand men against battalions none of which is half what it should be; the colony has only “dix[…] milliers” of powder (between ten and nineteen thousand pounds; the end of the figure is lost in the binding), which would be used up fast. Murray’s circular to the militia captains, a copy of which is enclosed, was written to discredit the bills of exchange and the paper money that Bigot and Vaudreuil had tried to protect; the munitionnaire and Vaudreuil himself offer bills on their own pay to reassure the habitants, and the Intendant and Lévis follow his example. The request. “Je vous … Monseigneur, de vouloir favorablement assurer Sa Majesté que si nous succombons ce ne sera qu’à la dernière extrémité.” With the stores waiting at Restigouche he could take the troops to a retreat and hold it as long as possible; without them he cannot. The clear letters beside this one in COL C11A 105 confirm the cast: the Machault , the Bienfaisant and the Marquis de Malauze with the troops, d’Angeac, La Giraudais, Villemont, the Extravagante , Bigot, Amherst.

The letter was transcribed from enlarged crops, one token per group, with a mark for digits lost in the binding, then decoded with tools/decode.py from the 700-cell table plus a file of context corrections. The first decode read as French at once. Where a sentence would not form, the group was looked at again on the image. The table was then corrected from the letter, 33 cells in all, each with its reason in key/overrides.json : long s read as f, l as t, c as e and b as h were the usual errors in reading the table, and two cells were settled on the alphabetical sheet e001295269 (rotated and enlarged: moyen 473, ton 152, bateau 671; cell 2 is campagne , not compagnie , which is 102). Three passages gave way to the sense, not to the table. A small line written between two lines of f.150v has a caret and is to be read inside the line below; read in place it made nonsense, and a second 51 that the transcription carried there is not on the image. “qui~ | z e diver s” is quinze diverses with the last group of the line lost, and “je~ | i s bou r g on” is [Lou]isbourg, on . Twenty-five groups cut by the binding were restored from their visible leading digits and the sense; they are counted separately (97.1% with them, 96.0% without). No control was run, because the key was found and not recovered from the ciphertext. The check is that a 700-entry table made for another year reads six folios of French, with the right ships, officers and enemy commanders in the right places, and reads two other letters of 1759 as well.

Of 2,424 groups, 2,328 (96.0%) read from the image as written, 25 (1.0%) were restored from visible digits and the sense, 24 (1.0%) are legible and unread, and 47 (1.9%) are lost in the binding. The reading was built from the table and the context by a model, and no person has checked a passage against the images. Cells read doubtfully from the table and settled by the letter are grade M. Forty-seven groups cut by the binding at the right edge of ff.147v–151v (20 partly visible and not restored, 27 wholly lost). The microfilm cannot show them; a clear copy would. f.147v line 4, “et i” after “tiennent ce poste”, and f.147v line 9, “mais son se le pour-ra-t” (eight groups): the cells are transcribed, the words are not identified. f.147v lines 24–25, “au pre[…] i si un instant favorable”, after the order for the Machault (three groups). f.148r lines 13–14, “fin i ra bateau campagne” after “rempli de zèle” (five groups): the cells are confirmed, the phrase is not. f.148v line 17, “de b l[…]” after “quinze diverses charges du” (two groups); f.149v lines 17–18, “ceux un | ton” (two); f.150v line 24, “de moyen” (two); f.151v line 6, “nt s” (two); f.151v lines 19–20, “je vous ent[…] e” before “Monseigneur” (two). Cell 656 of the table is illegible and doubtful readings remain for 323 and a few others; they are marked ? in key/key274.json . Monseigneur, J’ay receu les deux lettres que vous m’avés fait l’honneur de m’escrire des 14e et 15e de ce mois. Comme je n’ay eu aucun rapport particulier à faire au Roy d’Angleterre , je n’ay pu m’insinuer bien particulierement dans son esprit . Cependant je luy fais une cour très assidüe . Il m’addresse assez souvent la parole et escoute volontiers ce que je luy dis. M. de Louvigny n’allant point à Boulogne, je l’ay prié, et il m’a promis de m’addresser le plus qu’il pourra des nouvelles ou autres choses, qu’il faille rapporter au Roy d’Angleterre , affin d’avoir par là occasion d’insinuation f247v auprès de luy . Et je vous supplie très humblement, Monseigneur, de vouloir bien par les mesmes moyens y contribuer de vostre costé. Le Duc de Berwick n’a esté icy que peu de jours depuis que j’y suis, en estant parti pour Paris il y a plus de huit jours . À l’égard des Anglois qui sont auprès du Roy d’Angleterre , je suis parfaitement avec eux. Et j’espere m’y mettre mieux encore à Boulogne , parce que je tascheray d’estre logé assez commodement pour pour leur donner souvent à manger , ce que je n’ay pu faire icy par le deffaut de logement . Et vous savés que le vin [et] un peu d’adresse de discours sont de puissan [t] s scrutateurs des cœurs. Les ennemis sont tousjours mouillés au mesme endroit et en mesme nombre, c’est à dire vingt-trois ou vingt-quatre vaisseaux. Les corsaires de Dunkerque ont pris des bastiments chargés de troupes pour Angleterre. Il en entra un hyer dans lequel estoient trois compagnies angloises avec les lieutenants et enseignes. Les capitaines n’y estoient pas. Et l’on en voyoit trois autres prests à entrer. Vous saurés cette nouvelle plus precisement par Mr L’Empereur. f248r Je suis avec un profond respect, Monseigneur, Vostre très humble et très obeïssant serviteur, Vergier. f249r M. Vergier à Boulogne ce 26e mars 1696 Monseigneur, Depuis la derniere lettre que j’ay eu l’honneur de vous écrire, j’ay esté deux jours à Dunkerque, ainsy que ce m’estoit donné l’honneur de vous le marquer. Et Mr de Louvigny m’a obligé d’en retourner à Calais pour y expedier et payer la conduite de Calais à Dunkerque à l’equipage du Lutin, et enfin j’arrivay icy hier au soir. f249v J’ay veu ce matin Milord Myddleton et j’ay eu une longue conversation avec luy . Il m’a paru beaucoup plus empressé que de coutume pour l’entreprise Il m’a dit seulement qu’il croyoit, et je trouve que c’est avec assez de raison, que l’affaire est à present presque impraticable sur la coste de Kent , à cause des forces que le Prince d’Orange a mises de ce costé-là. Et qu’il seroit à present necessaire de tenter le debarquement dans la province d’York, où sont presque tous les haras d’Angleterre , et où par consequent on trouveroit les chevaux necessaires pour l’armée, ou bien dans une des provinces de l’Ouest , parce que le pays y est abondant en sorte que l’armée y subsisteroit aisement . Ou mesme de faire la descente dans ces deux lieux-là à la f250r fois. Et pour cela de faire embarquer à Brest les troupes destinées pour l’Ouest, et à Calais celles destinées pour York . Voilà, Monseigneur, son projet . Il peut y avoir quelque chose de bon, mais je ne sçay si l’execution n’en seroit pas plus difficile que du premier. D’ailleurs il compte sur la fidelité de plusieurs per [so] nnes dans ce pays-là , et je veux bien le croire, mais je juge par tout ce que j’entends dire et à luy et aux autres qu’ils n’y ont guere d’intelligence ny mesme de correspondance, car ils n’en reçoivent aucune nouvelle, ny par la Hollande ny d’ailleurs . Et tout ce qu’ils en apprennent leur vient du chevalier Girardin , qui est un Irlandais estably à Dunkerque . Je suis avec un profond respect, Monseigneur, vostre tres humble et tres obeissant serviteur, Vergier f251r Mr Vergier à Boulogne le 29e mars 1696. Monseigneur, Nous avions appris par des lettres particulieres de Toulon que l’armée en estoit partie le 13e de ce mois. Cependant le Duc de Berwick a mandé au Roy d’Angleterre qu’elle y estoit encore le 18e de mars. Cela le tient fort en peine, et il m’a fait prier ce matin par Milord Myddleton de tascher de sçavoir ce qui en est. Comme je ne veux sça [vo] ir ny debiter de toutes ch [o] ses que ce que vous jugerés à propos que j’en f251v sçache et que j’en debite , je vous suplie très humblement, Monseigneur, de vouloir bien en cette occasion estre mon nouvelliste . Aussy bien que sur les choses que j’eus hyer l’honneur de vous mander. Je suis avec un profond respect, Monseigneur, Vostre très humble et très obeïssant serviteur, Vergier. f256r À Calais ce 10e mars 1696. Monseigneur, J’ay receu les deux lettres que vous m’avés fait l’honneur de m’escrire des 6e et 8e de ce mois. Les ennemis qui avant hyer avoient paru sous Douvre au nombre de quinze vaisseaux, parurent hyer en cette rade au nombre de soixante voiles, vingt deux desquelles sont vaisseaux depuis cent iusques à cinquante canons ; quinze fregattes de dix huit à trente canons ; dix ou douze galiottes à bombes, les reste caiches ou autres petits batiments de charge. Ils passerent à une portée et demye de canon des forts des jettées sur une colonne, les anglois estant à la teste avec pavillons d’admiral, de viceadmiral, et de contreadmiral, et les hollandois à la queue f256v avec un pareil nombre de pavillons. En passant devant les testes des jettées, trois vaisseaux anglois s’en approcherent à la portée du canon sur les deux heures et demye et donnerent leur bordée en faisant leur route. Toute cette flotte portant tousiours le cap à l’est alla mouiller sur les cinq heures entre la fosse de Mardic et ce port à environ une lieüe d’icy, et y est encore. À la veüe des galiottes nous crumes qu’ils vouloient bombarder cette ville et y brusler les bastimens qui sont dans le port. Mais il faut ou qu’ils n’ayent pas les choses necessaires pour cette execution, ou qu’ils ayent un autre dessein, puisqu’ils ont perdu hyer et aujourd’huy le temps le plus favorable qu’ils puissent desirer. Le Roy d’Angleterre et le duc de Berwick , pendant que tout cela se passa, furent constamment sur le rempart occupez à distinguer avec des lunettes le nom des vaisseaux anglois , et à tascher de deviner le nom de leurs commandans. Les ordres qu’on a donnez icy pour les entreprises des ennemis consistent en trois cables qu’on a entraversés à la teste des jettées pour empescher les brulots et autres bastiments d’entrer dans le port. On a fait mettre le plus qu’on a pu les bastiments qui estoient dans le port entassez, affin qu’ils soient obliques f257r les uns des autres, et que le feu prenant à l’un par une bombe on puisse plus aisement en garantir les voisins. On a retiré de ces bastiments la paille et autres choses combustibles, et on a mis sur chacun des bailles et autres futailles pleines d’eau. On a armé six chaloupes commandées par des officiers de marine dans lesquelles on a mis des grenadiers de terre, douze dans chacune. Et enfin on a mis les batteries des forts en estat d’incommoder les ennemis avec les bombes et avec le canon s’ils tentoient de s’approcher de trop près. Comme on vit que les ennemis avoient dépassé cette rade portant tousiours à l’Est, on appréhenda qu’ils n’en voulussent à l’escadre de Mr de Gabaret. C’est pourquoy Mr de Bouflers despescha hyer un courrier à Dunkerque pour le faire avertir qu’il se tinst sur ses gardes et qu’il rentrast dans les jettées s’il le pouvoit ou s’il le trouvoit à propos. On observe sans cesse la contenance des ennemis, et s’ils font mine d’aller à Dunkerque, Mr le mareschal de Bouflers se prepare à s’y rendre. Mr de Bouflers et Mr d’Harcour paroissent fort d’intelligence . Le premier tousiours plein de circonspection pour le Roy d’Angleterre. Mais et les uns et les autres passent les trois quarts du temps en pourparlers f257v inutiles , et fatiguent fort Mr de Louvigny qui ne songe qu’à aller au fait . Je suis avec un profond respect, Monseigneur, Vostre très humble et très obeïssant serviteur, Vergier. f260r À Boulogne ce 30e mars 1696. Monseigneur, Mr le marquis de Harcourt est party ce matin pour Versailles après avoir eu depuis six iusques à sept heures une conference avec le Roy sur une lettre de Mr de Barbezieux qu’il receut hyer. Vous savés le veritable sujet de son voyage. Tout le monde françois et anglois conjecture icy que c’est pour concerter quelque nouveau projet pour l’entreprise d’Angleterre. Le Roy d’Angleterre m’a dit aujourd’huy que la Reine luy mande avoir appris de vous, Monseigneur, que l’armée navale avoit relaché à Toulon le 18e de ce mois, et en estoit f260v repartie le 22e. J’ay eu plusieurs conversations particulieres avec Milord Myddleton, dans lesquelles j’ay tasché de descouvrir ses sentimens. Je le croy bien intentionné , et je ne doute plus que Mr de Louvigny ne se soit trompé dans le soupçon qu’il en avoit conceu . Je ne laisseray pas de le sonder en toute occasion et d’observer ses discours et ses demarches . Je suis avec un profond respect. Monseigneur, Vostre très humble et très obeïssant serviteur, Vergier. f261r À Boulogne ce 6e mars 1696. Monseigneur, Je receus hyer les lettres que vous m’avés fait l’honneur de m’escrire des 28 mars et 2 avril. Celle du 28 mars m’a esté rendüe tard parce qu’elle estoit adressée à Calais et qu’on y a esté peu exact à me la renvoyer. Je n’aurois pas osé vous faire faire le premier, Monseigneur, la reflexion que vous faites dans vostre lettre du 24 mars et que vous confirmez par celle du 2e avril, de peur que vous ne soupçonnassiez f261v cet advis d’ennuy et d’inquietude de ma part plustost que de prudence et de bon conseil. Cependant cela me frappoit depuis long temps et surtout depuis qu’on sçait icy qu’on arme à Dunkerque, où je pourrois estre utile pendant que l’on me voit très inutile icy. C’est pourquoy je n’ay pas cru devoir essayer d’y rester davantage. J’ay seulement donné à mon depart un tour qui n’a pas deplu au Roy d’Angleterre et que je croy que vous ne desapprouverés pas. Je luy ay fait entendre que me voyant icy inutile pour son service , j’avois demandé il y a quelque temps à Mr vostre pere la permission de m’en retourner à Dunkerque pour y ayder à avancer l’armement , et qu’il m’a répondu que si je me voyois inutile à Boulogne je pouvois m’en retourner à Dunkerque, pourveu que le Roy d’Angleterre approuvast mon depart ; que mesme il m’avoit fait l’honneur de me mettre sous ses ordres , je ne devois faire aucun mouvement sans son ordre exprès . Il m’a paru fort touché de f262r cette honnesteté de Mr de Pontchartrain et de mon empressement pour son service, car il est très persuadé que l’armement de Dunkerque regarde sa descente et doit se joindre à Mr de Chasteaurenaut, et il m’a dit qu’il croyoit qu’effectivement je serois plus utile à Dunkerque. D’ailleurs, Monseigneur, je suis parfaitement avec Milord Myddleton et avec tout ce qu’il y a icy d’anglois un peu considerable, estant avec eux en coterie journaliere de debauche et de plaisir . Je n’ay rien remarqué en Milord Myddleton qui ne me confirme ce que j’ay eu l’honneur de vous en marquer en dernier lieu. Je suis avec un profond respect, Monseigneur, Vostre très humble et très obeïssant serviteur, Vergier. Daniel Bourdeau · posted 23 October 2026 Method: read after matching with key from external sources · Extent: complete Credits · Contemporary key or decipherment (key or decipherment used) key matched At a glance External key matched · complete The letter László Vetési Kökényesdi, Rákóczi's agent abroad, signing as “Cassimirus Miloftzki”, to Ferenc Rákóczi II, dated 9 January 1706: clear Hungarian with numerical cipher runs. Where Ráday Archives, C64-4d2-10, ff. 92–95; DECODE R473 (three images), catalogued 1 Jan 1705–1706 with Pál Ráday as receiver. The cipher A one-part Hungarian syllabic nomenclator: letters and syllables in two- and three-figure groups, names and words in larger ones (276 Franciaország, 1190 Kegyelmes Uram), 9 and 8 as nulls. How it was deciphered A hand of the time glossed nearly every group. On 23 Oct 2026 the gloss was transcribed afresh and Rákóczi's key DECODE R446 was found by testing the neighbouring key records against 18 glossed groups (16 agree); applied to all 380 groups it agrees with the gloss at 253 of 304 where both give a value. What it says The post from France: Nice castle surrendered to the French king, Valencia in revolt, the coming war in Italy and Spain, Holland tiring of the war, and Vetési's anxious report on an order of Rákóczi's he never received. Still open About a dozen clear words in a faded part of ff. 93–94, read with doubt; the printed note in Ráday Pál iratai I (1955) not compared (not online). With the doubtful words as holes, the reading builds coherent sentences but reads at 90.6% of its words (measured 24 October 2026), under the 95% a complete reading needs.

The letter opens “Méltóságos Fejedelem” (Most Illustrious Prince), part of it in cipher, calls the addressee Nagyságod (Your Highness) and Kegyelmes Uram , names “Rádai uram” in the third person and is signed Cassimirus Miloftzki , a cover name of László Vetési Kökényesdi. The addressee is therefore Rákóczi; DECODE's receiver, Pál Ráday, is the secretary in whose papers it survives. The closing reads Költ azon, Kilenczedik Januarii , the place in unglossed cipher, and the archive's endorsement at the head of f. 92 gives 1706 I. 9 ; DECODE's “1 Jan 1705–1706” is a placeholder. A pencil note on f. 92 cites Ráday Pál iratai I (1703–1706), ed. Benda Kálmán and others (Budapest 1955), item 102, footnote 1, p. 494. The volume is not online, so whether it prints the letter has not been checked. The images of the Ráday Archives are not in the public domain and are not reproduced here.

A hand of the time wrote the plaintext over almost every cipher group: Francziaország , Olaszországban , Spaniolországban , Holandia és Anglia , Ráday uram . DECODE's transcription renders this gloss as garbled syllables (“Fejedehd”, “ttolendia”), and an attempt in September 2026 to rebuild the key from it by alignment gave a noisy table. The key turned out to be in the same archive. The DOC files of the DECODE key records R380–R520 were scanned against 18 glossed groups of R473; only R446 (Ráday Archives C64-4d2-25 no. 6, Rákóczi's Hungarian key, original) fits, with 16 of 18, and no other record scores above 1. DECODE's transcription of R446 was then corrected on its image: 69 is al , 71–74 an, ar, as, at , the ö/ü groups are distinct, 35 is ly and 296 Belgium ; the last column, headed x , holds the nulls 9 and 8. Applied to the 380 groups of the letter, the key and the gloss both give a value at 304, and agree at 253. The rest are spelling variants, misalignments of the gloss over long runs and a few writer's slips. Where the gloss is garbled the key gives the word: Niszevárat ... az Franciaországi király kezében adta , az király táborba , Belgiummal , hogy Herbaville ujjobban gyözidelmeskedet .

Tegnap előtt Franciaországbul érkezett posta ad okot Nagyságodnak alázatoson udvarlanom. [...] Kegyelmes Uram, Niszevárat az Franciaországi király kezében adta, mellyért örömet itten tegnap estve az öreg templomban solenniter [?celebraltak]. “The post that arrived from France the day before yesterday gives me occasion to pay my humble respects to Your Highness. [...] Most Gracious Lord, [it] gave the castle of Nice into the hands of the King of France, for which they [?celebrated] the rejoicing solemnly here yesterday evening in the old church.” Nice castle surrendered to the French on 4 January 1706. Vetési goes on to Spain, where the court is discontented, Valencia has rebelled and Aragon wavers, and the Queen will not take up the administration; the King of France must send money there. Next year's war, he expects, will be in Italy and Spain, with the Empire on the defensive; taking Antwerp would not suit Holland's trade with Belgium, and people say Holland, tired of the useless expense, will leave the House of Austria. He has heard that Herbeville has won a victory, and he reports anxiously that he never received an order of Rákóczi's of 30 November, of which Ráday's December letter says nothing.

About a dozen clear words in the faded part of ff. 93–94, read with doubt and marked [?word] in the reading ( [?esmiten] , [?viretelu] , [?mandilat] ...): blocker, illegible on the scans. The place in the date line, in cipher and unglossed. Ráday Pál iratai I (1955), item 102 n. 1: not compared (not online; blocker, needs physical access).

Modern spelling of names here only (Nice, Valencia, Aragon, Brussels, Herbeville, Sopron). ## Translation Most Illustrious Prince, my great good and Most Gracious Lord! The post that arrived from France the day before yesterday gives me occasion to pay my humble respects to Your Highness. […] Most Gracious Lord, [it] gave the castle of Nice into the hands of the King of France, for which they [?celebrated] the rejoicing solemnly here yesterday evening in the old church. In Italy affairs are [?going] well; but in Spain, things not being [?…], it is [?accordingly] plain to the court, Most Gracious Lord, that the courtiers at that court have become malcontent, although the king's going to the camp also [?…] and costs a great deal. Nevertheless the great men here have doubts about it; Valencia too has rebelled, Aragon too is coming close to wavering. For which reason the Queen has by no means taken up the administration, but [?wants] to go to the camp; and there is no money, Most Gracious Lord, nor is any [?ready]. [?Many] are the men. Above all the King of France must send money to Spain. It seems, Most Gracious Lord, that next year the war will be wholly in Italy and Spain; here and in the Empire they will [?be] on the defensive, although Holland and England are preparing hard, and against Antwerp [?in Flanders]. But it does not seem to be to Holland's advantage if the English should manage to take the said place, since thus Holland's trade with Belgium would be wholly [?…]. Had Holland as well as England wanted it last year too, Brussels could easily have been taken, and us [?pressed] across towards Namur. The people here flatter themselves that Holland, tired of the useless expense, will one day leave it there and step away from the side of the House of Austria [?…] concerning Hungary, Most Gracious Lord! That […] Your Highness gave up [?Sopron], whereas [they say] that Herbeville has lately won the victory. Before […] be given, I humbly wish [?…]. Writing [?…] Your Highness's gracious order dated [?30] November, as I wrote in my earlier humble letter too, Most Gracious Lord, I reported that Your Highness had given no order at all [?about] it concerning the past [?month]. Indeed Mr Ráday does not mention it to me in his letter written in December either, from which I concluded the news was untrue, [?since] […] had happened. The […] I enclosed to Your Highness [through] Ráday, my two letters with their copies, that he should humbly represent [them] to Your Highness; in which matter, asking and living wholly in Your Highness's [?grace], falling at Your Highness's feet with great humble devotion, I commit my humble small person to Your wise decision and disposal. Let Your Highness's wise decision in this matter rest in Your Highness's hands. Though by my small understanding I have no merit for that [?letter], yet knowing that my life too stands in Your Highness's gracious command and humility, I humbly rest in Your Highness's gracious decision and command, remaining so until my death. Given at the same [place], on the ninth of January. Most Illustrious Prince, my great [?good] Most Gracious Lord, Your Highness's humble servant and faithful, Cassimirus Miloftzki. Between a clear opening and close are 173 groups of a code with values to 560, a different code from Torcy’s letter in the same volume. Tomokiyo’s table of the 1710 Desmarets code and the marquis de Rose’s code (R8768) were tried. Neither fits.
